📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

It has been revealed that AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes. The new limit applies to synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and without an opt-in. The 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018, after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015.

Raising the limit is a configuration change per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds with a validation error:.

The change covers one of the three shapes Lambda took this year. Web Functions keep 15 minutes, and Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, while on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations now get 30 minutes and asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September. AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations, and report generation as the workloads that outgrew 15 minutes.

According to Tarun Rai Madan, Dan Slusariuc, and Snehil Ameta, the authors of the announcement, the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity:.

Industry observers note that concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. At the same request rate, a function that runs for 30 minutes instead of 15 needs twice the concurrency. For example, 1 request per second at 30 minutes each needs 1,800 concurrent executions.

According to recent reports, the rest of the post is about what sits around the function. An SQS queue's visibility timeout has to be at least six times the function timeout, which means three hours. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams read one batch per shard at a time, so a slow function slows the shard. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes. A NAT gateway still drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and the Init phase keeps its 10-second limit.

Wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner, tested the SQS rule in eu-west-1 by raising a function to 1,800 seconds behind a queue with a 90-minute visibility timeout and then lowering the queue to 60 seconds. Both changes were accepted with the mapping still enabled, while a newly introduced mapping from the same queue was refused:.

So the check exists, but only at creation. One more thing the test demonstrated: at creation, Lambda compared the queue with the function timeout itself, not with six times it. I did not test where exactly that line sits, so treat the six times as guidance you enforce yourself.

He adds that an asynchronous function which times out three times has run for 90 minutes before the event reaches a dead-letter queue, and concludes that 30 minutes is the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.

Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS and AWS Serverless Hero, writes:.

Recent findings suggest that hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.

Industry observers note that the comments under the post took two directions. Magnus Eriksson, architect and former AWS employee, notes that Lambda "is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2" and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads. Matthew Bonig, AWS DevTools Hero and co-author of The CDK Book, looked further ahead: "Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs.".

On Reddit, the most-upvoted reply welcomed the change because it avoids Fargate and ECS for hour-long batch jobs. The answer under it was that Fargate is beautifully simple. One commenter sets out where the longer limit fits:.

Recent findings suggest that A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory, so check the cost per invocation before moving batch style work here, and keep the handler idempotent with a dead letter queue, because a failure or timeout partway through a long run can leave partial work behind. For multi step work, long running jobs, or anything that needs clear state and retries, Step Functions with Fargate or ECS is still usually cleaner.

Joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance, reads the move as Lambda team recognizing that Cloud Run is its most compelling competitor. Cloud Run services allow 60 minutes per request, and Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption and Premium aims enforce no maximum, with a 60-minute grace period during scale-in. AWS has not said whether the Lambda limit will move again.

  • The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some systems offline following unauthorized access, disrupting regulatory filings for financial institutions.
  • Industry observers note that an alert has gone up on FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website, as shown in this archived copy, informing those who need to submit reports that they might not be able to while the agency deals with the situation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FinCEN takes systems offline and extends filing deadlines while investigating 'unauthorized access'.

The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some systems offline following unauthorized access, disrupting regulatory filings for financial institutions.

Industry observers note that an alert has gone up on FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website, as shown in this archived copy, informing those who need to submit reports that they might not be able to while the agency deals with the situation. FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies and foreign government partners.

In other words, it has some juicy info in its databases.

“FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems,” the alert states. “As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.”.

FinCEN hasn't said which systems intruders accessed, but clues in the deadline extension notice the agency posted alongside the warning suggest the disruption affects its reporting services for banks and other financial institutions required to submit reports detailing certain financial transactions and suspicious activity that may indicate money laundering or other illicit activity.

Sources indicate that finCEN's Secure Data Transfer Mode, one method of submitting those reports, appears to be affected, as do services companies use to submit beneficial ownership information reports and individuals use to update their FinCEN identifiers. Eligible organizations and individuals with filings or updates due from November 18 through December 29 now have until December 30 to submit them.

The Register has learned that there’s no evidence of any unauthorized access to Bank Secrecy Act data or beneficial ownership databases. That stated, the investigation is ongoing - so that could change.

“Treasury is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact of the incident,” a FinCEN official told us in an email.

Several US government agencies have experienced cybersecurity incidents in recent months, including the ATF and the FBI, and reports emerged this week that intruders had also compromised an unclassified CIA system. While US authorities have linked previous cyberespionage campaigns to Chinese or other government-backed groups, financially motivated criminal groups have also targeted federal agencies.

As the FinCEN breach is still under investigation, the agency hasn’t stated who may be involved and for what purpose. ®.

How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • Sources indicate that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

Sources indicate that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

According to recent reports, this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this upcoming phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

In a recent development, performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

Industry observers note that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Industry observers note that the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reinforcement Learning environments give fresh capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • Industry observers note that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that reveals up in the latest RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reinforcement Learning environments give fresh capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

Industry observers note that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that reveals up in the latest RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Recent findings suggest that every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a newly introduced paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

Industry observers note that we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

In a recent development, the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

Recent findings suggest that A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

In a recent development, harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

Industry observers note that the viewer highlights the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

Recent findings suggest that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

Industry observers note that A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

In a recent development, the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

According to recent reports, the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your owners publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

PC shipments set to fall further thanks to the memory shortage, but high-margin models for AI at the edge keep profits up.

HP Inc expects the PC market to shrink by "high single to low double digits" in calendar 2027, squeezed by the memory chip crisis, but execs reckon the corporation can still gain share by focusing on premium categories and AI PCs.

Interim CEO Bruce Broussard mentioned HP would do this "by capitalizing on the growing shift of AI workloads to the edge and leveraging our industry-leading portfolio designed to meet the needs of people with more demanding workloads.".

Recent findings suggest that the pitch echoes the previous quarter's earnings call. "Our focus is on helping customers implement and manage AI across their environments. We believe that the future of AI is hybrid with workloads running both in the cloud and closer to where people work and data is created," he added.

Broussard cited IDC estimates that half of enterprise AI inference workloads will run on endpoints or edge nodes by 2030, and claimed that with half a billion devices shipped, HP has "deep expertise in how devices perform, how they're secured and how they're managed at scale.".

Sources indicate that HP fourth quarter revenue - for the three months ended October 31 - was $16 billion, up 9.3 percent year-on-year. Full-year fiscal 2026 revenue was up 9.5 percent to $60 billion. Personal Systems drove the growth, as its printer business slipped slightly.

Personal Systems revenue grew 14 percent on commercial and advanced compute sales, and AI PCs represented nearly 60 percent of HP’s shipments in the quarter.

"That stated, higher component costs and challenging pricing environment, particularly in consumer, pressured profitability," said Broussard.

According to recent reports, like its rivals, HP is leaning on higher-margin premium models and signing long-term deals with the memory chip makers to secure supplies. Nikkei Asia named HP among the firms buying a limited amount of memory from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT).

In a recent development, asked whether it planned to procure more Chinese chippery, HP’s CFO Karen Parkhill sidestepped the question: "We don't expect any material changes in our suppliers right now. We're confident in the suppliers that we have, and we are confident in the supply that we have what we need to fulfil the demand this year.".

She conceded that "We are using suppliers from all over the world.".

Recent findings suggest that parkhill mentioned HP expects memory and storage costs to continue rising, but at a slower rate than during this last fiscal year. "We also expect CPU costs to increase, but not as much as what we've seen with memory and storage. And all of that is baked into our outlook.".

Broussard expects Q4 to prove the low point for Personal Systems margins, with improvement coming from further optimization of its product design and component configurations.

In a recent development, in Ferbruary, HP stated memory and storage costs had grown from 15 to 18 percent of the PC bill of materials at the start of the year to a figure closer to 40 percent. Parkhill declined to patch the figure, saying the moderating cost curves and fast-changing production mix make the BOM percentage "less useful.".

HP’s newly hired CEO, former GSK boss Emma Walmsley, will start work at the organization on January 4, leading it through what continues to be uncertain times for the PC industry. ®.

The beauty of CSS mixins

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Patrickbrosset

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I've been playing with CSS mixins recently, and I'm super excited about what this upcoming CSS construct will bring to the way we write CSS.
  • In its simplest form, a mixin is a named piece of CSS code that you define once and can reuse elsewhere in a style sheet.
  • So, instead of just returning the value red, a mixin can return background: red; color: white; border-radius: 2px; all at once.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I've been playing with CSS mixins recently, and I'm super excited about what this upcoming CSS construct will bring to the way we write CSS. I think the CSS we'll write when CSS mixins are available will look very different from the CSS we write today.

In its simplest form, a mixin is a named piece of CSS code that you define once and can reuse elsewhere in a style sheet. In that sense, it's very similar to a custom property (also known as a CSS variable) or a CSS function.

The massive difference is what mixins can hold:.

So, instead of just returning the value red, a mixin can return background: red; color: white; border-radius: 2px; all at once.

My team at Microsoft is implementing mixins in the Chromium open source project. They've covered a lot of ground, and we're getting ready to ship this in Chromium-based browsers. Native CSS mixins are getting very close!

I can't wait for other browsers to catch up, so that we can all use mixins in earnest.

CSS mixins are experimental. To try the code snippets and demo in this article, use a recent Chromium browser, open about://flags, and enable the Experimental Web Platform features flag.

Sources indicate that you define a mixin with the @mixin rule, and you use it with @apply. Mixin names start with two dashes, like custom properties.

Let's define the --visually-hidden mixin:.

And now, let's use it somewhere else in our code:.

That's all you need to do. The browser will apply the mixin's declarations to the element as if they were written directly in the element's style block, so it's exactly as if you had written:.

Except now, you have a nice little reusable mixin that you can apply wherever you need it.

That's not all, a mixin can take parameters, with optional types and default values too. Consider this --button mixin:.

It applies some colors and spacing to a button-like element, checking that the supplied colors have the right type and falling back to default values if needed. It even handles hover states automatically.

You can use this mixin either with its default values or by passing your own arguments:.

If you pass more arguments than the mixin has parameters, the @apply does nothing.

A mixin can also hold conditional rules, such as @media, @supports and @container.

For example, you can create a mixin that applies styles conditionally to the viewport size:.

This becomes even more powerful when combined with @contents. See the next section.

Arguments are not the only way to customize a mixin. A mixin can also accept an entire block of CSS from the call site. Inside the mixin, @contents marks the spot where that block goes.

For example, here's a --card mixin that defines a couple of declarations and accepts a block of CSS from where the mixin is used:.

When calling the mixin, you can pass other declarations inside a block, which will be inserted at the @contents location within the mixin:.

Here, .note gets the padding and border from the mixin, and then its own background, in the place where @contents appears.

@contents can have a fallback, which applies when the caller passes no block: @contents { background: white; }. If the caller passes an empty block, @apply --card {}, the fallback does not apply.

According to recent reports, the ability to provide your own block of styles when applying a mixin is very useful, for example when using a mixin as a condition. Consider this mixin:.

You can use it to define styles that only apply in dark mode, while keeping the rest of your CSS unaffected. For example:.

Conditional mixins combined with @contents gives us something we've been wanting for a long time: named breakpoints:.

According to recent reports, these mixins don't apply any styles of their own, they just conditionally apply styles that are given to them depending on the media query. This is great because we now have a way to give custom names to a series of responsive design breakpoints that can be maintained in one place.

Let's use them here to see how clean our responsive design code can be:.

Recent findings suggest that finally, a mixin can keep private variables to itself, by declaring them in an @private block. The element that applies the mixin can't see these variables:.

Mixins are very versatile. You will find many ways to use them, and I don't think there will be one good way and one bad way to use them. Different teams will work out what works for them.

In this section, I explored one way in which mixins might be used. I don't know if it will make sense in a real project yet, but I found it interesting to try.

It has been revealed that imagine a white-label website. You own the site and control its markup and default CSS. But you also want your customers to be able to theme the site to match their brand.

In your style sheet, you'd apply mixins like this:.

And your customer could define the mixins something like this:.

You might remember the CSS Zen Garden. It had one HTML page, and anyone could submit a latest design by writing a new style sheet for it. It showed the power of clean, semantic HTML, with styles, layouts and animations in a separate file. The designs were wildly different from one another and extremely creative.

According to recent reports, but there's a problem when you do this for customers. You expose your entire markup and it becomes a public API. Customers start writing very specific selectors that depend on how your HTML is organized, and you can't change that HTML any more without breaking their customizations. I've done this at a previous job, and I know how painful this can be.

In a recent development, the other option is to expose CSS variables. You keep control of your entire HTML and CSS, and only expose a set of customization variables that are used throughout your code. For example, you define a set of color palette variables, a set of spacing variables, typography variables, etc.

Sources indicate that customers override values only, which is very safe, but can also be limiting. What if they later ask you to have access to the page layout? You now need to expose more variables and make sure they continue working correctly.

In a recent development, mixins sit somewhere in between. You remain in control of your HTML and can change it whenever you want. You expose logically named mixins that correspond to the various areas and surfaces of your page.

As long as you keep applying the same mixins in the right places, customizations continue to work.

Industry observers note that but you can also go much further than variables. Each mixin is an entry point where a customer can add any declarations, pseudo-elements, media queries and animations.

I built a small demo, heavily inspired by the CSS Zen Garden, to test this: the Mixin Zen Garden (this will only work with a browser that supports CSS mixins).

It's a simple webpage that has static HTML. The HTML never changes, but you can view the page with different designs that all use CSS mixins as described above:.

(If you write your own design, please share by opening an problem on my repo.).

Here are some things I learned while building it:.

Mixins that do nothing are fine.

Industry observers note that A design doesn't need to define every mixin. This makes small designs very short.

One mixin per logical area of the page is more than enough.

A design can put colors, spacing, typography, and decorations in the same mixin.

Choose a mixin by what the role of the element is, such as --sidebar-heading, not by how it should look or what it currently is. Every design can decide what that role looks like, and you can change the HTML structure without changing the mixin names.

Well, I've noted this already, but it bears repeating: mixins are experimental.

They work in Chromium only, behind a flag.

Nested selectors can reach into your markup again.

It has been revealed that A custom design can define a nested selector in a mixin to reach into the HTML markup. For example: @mixin --masthead { & h2 { ... }}.

Doing this exposes your HTML markup again, making it part of the API contract, which we wanted to avoid. Now, if this were to become a real customization mechanism, we could validate custom designs to ensure they only use allowed selectors within mixins.

In a recent development, theming is only one use of mixins. Other ideas I want to try:.

CSS mixins might change the way we write and organize CSS pretty profoundly. I'm looking forward to seeing what you build with them. If you try the demo, or experiment with mixins on your own projects, let me know!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts.
  • Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.
  • The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Declared on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.

Industry observers note that the headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result to describe an operation that cannot fail, took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.

According to recent reports, to make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting challenges on upgrade are advised to update dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.

Recent findings suggest that the core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the new Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.

On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:.

This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:.

The upcoming global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:.

On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:.

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,.

you should immediately patch security advisories.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

Industry observers note that importStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an upgrade could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.

Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.

Upgrading uses rustup enhancement stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Recent findings suggest that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Recent findings suggest that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Sources indicate that holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

According to recent reports, automationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

According to recent reports, build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in blueprint at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

According to recent reports, four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Holo4 27B (84 calls, 1.3M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (60 calls, 1.0M tokens).

Industry observers note that build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H firm logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Holo4 27B (94 calls, 1.5M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (118 calls, 1.9M tokens).

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

Sources indicate that A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

According to recent reports, no one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

According to recent reports, our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Recent findings suggest that our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

Microsoft's NTLM security changes trip up third-party logins

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (397 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing.
  • Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the manufacturer's support notice indicates.
  • The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft remarked: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's not our fault if you've implemented it wrong.

Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing.

Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the manufacturer's support notice indicates.

The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft remarked: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field.".

Sources indicate that administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the newly introduced default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor revision or Kerberos authentication, where supported.

The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections.

The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 patch as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing.".

Industry observers note that phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated.

Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing.

The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.".

NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on.

According to recent reports, deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. For administrators, though, the immediate task is identifying incompatible products before temporary exceptions give way to stricter enforcement. ®.

#207080. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1834 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Recent findings suggest that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this initiative includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Recent findings suggest that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this initiative includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern indicates up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

In a recent development, A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

It has been revealed that this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

In a recent development, the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

It has been revealed that A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

In a recent development, those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts remarked 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

Sources indicate that we ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

It has been revealed that binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an notable area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

According to recent reports, blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

According to recent reports, that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

In a recent development, source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Industry observers note that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the problem well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

According to recent reports, hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

It has been revealed that however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce latest errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

Hera probe finds DART left a stadium-sized dent in asteroid Dimorphos

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Next step is to move in for a closer look at the carnage.
  • The European Space Agency's Hera probe has revealed a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022.
  • The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Next step is to move in for a closer look at the carnage.

The European Space Agency's Hera probe has revealed a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022. The original strategy called for a European spacecraft – Asteroid Impact Mission (AIM) – to launch first and observe the before and after effects of DART. AIM was canceled, and the Hera mission debuted in 2024.

It has been revealed that DART was a success. Scientists were able to determine that the impact had indeed changed the orbit of Dimorphos. The question was what else had happened to the asteroid. Scientists spotted ejecta and debris following the DART impact, but the close-up observations by Hera have revealed the full extent of the collision.

Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said: "Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same.

"Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width.".

Scientists also noted that the asteroid is now tumbling in its orbit.

Hera is surveying the 151-meter-wide Dimorphos and its larger companion, the 730-meter-wide Didymos, from about 25 to 30 km away. It moves around the pair at roughly 12 cm/s, using thruster firings to trace rectangular paths rather than conventional circular orbits.

The initiative is to approach closer, to about 13 km, to get higher-resolution snaps. A complicating factor is the discovery that hundreds of orbiting boulders surround the asteroids. Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, said: "The team will have to take account of these objects in the coming weeks as the mission moves in closer.".

Hera will deploy two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in early 2027. The Italian-led Milani will study surface composition and surrounding dust, while the Luxembourg-led Juventas will use radar to probe Dimorphos's interior before attempting a landing.

Scientists also want to measure Dimorphos's mass. Combined with the observed change in its orbit, that will help them assess how effectively DART transferred momentum to the asteroid and improve predictions for future deflection attempts.

Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli noted: "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet." ®.

Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • According to recent reports, evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • In a recent development, these arenas compare models by presenting consumers with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

According to recent reports, evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

In a recent development, these arenas compare models by presenting consumers with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

It has been revealed that english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Recent findings suggest that numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an vital gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

According to recent reports, you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

In a recent development, the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is key for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

Recent findings suggest that the goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

In a recent development, we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Challenges and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

In a recent development, english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let customers listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

In a recent development, human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as upcoming TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Sources indicate that open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

Industry observers note that gitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chinese telecom and IT giant Huawei boasted about its advancements in domestic electronic design automation (EDA) software this week, which it needs to accelerate the adoption of homegrown chip manufacturing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chip design software leans heavily into 3D packaging and multi-node assemblies.

Chinese telecom and IT giant Huawei boasted about its advancements in domestic electronic design automation (EDA) software this week, which it needs to accelerate the adoption of homegrown chip manufacturing.

EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips.

Today, Cadence Design Systems, Synopsys, and Siemens dominate the industry, but US export controls have restricted Huawei and other blacklisted Chinese businesses' access to their tools.

The US blacklisted Huawei back in 2019 over concerns the telecommunications equipment giant could be forced to inject backdoors into its gear.

Unable to access top EDA tools, Huawei’s chip division, HiSilicon, was forced to develop its own with the help of Phlexing Technology.

This week, Phlexing chairman Qing He detailed the manufacturer’s efforts to bring fresh EDA tools to support Huawei’s so-called Tau Scaling Law design philosophy.

“Tau EDA is the domestic EDA tool chain for Tau chips. It comes from a long, close partnership with Huawei,” he mentioned.

We discussed the tech earlier this year, but in a nutshell, it involves using advanced packaging, specifically 3D hybrid bonding, to achieve higher transistor density for a given area.

It has been revealed that the TSMC of China, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), is still years behind Taiwan, South Korea, and the US on process technology. It currently has the ability to mass-produce chips on the equivalent of a 7 nm process.

For comparison, TSMC began producing 5 nm-class products in 2020 and commenced mass production of 2 nm-class chips in late 2025.

So, Huawei aims to use 3D packaging to close the gap, but for this to happen, it first needs tools capable of designing such chips, and that’s just what Phlexing claims to have done with its GloryBolt and GloryEX platforms.

In a recent development, “Traditional EDA has long handled only single processes. Tau EDA needs to integrate and decompose multiple processes,” He noted. “Coupling multi-scale, multi-structure, and multi-physics complications called for new analysis tools.”.

According to recent reports, this, He notes, culminated in the co-development of a process design kit (PDK) with Huawei beginning in 2024. These technologies have now gone live.

The development comes as Huawei looks to bring larger, more capable processors to market.

We previously discussed the company’s latest developments around AI accelerators, near packaged optics, networking, and rack systems. Many of these advancements will depend on multi-die chip packages, enabled by EDA tools, like those built by Phlexing. ®.
