Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.Sponsorship updateIt’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction, possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations. Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos. Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately? I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from, how many owners I have, or what they’re up to.At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet, but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key, I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key, and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to, and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again (ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good part of my career helping people streamline and automate).C++ Index…?Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go, in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement, but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax, and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms that already exists for on-heap structures but not off; bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow, it just chafes.Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine, performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact, and if we do I doubt it will be massive, as the Java implementation is already very optimized, and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor for continuing this even if the performance doesn’t materialize.I’m doing this quite slowly one component at a time, measuring twice and cutting once, finding good abstractions that lean into C++’s strengths rather than doing a straight translation. In part because this is supremely fiddly and technical work, and in part because there genuinely isn’t any rush and if there is much performance to gain it’s probably in staring at the problem long enough I find better alternative approaches. I did manage to lean more into lock-free algorithms in the buffer pool for example. Translation probably won’t be finished this year at this pace.Many things are undecided: Haven’t decided on where to draw the interface boundary yet. Neither do I have a public git repo for this. May still scrap the entire idea as a silly boondoggle. We’ll just have to see where it goes.On the off chance this rambling mess gets posted on a link aggregator somewhere, I anticipate two types of people will crawl out of the woodwork. I’ll address their concerns in advance.“Why not Rust/Zig/Odin/${MY_HOBBY_HORSE_LANGUAGE}? C++ is not memory safe! Haven’t you heard that C++ is bad? Look at this diseased rat comic I found on /r/programming!”My friend in Christ, I use C++ because I’m experienced with C++, and have built nontrivial stuff with in in the past, I’m familiar with the tooling and also kinda enjoy it. It can not be overstated how technical this code is, it’s more than hard enough in a language I’m familiar with, let alone one I’d have to learn as I go. I don’t need to do it blindfolded using a dance mat in a barrel going down the niagara falls for this to be difficult."${FRONTIER_MODEL} could one-shot this in less than ${TIME}!"Probably true? The source is all pretty well tested, with a reference implementation to boot. Seems like very favorable circumstances for a competent coding model.That noted, even without turning over rocks such as “externalities of the datacenter buildout”, “externalities of AI training”, and “legal ownership status of AI-generated code”âI don’t think such angles of attack do much to convince anyone who isn’t already convincedâif AI did the translation I sure as heck couldn’t go on to then maintain that code[1][2].Even in the best case, this is me at the edge of my programming abilities. Performance critical low level programming is hard enough to wrap your head around if you were the one who designed the code, let alone if it was vibe coded. I’d be on the hook for an AI subscription perpetually hoping and praying the token prices wouldn’t ever go up. This is a nonstarter for the same reasons the search engine runs on its own hardware and not in the cloud. You can’t be truly independent if you’re subject to the whims of a landlord.From a project management perspective, I’m not rushing anything to market. Project still has years of runway. I’m not beholden to any investors to deliver profits. Even if I wanted to, I have no employees to replace other than my self. What I would trade away is the very immersion in the problem domain that’s allowed me to get as far as I have with this project. What I’m expecting to be getting out of it is improved developer ergonomics and maybe a bit of performance if the aforementioned problem-immersion-thing pans out. That’s not something that brings me money, and something I can do because the project is in a fairly stable and mature state.Thus, regardless of what happens in the future with AI, there isn’t an obvious opportunity cost to holding off.Heck, let’s just consider popular future predictions about AI, where does this leave me?AI bet pays of and models become exponentially more powerful, much cheaper, and ubiquitous like tap water: How shortsighted would it be to pay for crappy AI today when I could save my money and get exponentially better or more AI for the same dollars in the future? I’d have to really hate having money to do such a thing.OpenThropic IPOs, vocal shareholders from Ferenginar quite insistently ask where they money at, token prices go up singificantly: Only a problem if you’re dependent on AI.AI investment bubble crashes and it’s raining bankers like October 1929: Bad for everyone, but especially bad if you’re dependent on AI.Tech prists in SV chant binharic hymns as the Machine God emerges and the chosen of humanity transcends into the cyber rapture: Kind of orthogonal to whether I build this index port by hand.Zoomers decide that Kazcinski was right all along and instigate a Butlerian Jihad: Mostly a problem if you’re dependent on AI.Rise of the Machines, hydraulic press youtube channel stomping on a human face forever: Inconvenient regardless of choice of action.[1] Lesser minds would think models outputting unmanitainable code is a sign of the superiority of AI. Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.

It has been revealed that not much latest functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most major parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.

It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.

Recent findings suggest that serpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.

The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction, possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations. Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos. Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately? I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from, how many consumers I have, or what they’re up to.

At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet, but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.

On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.

I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key, I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key, and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to, and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again (ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good part of my career helping people streamline and automate).

Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.

I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go, in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement, but we’re presently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax, and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.

Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms that already exists for on-heap structures but not off; bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow, it just chafes.

Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine, performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.

To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact, and if we do I doubt it will be massive, as the Java implementation is already very optimized, and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.

Sources indicate that thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor for continuing this even if the performance doesn’t materialize.

I’m doing this quite slowly one component at a time, measuring twice and cutting once, finding good abstractions that lean into C++’s strengths rather than doing a straight translation. In part because this is supremely fiddly and technical work, and in part because there genuinely isn’t any rush and if there is much performance to gain it’s probably in staring at the problem long enough I find better alternative approaches. I did manage to lean more into lock-free algorithms in the buffer pool for example. Translation probably won’t be finished this year at this pace.

In a recent development, many things are undecided: Haven’t decided on where to draw the interface boundary yet. Neither do I have a public git repo for this. May still scrap the entire idea as a silly boondoggle. We’ll just have to see where it goes.

On the off chance this rambling mess gets posted on a link aggregator somewhere, I anticipate two types of people will crawl out of the woodwork. I’ll address their concerns in advance.

“Why not Rust/Zig/Odin/${MY_HOBBY_HORSE_LANGUAGE}? C++ is not memory safe! Haven’t you heard that C++ is bad? Look at this diseased rat comic I found on /r/programming!”.

In a recent development, my friend in Christ, I use C++ because I’m experienced with C++, and have built nontrivial stuff with in in the past, I’m familiar with the tooling and also kinda enjoy it. It can not be overstated how technical this code is, it’s more than hard enough in a language I’m familiar with, let alone one I’d have to learn as I go. I don’t need to do it blindfolded using a dance mat in a barrel going down the niagara falls for this to be difficult.

"${FRONTIER_MODEL} could one-shot this in less than ${TIME}!".

Probably true? The source is all pretty well tested, with a reference implementation to boot. Seems like very favorable circumstances for a competent coding model.

That remarked, even without turning over rocks such as “externalities of the datacenter buildout”, “externalities of AI training”, and “legal ownership status of AI-generated code”âI don’t think such angles of attack do much to convince anyone who isn’t already convincedâif AI did the translation I sure as heck couldn’t go on to then maintain that code[1][2].

Recent findings suggest that even in the best case, this is me at the edge of my programming abilities. Performance critical low level programming is hard enough to wrap your head around if you were the one who designed the code, let alone if it was vibe coded. I’d be on the hook for an AI subscription perpetually hoping and praying the token prices wouldn’t ever go up. This is a nonstarter for the same reasons the search engine runs on its own hardware and not in the cloud. You can’t be truly independent if you’re subject to the whims of a landlord.

Industry observers note that from a project management perspective, I’m not rushing anything to market. Project still has years of runway. I’m not beholden to any investors to deliver profits. Even if I wanted to, I have no employees to replace other than my self. What I would trade away is the very immersion in the problem domain that’s allowed me to get as far as I have with this project. What I’m expecting to be getting out of it is improved developer ergonomics and maybe a bit of performance if the aforementioned problem-immersion-thing pans out. That’s not something that brings me money, and something I can do because the project is in a fairly stable and mature state.

Thus, regardless of what happens in the future with AI, there isn’t an obvious opportunity cost to holding off.

Heck, let’s just consider popular future predictions about AI, where does this leave me?

[1] Lesser minds would think models outputting unmanitainable code is a sign of the superiority of AI. I’ll refer you to the most problematic prophet, Terry Davis, for that one.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure).

Laura Savino discusses the psychological friction of AI adoption for senior engineers & architects. She explains how shifting from static expertise to learning in public lowers anxiety, accelerates tooling fluency, and prevents burnout. Leaders will discover actionable strategies to support their teams, debunk tech zealotry, and foster an adaptive engineering culture that thrives during upheaval.

Laura Savino a software engineer at Adobe Photoshop. She brings her background in education and humanities to technical topics, creating talks that spark ongoing conversations.

Industry observers note that software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

In a recent development, laura Savino: Several friends and colleagues have come to me to tell me recently that they are pregnant with their first child, and have taken comfort from a really odd bit of perspective that I've given them, because I have two lovely kids, two very much wanted and uneventful pregnancies. I hated being pregnant. Every so often, I look around a crowd of people, and I'm like, everyone here is the result of a pregnancy, and it creeps me out. It's beautiful. It's a miracle of life. It is also not my jam. The thing that made me willing to do it at all and that gave me great comfort along the way was actually the myth of the frog. This frog is swimming around in water that starts at a comfortable temperature, but is slowly heated through to a boil, and if you do it gradually enough, the frog won't really notice that its environment is no longer like anything it's ever experienced before, and the frog is eventually cooked.

This odd myth gave me a lifeline of hope, because if that frog can adapt to extreme, unprecedented conditions, so can I. Because the difficult parts usually come on gradually, day by day. If having a child started with the eighth-month pregnancy discomfort, very few of us would do it. It would be banned as inhumane torture if we could instantly make people eight months pregnant.

Sources indicate that some of you are like, "It's 9:00 in the morning. We're at a software conference. Can we please not talk about spontaneous advanced gestation? It is a repulsive idea." When we see a person eight months pregnant who got there gradually, the way we all luckily do, we just think, how nice. It's not repulsive at all, it's beautiful. It's usually obvious that they're just handling it like champions. It turns out the frog thing is thoroughly debunked. At a certain point, ectotherms change locations to keep themselves safe. The myth works to reassure me and my pregnant friends because of the way I frame it. It's not that the thing gets worse and worse slowly, and you don't notice and eventually are cooked. It's that you yourself change. You adapt. Yes, your context becomes more and more difficult, but if you're committed to sticking it out, you flex some increasingly creative coping strategies and skills, you become able to handle it. You worry about eighth month after you've figured out the seventh month and the sixth month, you'll be fine.

According to recent reports, let's tangent from there. I have these two amazing kids, one is 8. We've had Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse on repeat in our house this past month. There's this one scene that captures me. A newly bitten Spider-Man is trying to learn to thwip, that's the technical term, and he's doing it while being chased by an evil giant robo-scientist through the trees, so Spider-Man is like dodging trees, and he yells, "Whoa, whoa, I can't do this yet." His trainer quips, "Everyone knows that the best way to learn is under intense, life-threatening pressure." Another anecdote. My friend TJ. TJ is an all-around delightful person, but their rarest trait and the highest compliment that I can reach for is that they are a functional programming language aficionado and are not an asshole about it. These days we're all a little or a lot more on board with the functional aspects of Rust and Kotlin and Swift, and strongly preferring pure functions is just mainstream now.

Side Effect punk is dead. Remember Haskell, the language? Remember when there was a whole functional programming dogma with true believers, with the hyper-conviction of the newly converted, and there were memes about monads. If your brain could follow certain logical compressions, you were with it. You were good. You were likely to survive, and everybody else was getting left in the imperative rubble. When I learned TJ appreciated Haskell, I was like, but you're so chill about it. They were like, it's a really interesting tool. This was the first time that I'd met a functional programming enthusiast that I could relate to.

In a recent development, I am Laura Savino. I'm a developer on Photoshop, somewhat on the iOS UI, but also on the C++ library that supports real Photoshop PSD file editing on your phone. Before I became a software engineer, I thought I was going to be a language teacher. I was for a minute. I took master's-level courses in things like how to teach American English pronunciation, how to design a test that tests what you want it to evaluate, which is hard. I taught English in France and French in Seattle, and English again at that time in South Korea, and eventually learned to code. Fast-forward several years, and here I am on the QCon London stage. Today's talk, I hope, will start to shift your identity from someone who's good at doing a specific thing to someone who's good at learning near anything. I'm taking it as an anthology of vignettes with research for structural support. In rough order of appearance, so you have a sense of time passing. There will be cabinet-making, teen vampires, December-born horses, a Zen priest, football kits, awkward dance floors, and a puppy. I will provide a slide with references at the end, so you can settle in.

In a recent development, I started with three stories, one about a frog, one about Spider-Man, and one about these monad pushers, and this is not exactly an un-telegraphed reveal that these stories map shockingly neatly onto the onslaught of AI. The first one, the frog metaphor that comforted me so much in my pregnancy, part of what makes the AI transition so disorienting is that we're being asked, many of us, to take it on. Like, now, now, now, the water is plasma, and you frogs will get in there, and you will like it. If you're not already orchestrating, you're so far behind, you might as well take up goat herding, because the goats are more your speed. For Spider-Man, a major reason the AI transition is so daunting is that many people's livelihoods are directly tied to how well we adapt. It's fine. The robot arm's chasing us, they're motivating. We all just ducked in here for a minute to throw them off our trails.

Lastly, about my chill friend, it's tough out there because of all the zealots. I think most of them are not actually assholes. I genuinely believe they're mostly just excited, and they cannot imagine a reasonable person in possession of all the facts who's not exactly as excited as they are. They respond by either assuming you're an unreasonable person or giving you more facts, and I'm not sure which is worse. The ultimate well-meaning zealot is the Chris Traeger character on Parks and Rec played by Rob Lowe. This character is intense, precise, and painfully optimistic. There's this one scene where he says he's logged 65,000 miles running in his lifetime, and his goal is to run to the moon. Some AI enthusiasts are giving a little Chris Traeger running to the moon. We recognize they're telling us about something healthy and good, and they may even have our best interests at heart, but no part of me wishes I had my running shoes on so I could join him to the moon. How do we bring people with us?

I experienced a massive at-the-time transition in Cocoa, in the Apple development community that did this well. See, it was possible for a long time to go into Apple development with a great deal of hubris. You were an Apple developer. You knew all the tricks and tips. You'd hand-molded a lock and knit release cycles. Back of the cabinet here means, sure, no one's going to see this part of the code, but we're still going to make it just so because we take pride in our work. For a minute there, you could be confident that your deep UI kit and Objective-C knowledge meant that big companies would pay you and a team of three or four devs and a crack designer, absolute truckloads of cash to write them an app because everyone needed apps and no one knew how to write them except us. It was a really good time to be an Apple developer.

Then Apple dropped Swift, brand new language. You're welcome, everyone. Soon all our new APIs will be in this brand-new language that you have to use. We were willing to give up our semicolons. No one likes those, but they ripped away our square brackets too. This was one of those watershed community moments. One perspective I really liked at the time was, we're knocked back to being beginners again, and we like it. We're on even footing. We're learning together. Isn't this exciting? The change electrified us in good and bad ways. On the good side, I distinctly remember watching people who'd shipped indie software on CDs, people who were intimately familiar with why NSString is prefixed that way because they used to code in NEXTSTEP. These developers dived headfirst into the new language. I was sitting around with The Omni Group folks, like OmniFocus, OmniGraffle, these are Apple ecosystem legends, with our laptops out in the hotel lobbies of San Francisco, just trying to figure out, what can I do with this new language? On the less good side.

It has been revealed that swift was confirmed in June, and on my production app, we had an intern who waited several weeks till late July, before Xcode, our IDE was even out of beta, the intern added Swift to the project just for fun. The tool chain support was abysmal. I couldn't exactly embrace the beginner's mind when I was trying to ship a feature and couldn't even type because my IDE kept lagging out with this message. It was frustrating and not at all production ready because the tool chain was literally in beta. On the whole, with the benefit of rose-colored nostalgia, it was good. Most super senior principal developers, these pinnacles of technical excellence, were having to relearn how to get the eighth element out of a string, like just rookie stuff. The behaviors that got rewarded were the ones where people learned in public. The people who learned the most were the ones who asked the most questions, who'd notice when they didn't understand something and say, this is something I don't understand.

How interesting? They'd post forum questions and ask each other how things worked. They would post early code samples where they did not look like geniuses who knew all the answers, but just enthusiastic rookies who wanted to learn. You know how much people love correcting people on the internet, so anyone who posted something inaccurate got told about it real quick. How do you be ok with that, though? How do you psychologically handle going from the expert hot commodity to a total noob and keep up decent spirits while you do it?

My friends, has anyone considered the old standby straight-up denial? I don't think any of us are in first-order denial about AI where we refuse to accept that it exists or is changing things, but for myself, I am absolutely deep in second-order denial where you acknowledge the basic facts of the thing, but you deny the implications of those facts. Sure, the technology is here, but I am not ready to face its implications. I usually try to add a lot of details when I'm giving a talk, but here, I am going to kindly draw a veil and let the camera discreetly pan away because you do not need me to share my particular doomsday flavors. Besides, it weakens the denial. Denial can also stem from a fear that you or those you love lack the skills or resources to handle the consequences of a change. That's real.

Apparently, denial can have protective effects, though. This one study, "The role of denial in recovery from coronary heart disease," found that people who were in deep denial actually had better short-term outcomes than the ones who were actually facing reality. If you had deeper denial, you'd spend less time in intensive care and have fewer heart-related symptoms while you were in hospital. This rings true for me. Even if I've decided a thing is crucial to me, even when it's well-aligned with my values, if I face the full implications of how hard it's going to be, I will probably not do it. I might say, I don't have to exercise at the gym. I'm just going to put my shoes on and show up and we'll just see what happens. Denial can work to get us to start down a hard road and give us hope long enough to adapt to this ever-changing water.

It has been revealed that protective denial, it's incredibly common. We're also all going to die someday, but memento mori has somehow fallen out of fashion. If you want to sit in second-order denial with me for a little longer, that's ok. For a little longer, because the heart patients with serious denial had worse outcomes long-term. They didn't follow their medical advice, because why would they? They were fine. They got re-hospitalized more. Denial is not sustainable. If a little self-misdirection is what it takes to follow your values to stay in the room and not make a down payment on a yacht, go ahead, indulge. Let me suggest another indulgence, brain candy. When I was trying to improve my Spanish, I read the Twilight books, and I'm guessing most of you haven't read them or won't admit to having read them, because they're cloying vampire, werewolf, romance novels written for pre-teens. My Spanish became tan brillante como el pelo de Eduardo a la luz del sol, because brain candy, in the domain you're trying to learn, is just like the little carrot thrown down the path to convince the recalcitrant, what, I'm supposed to be good at this part of you, to at least look over and start to think about how to maybe head down this otherwise daunting path.

Sometimes you truly need to lower the stakes mentally just so you can push through. Get out of that intense, life-threatening pressure. Solve an actual problem that only you have. Make some tool, make some toy, make a flatulence app with your 8-year-old, something real, but where no one will evaluate you on the outcome because evaluation changes us. We don't learn so we can achieve the task we care about, we learn to pass the test assigned to us. This is bad even if you're an excellent test taker.

Industry observers note that I took a break from my French major one summer to spend eight weeks in an intensive Japanese language study in northern Japan, where they promised to teach us the equivalent of two university semesters of Japanese. I was very good at French at that point. I had just breezed through a pair of graduate seminars and my placement test in the Japanese program put me in the very lowest level class. I'd only taken two basic Japanese classes by this point, but I just still felt like, "Hello, don't you know who I am? I'm good at languages. Why am I in the beginner's class with these people who can barely put a sentence together?" Granted, I couldn't say, do you know who I am, in Japanese, which is maybe a sign that their class placement was somewhat valid, but I had a demonstrated skill in a fundamentally different but still related area.

Sources indicate that some of us are feeling this way about computing right now. I'm good at computers. I am a senior professional programmer. I once learned Python in an afternoon. If this newly introduced computing skill is hard for me, either is something is wrong with the system or something is wrong with me. Don't you know who I am? For me in Japan, my identity was so caught up in being good at languages that I worked hard to avoid ever making a mistake, not just on coursework, but asking the bus driver for a transfer ticket. I wanted my Japanese to be perfect. I actually learned the most about learning that summer on a weekend excursion, just me and a classmate, where we stayed at a family-run Buddhist temple out in the countryside. I won't go into the expectation thrashing experience of preparing myself for a solemn weekend of meditation and instead watching sumo wrestling on TV with a priest and his family, but the larger foundation-shattering surprise was the way my classmate spoke to our Japanese hosts and that she would just say things.

In a recent development, she'd trip over words. She'd mess up her verb endings. My grammar wasn't great, but I could recognize a bunch of mistakes even if I couldn't correct them. I was so deep in this prove to everyone that I'm good at this mentality that if I didn't know how to say something properly, I'd keep quiet so I didn't embarrass myself. Amy, though, just talked. They're like laughing, conversing. The priest gets another beer. What stuck with me long after I forgot all the extra kanji I learned that summer, is that interacting imperfectly builds fluency. You get early feedback before unwanted behaviors are calcified. Find your version of a Zen retreat where you can just play with the tools with no expectations of evaluation. You'll develop facility and fluency that much faster.

Another way to fail when something's not a test. Many years ago, as I was just learning to code, like mapping out how to do red-black trees on a whiteboard level, I went out with some friends and some friends of friends to rent a karaoke room. One of these friends of friends turned out to be an engineering manager at Microsoft, which is a hazard of where I live in Seattle. I remember the fear and dread and shame that I felt when I was unable to successfully navigate the karaoke interface via any of the in-room remote controls. See, I saw this as my chance to prove my technical prowess and maybe get hired on at Microsoft. Why would the engineering manager consider my resume if I couldn't even modify the output settings of a retro karaoke system? I don't remember what any of us saying, but I do remember holding that remote in my hand and thinking that I was never going to get a job in tech.

Sources indicate that now we're all looking back at 15 years ago me and inwardly shouting, everybody knows these systems are hard. Just try, don't give up, it's fine. We have so much compassion. What is your tool today that you're like, I still don't have this thing working. What are they all going to think of me? I better hide it and fake it and just play it cool. If you have that mental block, lower the stakes, make a tool, make a toy, something unspeakably inane that is tailored to exactly your interests. It can lower the activation energy required to take that next step towards learning.

Recent findings suggest that another way I make daunting things feel more approachable is thinking of them as a practice round. Picture this, every Sunday morning, I'm at a former aircraft hangar that's been turned into an indoor kids' sports hell hole arena. There are five football fields, a dozen simultaneous kid classes, there's adult workout classes, there's birthday rooms, plus an enormous bouncy house situation. I promise you whatever you're picturing, there are more bouncy houses. There's screaming and there's tears and there's kids running and begging for snacks, and I'm paying to be here. I went to great effort to dig the 4-year-old's soccer uniform out of his dirty laundry hamper and convince him to leave the house and convince him to leave the car. My reward for that is sitting on an uncomfortable bench drinking truly some of the worst coffee in Seattle. I want to paint for you this picture of aggressively, brightly colored despair, because what you need to appreciate is that it was a massive deal for me to change perspectives.

Because I realize that if you see this not as a whole collection of circumstances designed to maximize my suffering, but hundreds of families who each separately fought through the chaos that is having a child on a chilly, damp weekend morning and got them to leave the house. If we could see in a little heads-up display what people overcame to get through that door, we would be walking around high-fiving and pouring each other pints. Nobody mentions all these hurdles. They just act like, yes, kids are wearing their kits here on time, relatively few boogers, as if they didn't execute a dozen fancy maneuvers to get there. If I don't tell someone that I struggled to get my kid there dressed, I won't hear their advice. Yes, my kid sleeps in her football kit. Sunday mornings have become my time to bask in the glory that not only have all of us made it through a gauntlet, but we've also successfully identified flaws in our own getting-out-of-the-house systems.

Sources indicate that we're basically red teaming our own lives. How did you do at getting out of the house without yelling and tears? C-minus. How will you do at learning from what went wrong? Are you committed to bringing better snacks next time? The point isn't how well you executed the thing today, but how well you've internalized and applied the changes for next time. Put the snacks in the car right now, and today counts as a success.

In a recent development, when I was deciding whether to take this job I had at Photoshop, I called up a friend for advice, because I had two offers for very different jobs, one that I was sure I would be good at, that they would be lucky to have me, and the other was a stretch. It was on Photoshop, where I'd have to brush up on modern C++ and L1 caches and deal with real legacy code. My friend remarked that if I had the appetite to learn the new thing, the hard thing, that I should do it now. Because at some point, he said, you're like, I don't want to learn a whole new paradigm again. I've been there. I've done that. I'm good. This advice was perfect when I was choosing my destiny, and learning modern C++ was supposed to be my last major career challenge. Now, very few of us have a choice about whether to invest a ton of energy in learning this new thing.

According to recent reports, I have to somehow generate energy for learning or hit burnout real hard. I feel like maybe external energy building works for salespeople. Like I could just shout, are you ready? Let's get pumped. Everyone would be like, yes, let's go. We're engineers who got to where we are by taking skepticism to an art form. How many people have looked at some shiny latest tech, stated, no, and then just watched it crumble off into the sunset? No amount of like, rah, rah, do it, is going to convince us in all of the do it, learn, go. It's like being told by a scowling Simon Cowell to do a heartfelt interpretive dance. You're not at your best. How do we, the hopeful skeptics who do believe in a better future, in spite of it all, how do we generate energy to learn? Let's actually start by not spiraling, perhaps, by not leaking happiness.

AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • It has been revealed that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

It has been revealed that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

In a recent development, A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Industry observers note that feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

According to recent reports, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

Sources indicate that the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Recent findings suggest that consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Recent findings suggest that soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

According to recent reports, completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

Recent findings suggest that these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Industry observers note that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into fresh executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create newly introduced tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Industry observers note that identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a latest target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

In a recent development, the multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

Sources indicate that to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Industry observers note that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Recent findings suggest that generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Recent findings suggest that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

Industry observers note that the pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

Recent findings suggest that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

It has been revealed that A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

It has been revealed that passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

Industry observers note that the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We blueprint to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

According to recent reports, the synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

Recent findings suggest that the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, instead we'll see black blobs of data centers shadowing (as Star Link satellites do now) everything in the night sky and blocking sunlight during the day. Let's just hope the laser data transmission between space data centers to and from Star Link isn't using visible light.

Industry observers note that A million is a lot. I imagine this idea of putting data centers into orbit will stop being enticing when the AI bubble pops, which will be far before they get to 1 mil.

Industry observers note that the FCC is only responsible for US frequency allocation and making sure that the system doesn't cause interference. SpaceX will need to get their system submitted to the ITC after that, or avoid transmitting near the Canadian and Mexican borders. They might actually choose the latter option, at least initially.

Recent findings suggest that as for allocation of orbits, it's basically first come first serve. If you get a vehicle into an orbit that isn't in use, it's yours. By convention there is international coordination to try to avoid.

It's a paradox. The FCC is at times powerless and also too powerful, depending on what republicans want to accomplish.

Industry observers note that I'll be surprised if they get to ten. It'd be orders of magnitude cheaper to build them in Antarctica, and easier to maintain them once built. Not that building data centres in Antarctica is a good idea, or likely to be financially viable, but launching them into space isn't even good sci-fi.

The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And intruders don't always need to exploit bugs to break in.
  • American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems.
  • Sources indicate that the federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And intruders don't always need to exploit bugs to break in.

American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems.

Sources indicate that the federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A newly introduced index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23.

It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020.

However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted.

Industry observers note that five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords.

Industry observers note that the report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers, targeted more than 100 water systems, with incidents reported across at least 12 states, and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers.

According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17.

Sources indicate that additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique:.

According to recent reports, the authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [T0883]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22.

These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented.

Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo.

“Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®.

#207068. The Agent Remarked It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The Agent Remarked It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

According to recent reports, the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Sources indicate that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Recent findings suggest that two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

It has been revealed that an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

Industry observers note that that gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

In a recent development, want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

According to recent reports, A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

Industry observers note that an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Industry observers note that starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Sources indicate that only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Sources indicate that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

It has been revealed that kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

Industry observers note that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Sources indicate that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

According to recent reports, we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

In a recent development, figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

Recent findings suggest that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Industry observers note that cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

It has been revealed that now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

It has been revealed that none of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

According to recent reports, the practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

In a recent development, classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post reveals the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

It has been revealed that at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects.   • The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s proposal to launch a million datacenter satellites.
  • The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Approval for ‘Starmind’ granted but it’s a long way from the launchpad, or making sense.

The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s proposal to launch a million datacenter satellites.

The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”.

The order requires SpaceX to ensure its satellites’ radios don’t interfere with US government systems which use the 28.6-29.1 GHz band and requires the company to stick to operating within the parameters it files with the International Telecommunications Union.

SpaceX asked the FCC to waive its rule requiring the atmospheric disposal of dead satellites orbiting at 2,000 km or less.

Elon Musk’s company asked for “flexibility to dispose satellites operating above 600 km altitude into Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.”.

The FCC found SpaceX did not provide enough information to let it assess if proposed “alternative disposal methods” are compliant with regulations, so deferred its decision on the waiver request.

“SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules,” the order states. The firm must also file twice-yearly reports about “conjunction events” – moments when its satellites get dangerously close to each other, or other orbiters.

Whether orbiting datacenters are feasible, make sense, or will ever pay for themselves, remain open questions.

Analyst firm Gartner has described the idea as “peak insanity.”.

According to recent reports, google thinks orbiting datacenters become viable if launch costs fall to $200/kg, which would mean SpaceX needs to launch its massive Starship 1,800 times. SpaceX’s assumptions assume near-daily introduces, far better than its current cadence of a launch every three days or so.

Fundamental networking research must also come to fruition to handle the amount of traffic large constellations of orbiting datacenters will create.

Terrestrial manufacturing capacity will also need to increase to build all those satellites. Elon Musk’s companies and Intel have planned a giant newly introduced fab to make that possible, without explaining how the supply chains behind chip manufacturing will scale to make it feasible. That's a notable omission given that semiconductor supply chains are already extremely strained.

Approval for SpaceX is therefore nice but in no way a roadmap to a million datacenter satellites.

Google, ironically, is a little further along than SpaceX, having debuted a test sat in October and last week announcing it has hired Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch a larger satellite carrying the equivalent of a full datacenter rack in early 2029.

In a recent development, down on Earth, meanwhile, scientists trying to observe the universe continue to bemoan the obstructions caused by mega-constellations of broadband-beaming satellites. Proposals from across the USA, China, Europe and India presently call for around 100,000 satellites. SpaceX’s proposed million orbiters could run workloads which help us to understand the mysteries of the universe while also making them hard to see from down here. ®.
