AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post demonstrates you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Sources indicate that meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that aims, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Sources indicate that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the latest modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

According to recent reports, the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

Recent findings suggest that A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

In a recent development, the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

According to recent reports, the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

In a recent development, <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

Sources indicate that we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

In a recent development, once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Industry observers note that note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/newly introduced/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

Sources indicate that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

Industry observers note that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Recent findings suggest that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

Sources indicate that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

According to recent reports, we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

Sources indicate that we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

According to recent reports, we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Industry observers note that hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

bp has hired Wipro to help redesign its core finance operations using artificial intelligence, automation and changes to how work is done. Under the strategic supplier agreement, around 3,000 bp employees who support finance operations in India, Hungary and Malaysia are expected to move to Wipro. The companies expect the new operating model to take effect in 2027, subject to applicable conditions.

The move combines a technology program with a significant transfer of staff. Wipro will bring its finance and automation capabilities, while bp claims it will remain accountable for standards, controls, data and technology governance. PwC will provide controls oversight, according to bp’s November 25 announcement. The companies did not disclose the agreement’s value, quantify expected savings or detail which workflows would use AI first.

In a recent development, for bp, the partnership is part of an effort to simplify how it runs its finance operations and improve its long-term cost competitiveness. Chief financial officer Kate Thomson pointed to Wipro’s digital capabilities and investment as reasons for the move. Wipro CEO Srini Pallia cited the experience of the employees joining Wipro as well as the provider’s AI capabilities. The announcement describes a planned transfer of employees, not a reported reduction in headcount.

In a recent development, keeping accountability at bp matters because running a process and deciding what it is allowed to do are distinct jobs. A supplier can change how a team handles routine items, but bp still has to determine who may access finance data, what requires approval and how work can be audited. PwC’s oversight role adds another layer, although bp did not describe the scope of that oversight or how it will be conducted.

The handover also makes continuity key. Staff who know the existing systems can help identify which processes really follow a standard sequence and which rely on local judgment. That distinction affects what can be automated. A rule that works for routine transactions can create more work if it sends unusual items to the wrong person or makes the evidence for a decision harder to retrieve.

Wipro’s finance and accounting practice covers work ranging from paying suppliers and collecting customer payments to closing the books and producing reports. Its finance transformation practice also describes combining enterprise resource planning systems with automation, AI and data. Those services give a sense of the tools Wipro can bring to the engagement; they do not establish that bp has selected any specific products or workflows.

Invoice processing illustrates why the distinction matters. A system can extract information from invoices and send mismatches to the right queue. A person can then investigate an unexpected amount or a missing purchase order before releasing a payment. Used this way, AI can help prepare work for review without gaining the authority to make a payment. The same principle applies when a tool summarizes exceptions for a finance team preparing to close the books: someone still needs to verify the underlying entries.

Recent findings suggest that for a program this size, the useful measures will be operational. Faster invoice processing is meaningful only if error rates and the backlog of unusual items also improve. A shorter financial close matters more if teams can still explain adjustments and reproduce their audit trail. The companies haven’t published baselines or targets on those measures, so there are no results yet against which to judge the changes.

The 2027 transition will show whether Wipro can improve the day-to-day work while bp maintains control over the decisions that affect its financial records. That balance, rather than the number of tools added, is the more useful test of what AI contributes to the partnership.

Tech Report: Ansible Fails waiting for privilege escalation on Ubuntu 26

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (366 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jeffgeerling

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've slowly been moving my servers from Ubuntu 22 and 24 to 26 this year, and noticed my Ansible automation starts failing if I have password protection for sudo use:.
  • Apparently Ubuntu's been rewriting system utilities in Rust, and the sudo-rs version that ships on Ubuntu 26.04 has some incompatiblities with the sudo I've used on servers for 20+ years.
  • It prints an extra string before the password prompt, which sudo doesn't do, and that can confuse automation tools like Ansible that wait for a specific prompt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've slowly been moving my servers from Ubuntu 22 and 24 to 26 this year, and noticed my Ansible automation starts failing if I have password protection for sudo use:.

Apparently Ubuntu's been rewriting system utilities in Rust, and the sudo-rs version that ships on Ubuntu 26.04 has some incompatiblities with the sudo I've used on servers for 20+ years.

It prints an extra string before the password prompt, which sudo doesn't do, and that can confuse automation tools like Ansible that wait for a specific prompt.

Sources indicate that there's a thread in the Ansible project covering the problem: validate sudo become plugin against sudo-rs . The fix landed in Ansible Core 2.22.0, and is being backported into updates in 2.16, 2.18, 2.19, 2.20, and maybe also 2.21 (it's quite disruptive!). It looks like it also broke pyinfra, and their fix is in the latest release of 3.11.

I updated Ansible (pip install -U ansible) and now -K (--ask-become-pass) works again.

Another alternative is to use the traditional version of sudo that still ships with Ubuntu 26. For that, the easiest way is to set the become_exe inside your hosts file:.

Or you could even revert sudo systemwide on your Ubuntu host:.

Recent findings suggest that I'm not sure why Ubuntu sees the need to rewrite common Linux utils in Rust. I don't mind Rust, but these are foundational tools every Linux system relies on. This isn't a window manager, where experimentation is more acceptable1.

If other distros plan on moving to sudo-rs that's one thing, but if it's just Ubuntu, maybe I should hop back to Debian for everything, and not just my cloud servers.

Yes, I know this makes me sound like "old man yells at [rust]," but major changes to structural components of Linux should take longer, IMO. At least on the Red Hat side, we have Fedora, which is more bleeding edge, then at least a few years' gap before it hits 'production' systems. With Ubuntu, there is no cutting edge upstream where things like this can be fixed or worked around before hitting prod! (And no, I don't consider non-LTS Ubuntu releases the same thing.) ↩︎.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Expiring IPv6 routes can bring affected systems down, though corrective update doesn't require a restart.
  • Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security patch that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.
  • Recent findings suggest that the patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expiring IPv6 routes can bring affected systems down, though corrective update doesn't require a restart.

Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security patch that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.

Recent findings suggest that the patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes. When a route timer expires, affected servers can halt with error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE).

Issued on November 25, the corrective update takes effect without requiring a restart, according to Microsoft.

KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE means the kernel has detected corruption of a critical data structure and stopped the system. Microsoft has identified route-timer expiry as the trigger but hasn't explained the underlying coding fault.

Recent findings suggest that good to see the operating system being protected against the impact of the corruption. Less good for administrators wondering why their servers have suddenly misbehaved.

It has been revealed that lansweeper puts Windows Server 2025 at 7 percent of the servers it monitors, compared with 32 percent for Server 2022 and 33 percent for Server 2019. Only systems with the affected hotpatch and networking configuration are implicated.

Microsoft's Windows Server updates have not gone well over the last few months, with out-of-band updates issued in September, October, and November. An out-of-band upgrade to deal with a problem introduced in a hotpatch (in this case, KB5131077) therefore carries with it a certain sense of inevitability.

Sources indicate that hotpatches are a way of getting OS security updates on a Windows Server without requiring a restart and so are, in theory, a boon for administrators keen on maximizing uptime. According to Microsoft, in addition to faster installations and better protection, there is "lower workload impact with less need to restart your machine.".

In a recent development, avoiding a planned restart is less of a selling point when the alternative is an unplanned crash. ®.

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

It has been revealed that we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. Latest contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

According to recent reports, rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All upcoming data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Recent findings suggest that alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

In a recent development, while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

According to recent reports, we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

According to recent reports, apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

Recent findings suggest that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Industry observers note that structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Industry observers note that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Recent findings suggest that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been confirmed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Industry observers note that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In a recent development, in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

  • Industry observers note that titanium Innovations Investments participated alongside CSL Ventures, which led Mechademy’s seed financing.
  • It has been revealed that the expansion is aimed at utilities and independent power producers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, houston-based Mechademy noted in a November 25, 2026 announcement that it had completed a $9.5 million Series A led by Silverton Partners to expand its industrial AI platform from oil and gas facilities into power generation. The round closed earlier in 2026.

Industry observers note that titanium Innovations Investments participated alongside CSL Ventures, which led Mechademy’s seed financing. Total capital raised, including the Series A, stands at more than $12.5 million.

It has been revealed that the expansion is aimed at utilities and independent power producers. Mechademy attributes the opportunity to rising U.S. electricity demand from data centers, AI, electrification and industrial reshoring, together with multi-year delivery backlogs and higher prices for upcoming gas turbines. Its pitch is that operators need greater availability and efficiency from turbines they already own while new equipment remains difficult to secure.

It has been revealed that turbomechanica applies AI to critical rotating machinery, using live plant data and an asset-specific physics model of expected machine behavior. Machine learning identifies departures from that baseline, and a diagnostic engine maintained by Mechademy’s turbomachinery specialists turns the findings into maintenance recommendations.

Mechademy says its use of simulation-based transfer learning cuts the amount of historical plant data required to model a newly introduced asset, while connections to existing data historians and monitoring systems let plants retain their current data infrastructure.

The company reports detection on customer machines of declining performance, abnormal vibration, problems with dry gas seals and motor insulation, and gas contamination. These findings often came months ahead of failure and, in some cases, involved faults that other monitoring providers working on the same equipment did not identify.

Industry observers note that the platform covers gas and steam turbines, centrifugal, reciprocating and screw compressors, expanders, pumps and motors. Mechademy right now serves LNG, oil and gas and process-industry operators. Chief Product Officer Mark Weatherwax has more than three decades of turbomachinery experience, became a Chevron Fellow in 2019 and worked on the Wheatstone and Gorgon LNG developments in Australia.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, to untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, âmake the initiative a valueâ or âdecide what to do, and then do itâ.
  • Industry observers note that I really like this pattern because the âdeciding what to doâ part of a program is often more complicated than the âdoingâ part.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client token support provided by AWS. Implementing this required making some fairly substantial changes to the generator, the bespoke Haskell program that turns the service definitions in botocore into cabal packages. amazonka is over a decade old, and the generator has evolved as AWS have added upcoming styles of APIs for their different services. Some services return XML, some return JSON, some return raw bytes, some return additional information in HTTP response headers, and so on. As a result, the generatorâs logic had been extended each time and had grown gnarly.

In a recent development, to untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, âmake the initiative a valueâ or âdecide what to do, and then do itâ. This move decouples two parts of a program by introducing an intermediate data structure (a âplanâ, or a value of a âplan typeâ) describing what is to be done before any action is taken.

Industry observers note that I really like this pattern because the âdeciding what to doâ part of a program is often more complicated than the âdoingâ part. Separating the two often turns the âdecidingâ part into a pure function that produces a plan, making test cases simpler to write. And then if the âdoingâ phase is also complicated (because of remote API calls, rollbacks, parallel execution, or whatever else), itâs more manageable because those complications are not entangled with the planning logic. You also get to add a --dry-run flag almost for free, which is really useful for testing. (Henrik observes that testing for a dryRun variable everywhere pollutes the code somewhat. I think if he split his code into a planning phase and consumed that plan with either a âdry runâ printer or a ârealâ executor, the inline checks that he dislikes would disappear.).

Industry observers note that this technique isnât subtle or obscure. Iâve seen it called the initiative-execute pattern, and the ârouting slipâ enterprise integration pattern is literally about centralising the decision logic before execution. Iâve previously called it a âtiny DSLâ, and Matt Parsons sells its benefits in his Three Layer Haskell Cake article:.

In a recent development, having resolved to introduce a plan type, how do we work it into a venerable program like the Amazonka generator? For this part of the generator, it means separating the analysis of the loaded service definitions from the generation of the instance AWSRequest declarations. I did this by introducing a Config record of simple data and a function instanceD :: Config -> Decl () that builds Haskell code from that config record.

According to recent reports, I found the generatorâs logic too difficult to understand and replace in a single change, so I replaced it incrementally using the strangler fig pattern. The most complicated part of this change was response parsing, so I added to the Config record an enumeration of ported response parsers, and a fall back to âdo things the old wayâ for everything else:.

It has been revealed that one thing that makes Amazonkaâs generator rewarding to hack on is that the service bindings act as an extensive and automatic golden test suite. Any changes to the generated bindings show up in diffs, and so if there are no diffs and the generator doesnât crash, the change probably didnât break anything. This makes the process of replacing the entangled code relatively simple (not easy):.

According to recent reports, the end result worked well and kept the individual commits readable (example: factoring out status code parsing). Adding the idempotency machinery was then straightforward.

The data types in the Amazonka example represent parameters to a Haskell code template, but this refactoring also works for more expressive proposal types, such as âtiny DSLsâ, âlists of commandsâ, or âfree structuresâ. The trick is to keep a âdo it the old wayâ constructor in your plan type until the âold wayâ has been refactored away.

A well-chosen proposal type introduces a narrow waist that decouples producers and consumers of your plan type, and the most obvious wins come from introducing alternate consumers of the plan: things like testability, --dry-run, and simpler executors all follow from that. A less obvious benefit is that you can also analyse and transform the plan itself. This is a great place to add pre-execution sanity checks or access controls. I regret that my tiny DSLs post inverted a transformation by interpreting it as matrix multiplications and inverting the result; it would have been simpler to provide an invert :: [Transform] -> [Transform] function.

Introducing alternate producers of the strategy type can also pay off, but needs a bit more imagination:.

It has been revealed that âMaking the proposal a valueâ works well in any language, but Haskellâs laziness makes it especially nice. Lazy evaluation can avoid materialising the whole plan in memory if it is consumed right away. Even in strict languages, the decoupling benefits are great enough that the extra memory use is often worth it.

  • The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.

UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.

The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.

Sources indicate that LEPs brought together councils and businesses to promote economic growth in England under a coalition government initiative launched in 2010. Central government funding ended in April 2024, with their core functions transferred to local and combined authorities.

Sources indicate that among other things, Digital Royalty builds and looks after websites, which means chasing down old links. In August, it found that a link on Surrey County Council's website led to a former LEP address now displaying casino content. It went looking for more.

Digital Royalty founder Alex De Sousa said: "Slow is usually a sign of caution and diligence, but 31 months after the LEPs wound up, it's crossed into inefficient and dangerous.".

Sources indicate that the consultancy offered The Register four examples of websites run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), Hull City Council, Parliament, and the Local Government Association. One example is a government page about the Digital Skills Partnership, originally published under an earlier incarnation of DCMS.

The page includes a link that appears to be for the Humber Digital Skills Partnership within the Humber LEP website, but in fact takes customers to a site advertising "Independent Non GamStop Casinos UK – New Casino Sites Outside GamStop." GamStop is the self-exclusion scheme designed to help people restrict their online gambling, which makes the links more concerning than ordinary website clutter.

The same link appears on the Hull City Council website under a list of Joint Committees, Partnerships and Trusts where it appears as Local Economic Partnership (Humber LEP).

An old page for the Parliament website detailing the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy committee's Industrial Strategy report includes a footnote (135) that appears to be for the Business Central funding finder service, but takes the user to the "Highest RTP Non GamStop Casinos for UK Players.".

Sources indicate that the Local Government Association's (LGA) sustainability and waste route map included a link to the former York and North Yorkshire LEP website. The destination initially appeared legitimate but contained links promoting crypto casinos. The LGA now appears to have removed the link.

All the organizations mentioned have been contacted by The Register to offer them the opportunity to comment.

Digital Royalty checked former web addresses associated with about 70 LEPs and growth hubs, then used a backlink index to identify roughly 3,000 incoming links from public sector sites. Most were simply outdated rather than leading to gambling content.

Recent findings suggest that the findings are not exhaustive: the index may miss pages, and the research did not cover other types of defunct public body whose domains may have been repurposed. ®.

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR After Three-Year Migration.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub has published an in-depth account of a three-year effort to move github.com off CSS-in-JS and onto CSS Modules, reporting a 55% reduction in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer-powered design system.

Written by Primer engineers Josh Black and Marie Lucca, the post explains how component counts on certain pages began to explode in 2023, exposing scaling problems with the existing styled-components setup. Initial page loads, server render times and style update costs all grew with component count. The team picked CSS Modules because it kept native CSS features and co-location while removing client and server runtime work, letting styles roll up into static stylesheets delivered with the HTML.

In a recent development, for every Primer component the team added a CSS Modules variant, gated it behind a feature flag, verified parity with visual regression tests, then rolled it out from the Primer team to GitHub staff and finally all users. By December 2024, Primer itself was fully on CSS Modules. The harder half was the roughly 7,760 sx prop usages scattered across github.com, the de facto styling standard for years. A transitional @primer/styled-react package let sx keep working against migrated components during the crossover.

A typical conversion looks like this:.

According to recent reports, A rotation of eight engineers migrated 6,419 props over six months, seeing SSR improvements ranging from 3% up to 22% per page. The final 895 props were cleared in three weeks by two engineers leaning heavily on Copilot coding agents. GitHub also had to decouple theming for its seven themes and high-contrast variants before pulling styled-components out entirely. A VS Code plugin and internal codemod cut the manual burden, and GitHub notes that styled-components entering maintenance mode reinforced the direction.

Industry observers note that on Hacker News one commenter running a similar migration reported a 30% build time speed improvement and much better tree shaking on Next.js across a codebase over 1M lines. Others were sceptical about user impact, with one arguing that the reduction in size was not massive enough to justify making all CSS names unreadable, adding that hashed class names make ad-blockers, custom CSS and browser extensions harder to build. A separate thread noted that CSS-in-JS can be made zero-runtime without moving to Modules at all.

According to recent reports, gitHub joins a broader shift away from runtime CSS-in-JS. Linear recently completed its own 1,000-PR move from styled-components to Meta's atomic StyleX library, citing similar render-time concerns after upgrading to React 18's concurrent mode. Others using vanilla-extract or Tailwind have shifted style generation to build time entirely. The common thread is to pay the cost once at build, not on every request.

The Primer Design System is GitHub's open-source component library, providing the foundational building blocks used across github.com. Teams following the same path can start from the Primer React v38 release notes and the migration guide for CSS variables, which covers the move from sx props to CSS Modules.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • It has been revealed that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the latest US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

It has been revealed that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

It has been revealed that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

According to recent reports, beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

It has been revealed that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

In a recent development, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

Sources indicate that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Recent findings suggest that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Sources indicate that hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

Recent findings suggest that A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

According to recent reports, beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

According to recent reports, pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Sources indicate that beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

It has been revealed that beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

In a recent development, both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Industry observers note that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

In a recent development, on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

It has been revealed that * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

Sources indicate that you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

Recent findings suggest that the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Industry observers note that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Recent findings suggest that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can patch the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

In a recent development, sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

It has been revealed that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

According to recent reports, evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

It has been revealed that the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Recent findings suggest that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

In a recent development, if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Recent findings suggest that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

According to recent reports, we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Sources indicate that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

It has been revealed that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

Sources indicate that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

In a recent development, our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

It has been revealed that decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

Recent findings suggest that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

It has been revealed that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Industry observers note that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tempus AI entered a senior secured credit agreement on November 25, 2026, providing $385 million of term-loan commitments and $115 million of revolving commitments to help finance its pending Personalis acquisition, according to its Form 8-K.

It has been revealed that in a separate November 24, 2026 decision, Tempus elected to pay approximately $600 million in cash and issue approximately $900 million in Tempus Class A common stock to Personalis shareholders. These are financing commitments, not evidence that the full amounts have already been drawn. Initial funding requires the acquisition to have closed or be reasonably expected to close within one business day after funding.

Tempus expects borrowings to fund part of the acquisition consideration and related transaction costs, as well as working capital and general corporate purposes. Ares Capital Corporation is the administrative and collateral agent, Ares Capital Management LLC the lead arranger and bookrunner, and ACF Finco I LP the revolving agent.

According to recent reports, term loans bear interest at either the agreement’s Base Rate benchmark plus 4.50% or its Term SOFR benchmark plus 5.50%; revolving loans use Base Rate plus 2.75% or Term SOFR plus 3.75%. Term SOFR has a 1.00% floor, the Base Rate a 2.00% floor, and interest on the loans is payable solely in cash.

Both facilities mature on the fifth anniversary of the effective date. A springing provision can move maturity to 91 days before Tempus’s 0.75% convertible senior notes due 2030 unless those notes are repaid or converted first or specified liquidity requirements are met.

Certain Tempus subsidiaries will guarantee the obligations, which are secured by substantially all assets of Tempus and those subsidiaries. The agreement includes minimum-liquidity and minimum-revenue covenants. Revolving availability depends on eligible accounts receivable and certain qualified cash, subject to reserves and other limitations, and revolving interest can be charged on a minimum balance even when actual borrowings are lower.

It has been revealed that the cash election uses flexibility described in Tempus’s July 20, 2026 acquisition announcement. The merger agreement priced Personalis at $16.25 per common share, representing approximately $1.5 billion in enterprise value net of Tempus’s existing ownership. Consideration was originally structured as all stock, with Tempus holding an option to pay cash capped at 50% of the consideration and a floating exchange ratio capped at 0.3356 Tempus shares per Personalis share.

According to recent reports, the cash estimate assumes 108,740,631 Personalis shares outstanding immediately before closing and no perfected appraisal demands. The number of shares designated for cash can automatically decrease, with a corresponding increase in the stock portion, to satisfy the merger agreement’s reorganization threshold, determined using Tempus’s closing-date trading price.

Tempus states the acquisition pairs its multimodal data, AI capabilities and commercial infrastructure with Personalis’s tumor-informed molecular residual disease (MRD) technology, including the NeXT Personal test, which detects small traces of circulating tumor DNA to monitor treatment response, residual cancer and recurrence.

According to recent reports, the transaction builds on a partnership established in November 2023, through which Tempus invested in Personalis and commercialized NeXT Personal. Tempus CEO Eric Lefkofsky called MRD “a large and rapidly growing market” and said the collaboration had demonstrated the strength of combining Personalis’s technology with his company’s commercial infrastructure.

Tempus originally expected the acquisition to close in late 2026 or early 2027. Closing remains subject to Personalis stockholder adoption of the merger agreement and other customary conditions. Tempus has now aligned the debt package with its cash-and-stock election, but the borrowing timetable and the proposed AI-supported MRD expansion both remain tied to completion of the acquisition.

Company was religious about backups but sinned by leaving them exposed

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (468 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.
  • Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account.
  • Industry observers note that our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a firm that provides data protection and recovery software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.

Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

Industry observers note that our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a firm that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

Industry observers note that however, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.

Recent findings suggest that so the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.

Industry observers note that “Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”.

Industry observers note that have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

It has been revealed that the results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his manufacturer to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

According to recent reports, li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®.
