📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fireworks AI made Tencent’s open-weight Hy4 Flash available on its serverless API on November 25, 2026, pricing the Standard tier at $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens. The announcement adds benchmark tests that position the model as a low-cost option for professional and agentic work.

Sources indicate that cached input costs $0.003 per million tokens. A Priority tier is also available, and the service is served globally. Developers can instead use on-demand dedicated GPUs; the Hy4 Flash model page lists function calling as supported and fine-tuning and embeddings as unsupported.

Recent findings suggest that hy4 Flash uses a mixture-of-experts design, in which only about 12 billion of its roughly 220 billion parameters are active for each token. It accepts text and image input. The native context window is 1M tokens, while Fireworks is serving 512K at launch, a material constraint for applications built around very long documents or extended agent sessions.

Tencent introduced Hy4 Flash on November 16, 2026, as its most cost-effective Hy model for everyday productivity and released the weights on GitHub, Hugging Face, ModelScope, and AtomGit. Tencent says reinforcement learning reduced average end-to-end output tokens by 50%, while megakernels, 4-bit quantization, and DFly lifted decoding speed beyond 150 tokens per second.

It has been revealed that fireworks reports testing the model on seven professional benchmarks with the same harness used for other models on each leaderboard, at high reasoning. Costs are based on recorded tokens at Fireworks’ serverless prices, and the results are dated November 22, 2026. Hy4 Flash reached the score-cost Pareto frontier on every board where cost was recorded, meaning no listed model delivered a higher score at a lower cost.

It has been revealed that fireworks’ run of Epiq’s CorporateBench, which tests questions across thousands of internal firm emails and meeting notes, produced a 75.9% score for Hy4 Flash: sixth of 14 models and slightly above Claude Opus 5.5’s 75.4%. The respective costs were $0.013 and $2.80 per task.

Rogo’s Substantial Finance Benchmark produced a 49.2% tie with Claude Opus 5 in Fireworks’ tests, at $0.0065 per task for Hy4 Flash versus $1.83 for Opus 5. Hy4 Flash also placed above Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro, which each scored 48.2%. GPT-6 Luna was the only cheaper model on that board, but scored 35.3%.

According to recent reports, on Sierra’s τ³-Banking agent benchmark, Fireworks reports a 49.2% score for Hy4 Flash against 49.1% for Claude Opus 5. The cost was $0.012 per trial versus $2.59. Across all boards where it recorded cost, Fireworks found Hy4 Flash was the lowest-cost model except on Big Finance.

Sources indicate that fireworks’ rankings were weaker elsewhere: Hy4 Flash placed 16th of 18 models on HealthBench Professional and 19th of 22 on DeepSWE. Tencent recommends the larger Hy4 for long-horizon software engineering because of its higher intelligence ceiling, reinforcing that the cost results do not establish uniform superiority across professional work.

Before opening the endpoint, Fireworks ran Hy4 Flash through its launch-validation suite on FireAttention, its inference engine, and compared the results with Tencent’s official endpoint. The manufacturer reports that every score came within one point of Tencent’s. The Fireworks results were:.

The deployment’s appeal is therefore workload-specific: Fireworks’ tests pair near-parity with Claude Opus on selected professional tasks with much lower recorded costs, while the reduced hosted context and weaker health and software results set clear limits. Validation against Tencent’s endpoint gives developers a direct reference point for assessing whether Fireworks’ serving configuration preserves the model’s expected behavior.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, torchNeuron provides a latest native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • It has been revealed that starting Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, torchNeuron provides a latest native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

It has been revealed that starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron people use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Recent findings suggest that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

Sources indicate that the command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

According to recent reports, many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

In a recent development, make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, customers can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, S&P Global Ratings placed NVIDIA’s AA issuer credit rating and AA senior unsecured debt rating on CreditWatch with negative implications on November 25, 2026, citing concerns about board independence, executive oversight and succession planning. The agency remarked it could downgrade NVIDIA within 90 days if further due diligence finds that governance deficiencies remain.

In a recent development, the ratings were affirmed, with CreditWatch marking a review for a possible downgrade. The issuer rating moved from AA/Stable/A-1+ to AA/Watch Neg/A-1+, while the senior unsecured rating moved from AA to AA/Watch Neg. NVIDIA’s A-1+ commercial paper rating was affirmed separately.

It has been revealed that the concerns center on the board’s structure, composition and effectiveness. S&P stated events involving the CEO and questions about potential export-control violations exposed those weaknesses; the CEO’s departure and later reinstatement did not resolve its questions about oversight of the executive code of conduct. Weak executive oversight and a lack of succession planning also sharpened key-person concerns.

In S&P’s assessment, long director tenures may have compromised independence, while governance practices may have lagged NVIDIA’s rapid expansion and growing importance in global technology infrastructure. The agency revised the management-and-governance modifier used in its credit analysis to neutral from positive and was unaware of any remedial board action addressing the potential deficiencies.

S&P intends to meet NVIDIA’s board and management to discuss board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession strategy. It expects any downgrade to be limited to one notch unless investigations or disclosures indicate harm to NVIDIA’s reputation or future business prospects.

Sources indicate that export controls form a separate part of the assessment. NVIDIA’s China exposure raises questions about geopolitical risk management and internal controls, in S&P’s view. A conclusion that export-control rules were circumvented or violated, or that past disclosures about exposure to China and nearby regions were misleading or understated, would weigh on overall credit quality.

For now, S&P’s assessments of NVIDIA’s competitive position, technology leadership and financial profile remain unchanged. S&P mentioned stricter export controls could reduce future growth prospects, while its published scores still classify business risk as strong, competitive position as excellent, financial risk as minimal and liquidity as exceptional, with an aa stand-alone credit profile.

Sources indicate that the credit profile rests on a business S&P describes as data-center-scale AI infrastructure. Its platform covers chips, networking, systems and software for model training and inference, data analytics, scientific computing, robotics and 3D graphics. Compute and networking generated 90% of revenue in the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, while graphics generated 10%. Its core end markets are data center, gaming, professional visualization and automotive.

Sources indicate that the review therefore separates NVIDIA’s operating and financial strength from the governance controls around it. S&P is testing whether board oversight and succession planning have kept pace with the firm’s role in AI infrastructure; adverse export-control or disclosure findings could broaden the concern to its reputation and business prospects.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.
  • The Australian uranium producer stated on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peninsula Energy notes plant and wellfield control systems were affected, with no restart date yet.

Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.

The Australian uranium producer stated on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.

Peninsula Energy noted it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected.

"The manufacturer's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an patch to the Australian Securities Exchange.

The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing.

Industry observers note that peninsula has not given a restart date and notes it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it mentioned.

The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site.

According to recent reports, the November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's revision clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time.

Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance.

Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈.

Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors.

The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb.

Peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®.

#207027. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and fresh Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the significant matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Recent findings suggest that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

According to recent reports, in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The latest Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel reveals up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

According to recent reports, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

According to recent reports, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them newly introduced paths through Metal:.

In a recent development, token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Sources indicate that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

In a recent development, you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

In a recent development, work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

It has been revealed that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

According to recent reports, pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers face frantic scramble to migrate workloads and rotate compromised credentials.

Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.

In a recent development, in a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz said its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8. Any workloads still running at that point will be terminated, and customers will no longer be able to access their data.

Industry observers note that "Following the recent security incident affecting Rackspace Spot, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the service," the company stated. "Spot customers are being notified with the wind-down timeline, instructions for retrieving their data and steps to secure their environments.".

Customers will have to contend with the fallout from the breach while simultaneously trying to get their applications and data off the platform.

Industry observers note that according to a customer notification seen by The Register, the attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot over a period of almost 22 hours on November 17. Rackspace only learned of the intrusion the following day, after a customer raised the alarm.

The intruders impersonated legitimate users, created pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, gained access to stored credentials known as Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and storage volumes.

"With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held," Rackspace told customers.

Rackspace has since revoked the affected tokens and sessions, removed the pods planted by the intruders, and changed the affected platform and storage keys. Customers must also reissue API tokens, download new Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their clusters, including database passwords and third-party API keys.

Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and chief growth officer of Platform9, which co-developed Spot with Rackspace, shed some light on the root cause in a November 20 GitHub post.

"An observability system was breached using a compromised credential," Raghuram wrote. "This was obviously a critical error on our part and we are very sorry we let this happen.".

Raghuram stated the incident necessitated significant changes to the underlying infrastructure clusters, prolonging the outage.

In a recent development, spot's selling point was cheap compute. The service operated an auction-based pricing model, allowing customers to bid for cloud infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of conventional on-demand instances. Rackspace advertised savings of up to 90 percent for customers willing to tolerate interruptions to their workloads. A permanent interruption probably wasn't what they had in mind.

Rackspace hasn't explained why it chose closure over recovery, revealed how many customers were affected, or mentioned whether it will offer migration extensions. It did not respond to The Register's questions. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Sources indicate that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Sources indicate that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Sources indicate that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too significant to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

It has been revealed that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Industry observers note that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

According to recent reports, language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Donsz

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0.
  • This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.
  • And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can promptly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:.

The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

According to recent reports, many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here, and here.

It has been revealed that my work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team.

Industry observers note that on the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0. Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a upcoming trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Industry observers note that chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md indicates it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual new subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

Industry observers note that the goal of the latest trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero", referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one, that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed. Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Recent findings suggest that note: Chalk and the latest trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

According to recent reports, but what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

Sources indicate that the first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide". It indicates "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.". But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties. For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality. To codify these properties, we can use traits. In other words, a trait is a property of a type.

Notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties. The standard library's definition of Clone also includes two methods that can be called to perform this cloning operation.

In a recent development, to check whether the code you wrote is correct, the Rust compiler sometimes has to check that these properties hold. If you're trying to clone a value, the compiler has to check whether that value can be cloned.

Recent findings suggest that prolog is a cool programming language that works and looks very differently to what you may be used to. However, it is just as powerful (i.e. turing complete) as any other. The way it works has strong parallels to our trait system, let me show you. Here's an example:.

A Prolog program consists of a set of statements, called "facts", as well as relationships between facts. In the above program, there are two facts: u64 has the property Copy, String has the property Clone, And there's also a relationship between these two properties. If some variable x has the Copy property, it also has the Clone property.

Finally, we can ask the prolog program some questions. For example, Does the type u64 have the Clone property? To answer that question, the runtime of a prolog program has to analyze all the known facts and relations. In this program we haven't said that u64 has the Clone property. However, we have said that it has the Copy property. And by using the relationship between Copy and Clone, the solver can derive that both questions (starting with ?-) are true!

The reason Chalk was using a "prolog-like" solver, is because as you can see, the trait system is extremely similar to a logic solver. Both "facts" and "relations" can be written using impl blocks. In fact, I can write the above program as a Rust program:.

Neither the upcoming solver or the old solver state as plainly as chalk does that they're using a "prolog-like solver". However, given the similarities, both the old solver and the new solver really aren't so different from how you'd implement a prolog runtime.

Sources indicate that trait solving is not the same as type inference. This is a common misconception. Inside the Rust compiler, the two are completely different subsystems. Type inference is the process of replacing blanks with types. Throughout this text I'll refer to some the following example code (with slight variations):.

We use type inference to determine that the type of the variable a is an integer. The same for b.

Industry observers note that having remarked that, sometimes during type inference we do have to ask things about traits, and will call into the trait solver. Furthermore, the trait solver sometimes "unifies type variables", which means that while Rust makes a query about traits, we might make some progress on figuring out what the types of some variables are.

In the example code, one place where the trait solver comes into effect is when we call weird_add. On the function there's a where bound. A where bound is a requirement that the Rust compiler must check before allowing a call to that function. In this case, Rust has to make sure that i32 (a type we found through type inference) implements the Add trait. To do that, the solver can use one of a couple of strategies, and we'll look at each. In this case, we'll be looking for an impl block that mentions the i32 type, and we'll find one of those in the standard library!

Industry observers note that once the trait solver finds this impl block, it acts as an answer to the question "does i32 implement Add?". We somtimes refer to this answer as a a proof that the statement holds.

The example code contains several more calls to the trait solver. One you may not have thought about is that all local variables in Rust have to implement the Sized trait to be allowed on the stack. The Sized trait codifies that the compiler knows how many bytes of memory the value takes up, so it can be allocated on the stack. So, there will also be a query to the trait solver asking "does i32 implement Sized?".

The proof for this statement doesn't come from an impl block though. I did say that the compiler has several stratagies to derive proofs. In this case, the fact that some primitive types implement Sized is built-in to the compiler. i32 is inherently Sized, and there is no impl block anywhere that says so.

According to recent reports, answering Sized queries in general turns out to be quite hard because of the shear volume at which it occurs. To compile rust's standard library, we'll ask "does type implement Sized?" about 800 000 times! Additionally, answering it isn't always this simple. Let's take a slightly more involved example:.

To prove Kitten: Sized, a recursive process takes place. Both fields have to implement Sized too. So in the process of answering this question, the trait solver will produce more questions to be answered. Kitten: Sized leads to String: Sized & f64: Sized. f64 luckily is trivial again, and built into the compiler. String isn't though, and we go one more layer deeper to Vec: Sized, etcetera.

Sources indicate that in Rust, generic functions can be type checked standalone. The example using weird_add doesn't need a main function to be checked, and may emit its own type errors.

It has been revealed that this is where the trait solver actually does the most work. For example, to type check weird_add, we have to prove that a + b is valid. a + b desugars to a.add(b), and when finding the method add the trait solver gets invoked, since the add method comes from the Add trait.

Previously, proof candidates came either from impl blocks or they were built into the compiler. Not here though! A upcoming proof strategy is used here instead. When calling weird_add we saw that a where bound acts as a requirement that has to be checked before calling, but that means that inside weird_add we can assume that where bound holds and thus it acts as a proof strategy. Concretely, we know a has the type T, and to answer the question "does T implement Add" we find a where bound that says so.

Add isn't the only trait bound that has to be proven inside weird_add. This is another place where we have to prove that T: Sized. Again we have to look for candidates, and there's no built in one for generic types T, nor is there an impl block, nor a where bound that mentions Sized. So how does that work? Well, it turns out the where bound is implicit. T: Add really means T: Add + Sized, and so proving Sized works the same as proving Add.

On lobsters I got asked about whether the Add bound is required to add the Sized bound. The T: Sized implicit bound gets added for any generic. Even if there was not already an Add bound, T would still be Sized. Currently, you can opt out of that implicit bound using T: ?Sized (or in the example, T: Add + ?Sized). In the future we may change the syntax for that to T: MetaSized. Look for the keyword "Sized Hierarchy" if you want to learn more. This document should also give you a primer.

Finally, this code will actually give a type error, because there's one more trait to prove. Because b gets mentioned twice, we have to clone or copy values of type T. The function signature really should have been:.

Recent findings suggest that to summarize, trait solving is the process of answering questions about relations between types and traits. These questions are submitted to the trait solver, and the trait solver looks for candidates in the form of:.

When it finds one of these, we say we've found a proof, and if we cannot find one, a type error is emitted.

Sofar, all trait solving came down to finding a single candidate, but that's not always how it works. Let's look at the definition of the From and the Into traits:.

If the trait solver gets a question like u32: Into (does u32 implement the Into trait), it will find the impl block above. However, the impl block is generic, and has a where bound that states "T implements Into U IF U implements From T". Luckily there's another impl block that gives that implementation and so the initial statement can be proven.

According to recent reports, what this all means, is that while answering a question, the trait solver emits more questions. These subquestions get added to an internal queue in the trait solver, and this queue of questions will be proven one after the other. Like this, some questions can turn into several subquestions, which can even have their own subquestions again.

It has been revealed that also, in the example from above, the second question actually has two proofs! There are two impl blocks that apply, since there's also this blanket implementation for identity conversion:.

Recent findings suggest that some preference takes place here. Since this is a blanket implementation, the other more specific one takes precedence. We can think about the trait solving about answering a tree of candidates that may apply. In this case, the single candidate for u32: Into turns into two, u64: From and T: From.

Something we'll not cover today, but this tree of candidates in reality is not a tree, it can have cycles! This has been the cause of both many bugs, and many rust compiler developers' nightmares.

The trait solver doesn't just deal with traits. An notable thing it has to also consider is the associated types of traits. Let's look at the Add trait:.

It has been revealed that an implementation of the Add trait can decide what the Output type will be equal to. Remember the definition of Add for integers?

It has been revealed that it says that when you add two i32s, we get back an i32. The reason the trait solver cares about associated types is that sometimes answering questions creates subquestions that mention associated types.

Industry observers note that because we wrote Output = T, the trait solver has to check that the candidate impl block has an Output type that's equal to T. We could've also written a more general function signature to something like:.

Or really to make it works you have to go one step further (click to expand).

It has been revealed that hold on! impl blocks can define inputs they act on, like impl Foo for i32 applies when the input is i32. It can make these inputs variables, like impl Foo for T. And impl blocks can also define outputs thrugh associated types.

What we've done here, is make impl blocks powerful enough to act as functions, with inputs and outputs. And Alonzo Church proved that a language with only pure functions is in fact turing complete.

This is why Prolog is a fully-fledged turing complete programming language, and so is Rust's type system. People have defined numbers completely in Rust's type system in a crate called typenum, and have gone even further by implementing a chess engine inside the type system.

Trait solving ends up being a subsystem that the compiler spends quite a large portion of its time in. In general, there are two reasons for that:.

In a recent development, this ends up replacing the trait solver more complicated than you might think. People have already written many programs using the old solver, and because the upcoming solver internally makes different assumptions (sometimes in the name of soundness, remember the old solver has many bugs), we end up having programs that take both longer and shorter to compile. Sometimes with a polynomial factor, sometimes even with an exponential factor.

For example, the crate unic-ucd contains code along the lines of:.

Sources indicate that it lists a whole bunch of unicode characters, and each constant inside these slices are themselves string literals. That means each of them has an associated lifetime variable, that at some point gets inferred to 'static since we're assigning to a const. Now the fresh trait solver, in some cases where the old solver did not, reasons about lifetimes.

Now sometimes, the rust compiler attempts see if two types are equal. This process may have side effects, in that it may make some progress towards inferring other types in the program. Because these side effects are sometimes undesireable, we have a system to "attempt" to unify types, and then roll back the results. To be able to do rollbacks we sometimes keep a trace of all operations we perform, so we can run them in reverse to get back to where we started. However, sometimes this tracking is more expensive than simply making a copy of the state and putting that copy back.

In this case, during borrow checking, we call into the the trait solver and end up unifying two "lifetime variables", which we roll back. This specific rollback involves a copy, though there was a shortcut. We keep track of a single boolean: "was any lifetime variable modified". If none were, the rollback can be skipped. The old solver wouldn't do such unifications, so the rollback could always be skipped, while in the new solver we couldn't do so.

In a recent development, often, there are very few lifetime variables in scope, so doing a rollback isn't so bad. However, the example above lists every unicode character in existence, so the list is rather long. And for every item in the list, we'd do such a rollback, that copied all lifetime variables (for which there is one per element in the list). So N undos copying a list of N lifetime variables, that's a quadratic factor! So this crate would compile just fine with the old solver, and be 200 times slower with the fresh solver. Oops!

Industry observers note that there are two key strategies we use to make the trait solver faster. First of all, there's caching, and a lot of it. For example, in the following example we prove that i32: Sized three times:.

We'd like to make it so we only need to figure out whether a specific type is Sized once, and so we cache the result.

The second optimization we use a lot is not caching funnily enough. Accessing the cache can be rather expensive (we'll get to why). So in this case, since i32 is trivially Sized, we can answer the question faster by never looking in the cache. For more complicated types this is not true.

A naive cache would be a mapping from questions asked to the trait solver, to answers (errors or proofs). So, something like HashMap, but this wouldn't perform so well. Let's look at this example:.

Here we've renamed the variables T and U between foo and bar. We'll prove two question, that T: Into and later U: Into. Because of the renamings these two proofs are the same, but the questions are technically different. If we don't do something about variable renaming, we'd have cache misses all the time.

Industry observers note that another glitch is that this cache wouldn't even work. By now, we've learned that candidates for proofs can come from three sources:.

The first two play nicely, because the same impl blocks and compiler built-ins are around for all questions submitted to the trait solver. Howver, where bounds are different for every function, and thus a proof that a type implements a trait inside of one function, may not be reusable inside another function.

It has been revealed that in the example above, we prove that T: Into twice. Inside foo that's ok, but not inside of bar. So if we naively cached that T: Into we wouldn't notice that bar is incorrect.

It has been revealed that we call the set of bounds that are in-scope during trait solving the ParamEnv (parameter environment), and so the cache would really have to look like HashMap<(ParamEnv, Question), Answer>. Since for every function, the ParamEnv is different, we'd have even more cache misses.

According to recent reports, to improve our chances of a cache hit, we perform a process called "Canonicalization". During canonicalization, we do two things. First we'll rename all variables with numbers. So, T: Into will become ?0: Into (variable 0 implements Into variable 1). Since this process is consistent, another renamed input like U: Into also gets this numbering and is compatible.

In addition, we'll try very hard to figure out which where bounds in the ParamEnv actually matter. If there are bounds that won't affect the result of the query, we can avoid putting them in the cache key, making cache hits more likely.

So, in the rust compiler, the cache really looks more like a HashMap<(Paramenv, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer> Note that the answer of every query now has to be de-canonicalized. We call this "instantiation". When we turn T: Into into ?0: Into, and cache its result, and we later look for U: Into, we have to turn the answer (that mentions variables 0 and 1) into U and T respectively. In other words, by canonicalizing we make cache hits much more likely, but the process isn't free. Hence not caching is sometimes worth it for simple questions.

Sources indicate that now is this worth it? Below I've plotted the hit rate of the new solver's cache for various popular crates, and one internal rust compiler benchmark.

It has been revealed that as you can see, we can often avoid almost 80% of all trait solving by caching. The last two bars are for a crate called wg-grammar. It is a crate that used to be particularly slow with the fresh trait solver. Part of my job this year used to be specifically optimizing it.

The problem was that there's one more property that has to be part of the cache key: which opaque types are in scope. An opaque type is a type you write as a "return position impl trait". For example:.

Sources indicate that foo returns impl IntoIterator. By doing so, callers of this function don't get to know what specific type is returned. Only that they can iterate over whatever they get back. Inside of this function foo, the trait solver will infer which specific type gets returned (a Vec), but in other functions calling foo, this information is not available. So, this is another piece of information that may affect answers from function to function, just like the ParamEnv.

So, the real cache has one more input: HashMap<(ParamEnv, OpaqueTypes, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer>. What that really means is that the following two functions both submit the question i32: Clone to the trait solver, but cannot reuse the cache entry:.

This ends up mattering a lot in async code, or code like parser-generators that tend to return -> impl Parser from functions. That's unfortunate, because the fact that opaque types are different ends up almost never affecting the outcome of a question. Sure, we can come up with examples where it does, but in practice it almost never does.

So, the fix here is to remove opaque types from the cache key to the cached value like so: HashMap<(ParamEnv, CanonicalQuestion), (CanonicalAnswer, OpaqueTypeState)>. Then, every time we answer a question that may be different because of opaque types, we record in the opaque type state under what condition it may affect the answer, and continue assuming the answer is unaffected (this is often the case). Then, when we get a cached answer in a specific environment, we look at the opaque type state, to see whether the answer might be affected by current context. It almost never is, but if it ends up mattering, we retry the question but now no longer assuming opaque types don't matter.

Industry observers note that this sometimes makes performance worse (we sometimes do double work), but since its so rare, we get an improvement over all by having more cache hits. In the graph from above, there are two bars for wg-grammar. One where the hit rate is 73% and one where the hit rate is 79%. This 6% difference translates to some the wg-grammar crate first taking 28 seconds to compile, and afterwards only 14 seconds. That's 2x faster!

(click to expand for me going into a little more detail about this).

Recent findings suggest that technically even when we use opaque type tracking, the list of opaques is still part of the key. We just set it to be an empty list. That means that in the rerun, we un-empty it and we get a different cache key. Now because we keep the cache entry with the empty list around too, when a fresh query comes along it will also empty the list, find a cache hit that matches this empty list but with tracking information (so it's not redoing work getting that tracking). Then, if it decides it needs to rerun, it adds back the list of opaques and could totally get a cache hit again if we've tried with those exact opaques before.

Sources indicate that of note is also that sometimes we run multiple dependent queries without their opaques like this. We can only un-empty the list once we get back up to the root at the point where we emptied the list to see if they may be unnecessary. To make sure we don't spend too much time running giant query trees we have a bailing mechanism built in to the tracking. Once a query and it's dependencies try to access opaques more than 3 times (or when they do so in very specific ways) we assume that it's unlikely for opaques not to influence the outcome of the query in any way, and we bail out of the "erased" attempts (recording in each dependent result that it's likely a rerun is necessary) and rerun without every knowing the original (erased) result, since it's unlikely to be correct. Future queries will see that this happened in the tracking information, and never attempt to erase opaque types. They know that the attempt is likely wasted.

Now there's an even more subtle thing going on. Sometimes assuming that opaques are empty (in a specific path related to coroutines) leads to query cycles. So, in that case we are forced to do this bailing and to rerun with opaque types even if the answer would've maybe been correct with the erased environment, because the compiler would crash if it encountered the cycle and we want to avoid those at all costs. In this case we may end up rerunning with opaque types, get to the exact same point, and continue to return the exact same result as we would have when we erased the environment previously. This is sadly unavoidable.

This, and more optimizations meant that wg-grammar used to take almost 200 Billion cpu cycles to compile, and now only about 7 Billion.

Industry observers note that now this is my second blog post about trait solver optimization. The other one is a little more technical, and goes into all the different things we did over the past year to bring the latest trait solver towards stabilization. Go read it next if you're interested, and thank you for reading! If you're still interested in learning more about this, I'm happy to answer any questions if you reach out.

Also, hell yea! you made it to the end. Here's my cat.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • DeepL rolled out Aure v2 on November 26, 2026, at its inaugural Unmute Summit in Tokyo, reporting a 50% reduction in median translation delay from the original Aure.
  • Instead of passing audio through separate transcription, text translation and speech-generation stages, Aure v2 translates directly from speech to speech in one architecture.
  • Sources indicate that those results come from a November 2026 study of one-minute real-speech recordings across 10 language pairs with human-validated transcripts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DeepL rolled out Aure v2 on November 26, 2026, at its inaugural Unmute Summit in Tokyo, reporting a 50% reduction in median translation delay from the original Aure. The model is available across DeepL Voice for Online Meetings, DeepL Voice for In-Person Conversations and the DeepL API for Voice.

Instead of passing audio through separate transcription, text translation and speech-generation stages, Aure v2 translates directly from speech to speech in one architecture. DeepL’s internal benchmarks also gave it higher translation quality than six competing systems in every tested language pair, including 32% fewer English–Japanese translation errors than Google Gemini 3.5 Live Translate.

Sources indicate that those results come from a November 2026 study of one-minute real-speech recordings across 10 language pairs with human-validated transcripts. All models were accessed through public APIs without app overhead, and DeepL noted results may differ in real conversations.

Recent findings suggest that speed also depends on deciding when to begin the translated audio. Starting too early can sacrifice context and accuracy; waiting too long can produce a better translation while slowing the conversation. DeepL identifies German and Japanese as especially difficult because essential information can appear at the end of a sentence.

Recent findings suggest that high-quality recordings that demonstrate well-timed, expressive real-time translation are scarce, so DeepL used reinforcement learning rather than relying on large volumes of such examples. Aure v2 was rewarded during training for accurate translations that started rapidly, gradually learning when it had heard enough context to begin.

DeepL introduced the original Aure model on November 11, 2026. It continuously adapted translated speech to changes in tone, emotion, emphasis and pace, moving beyond an earlier system that derived vocal delivery from a static sample at the start of a conversation. The new model extends that work by targeting delay and accuracy as well as expressiveness.

Aure v2 supports six languages at launch: English, German, French, Spanish, Japanese and Korean. The original model’s launch list additionally included Italian and Portuguese, and DeepL noted other languages would remain available through existing voice models. The upcoming model is enabled automatically for supported languages without additional setup.

It has been revealed that for enterprise customers, DeepL says audio, transcriptions and translations are not used to train its models, and meeting data is deleted when calls end, subject to customer-controlled retention settings. DeepL holds ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certifications and supports GDPR compliance.

Sources indicate that deepL reports that total Voice minutes grew more than eightfold year over year in Q3 2026, while translated meeting minutes increased approximately sevenfold. As of October 2026, the number of active Voice subscriptions with meeting usage had grown approximately 12-fold year over year in Japan and South Korea combined, eightfold in the US and ninefold in Germany.

Aure v2’s significance for DeepL Voice therefore rests on a practical tradeoff: faster output can keep multilingual meetings and customer-support conversations moving, but only if the model starts speaking without losing the sentence context and vocal expression the original Aure was designed to preserve.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest attack in spate of similar incidents targeting booking systems globally.
  • Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) notes "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.
  • The Brisbane-headquartered tech giant said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest attack in spate of similar incidents targeting booking systems globally.

Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) notes "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.

The Brisbane-headquartered tech giant said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.

Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated.

Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident.

Recent findings suggest that an initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information.

Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company stated.

"FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes.".

Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said.

Industry observers note that the organization noted it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their prepares.

Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information.

The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels.

More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October.

Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time.

Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft.

Recent findings suggest that speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or rapidly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • Sources indicate that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

Sources indicate that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

According to recent reports, the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch owners had to work harder to get in.

It has been revealed that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

It has been revealed that to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a fresh backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

According to recent reports, the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

It has been revealed that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Recent findings suggest that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Recent findings suggest that models too significant for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

Industry observers note that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

According to recent reports, the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

In a recent development, decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

According to recent reports, it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an matter on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 problems, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel aims. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch consumers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.
