💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

Sources indicate that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Recent findings suggest that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

It has been revealed that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

According to recent reports, the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

It has been revealed that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table indicates that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Sources indicate that the table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

In a recent development, each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

It has been revealed that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

It has been revealed that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

According to recent reports, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

It has been revealed that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

It has been revealed that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

According to recent reports, the table highlights one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Sources indicate that key_averages() reveals which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Industry observers note that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned.
  • Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.
  • Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned.

Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.

Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Industry observers note that edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment.".

In a recent development, that investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to.".

Recent findings suggest that the new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.

The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Industry observers note that monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

According to recent reports, and if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.

The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.

The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.

"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.

The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®.

Microsoft Ignite 2026, held in San Francisco and online from November 17 to 20, centered on running AI agents in production, with Microsoft positioning Copilot as the operating system for work and extending agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender.

According to recent reports, CEO Satya Nadella opened the keynote by acknowledging the November 12 Microsoft 365 outage, then positioned Copilot as the operating system for work, combining chat, coding, and autonomous agents in one experience. In his edited keynote remarks, Nadella argued that customers must be able to examine and independently verify what AI does, announced an AI Transparency Initiative aligned with NIST's Agent Standards Initiative, and rejected setups where models audit other models:.

These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable.

The Book of News groups the announcements by product area, and many of them ship as previews rather than in general availability.

Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines are now generally available, a year after InfoQ reported on Microsoft introducing the chip at Ignite 2025 and two and a half years after the preview of Cobalt 100 VMs. According to the Azure announcement, the processor combines 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores on TSMC's 3nm process, and the VMs run in 14 regions today, with 23 planned by the end of 2026. Microsoft claims up to 50% better CPU performance than Cobalt 100, plus up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS through Azure Boost. Customers can run cores at a fixed 3.2 GHz in Deterministic Mode or let them boost up to 3.6 GHz in Opportunistic Mode, and the lineup adds Mpsv4 VMs for high-memory workloads and storage-optimized Lpsv5 VMs. Amadeus reported more than 30% higher flight-search throughput than on Cobalt 100, and OpenAI's Vadim Filanovsky described a similar result:.

We saw higher throughput and lower latency on Cobalt 200.

Confidential computing gains three previews: multi-GPU confidential computing on VR72 for models larger than a single GPU, Azure Confidential Enclaves with AKS Kata CoCo containers, and Azure Confidential Clean Room for multiparty analytics without exposing raw data.

Customers can now deploy Foundry open-weight models and agents to their own AKS clusters. At the same time, an Agent Sandbox extension provides VM-level isolation for agent-written code, and Agent Grid applies central policy to agent, model, tool, and service interactions. Flex nodes extend AKS clusters to servers outside Azure. According to the AKS team's Ignite post, managed GPU node pools, which handle GPU drivers, device plugins, and Azure Monitor metrics, are generally available, with NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 support and mixed multi-instance GPU in preview. Confidential VM node pools on Azure Container Linux are also generally available on both Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP VM sizes.

Recent findings suggest that on the operations side, Azure Monitor health models are generally available and build a real-time health graph from telemetry, ranking incidents by business impact. The Azure Copilot deployment agent, also generally available, turns natural-language requirements into deployed workloads, and Azure SRE Agent picks up previews for customer-managed keys, Entra Agent ID integration, cross-agent communication, and multicloud investigations. For migration projects, Azure Catalyst is now generally available, with its agent (formerly the Azure Copilot migration agent) handling discovery, assessment, and planning. Separately, GitHub Copilot modernization adds a preview of BizTalk-to-Logic Apps migration.

In a recent development, microsoft now pitches Sovereign Private Cloud as a full stack on Azure Local, with VMs and AKS at the base, followed by data services, Foundry Local, GitHub Enterprise Local, and Microsoft 365 Local. Darryl van der Peijl, a Microsoft MVP for Azure Local, Hyper-V, and Azure Arc, listed what shipped in his Azure Local Insider newsletter: Foundry Local on Azure Local and GitHub Enterprise Local are generally available, while a Sovereign control panel, Blob Storage and DocumentDB on Azure Local, multi-tenancy, and rehoming are in preview. The control panel assesses data residency, encryption, network exposure, and business continuity for Azure resources without enforcing any controls, and during the preview it runs in European regions only, with the service hosted in Sweden.

Van der Peijl singled out rehoming, which moves an Azure Local instance from Azure management to local management while VMs, AKS clusters, and data stay in place:.

In a recent development, until now, going from connected to disconnected meant a migration project. Microsoft revealed a script that does the rehoming in one run.

Industry observers note that azure Local also runs on arm64 for the first time, in public preview on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Development Kit, which hosts containers on bare metal without a hypervisor. Windows Server 2028 entered preview through the Windows Server Insider Program, bringing a hardened Server Core, post-quantum cryptography, native NVMe enabled by default, NVMe over Fabrics, and boot from ReFS. According to van der Peijl, Microsoft added inference as a new pillar for the release, calling on-premises inference servers token factories, and is moving network drivers from kernel mode to user mode as part of its Windows resiliency work. Windows Admin Center vMode is now generally available at no extra cost and manages up to 1,000 Hyper-V hosts and 25,000 VMs, which Microsoft described on stage as "kind of a replacement for SCVMM.".

According to recent reports, foundry's main theme was continuous improvement. Multi-turn evaluation and production insights that group recurring failures and rank fixes are now generally available, while the agent optimizer, human annotation, rubric evaluators, Managed Training, and Programmed Training for custom SFT and reinforcement learning loops on open-weight models are in preview. The optimizer adjusts an agent's instructions, skills, and model choice, with a human approving each change before it ships.

In a recent development, in a separate engineering post, the Microsoft team behind the optimizer described how the loop works. They reported that the reflector, a separate model that reads failing traces and diagnoses why an agent scored poorly, influenced results more than switching the agent's own model, for example between gpt-4o and gpt-4.1-mini. Developers drive the loop from the Azure Developer CLI:.

Writing on DEV Community, Hector Flores advised readers to treat Microsoft's claim that the model router saves up to 65% compared with a frontier model as a ceiling rather than a forecast, and he welcomed the human approval step in the optimizer loop:.

Self-modifying agents with no review gate are an incident waiting to happen.

On the model front, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is generally available in Foundry, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Built on Gemma 4 26B A4B with added image input, it scores 68 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 and runs more than twice as fast as its predecessor, and Copilot uses it to route requests. MAI-Code-2 and MAI-Code-2-Flash are generally available on GitHub, MAI-Image-2.7 is in preview, and the model router now covers the top 50 models in a catalog of more than 11,000. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol became generally available in Foundry, with Global Standard deployments covering 28 regions. On Standard deployments with short context, Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while Astra costs $8 and $40. Foundry IQ added knowledge graphs and an iterative retrieval model, Microsoft-Retriever-1, both in preview.

Industry observers note that microsoft also made Azure AI Gateway generally available as a standalone product, split out of the API Management AI tier, to govern, route, and monitor access to AI models and MCP tools across providers. It includes 10,000 free requests per gateway per month, with paid billing starting January 1, 2027, across 17 regions.

Industry observers note that microsoft IQ, which Nadella described as an externalization of the context system behind Copilot, is now generally available without a fresh SKU. It exposes Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ context to Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Foundry, and MCP-compatible harnesses, and Web IQ is now available to all Azure customers at a lower price. Business plugins, which package reusable context, skills, and tools with hierarchical inheritance and governance, are available through the Frontier program.

PostgreSQL got most of the attention on the data side. Azure HorizonDB is now generally available as a managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database with built-in vector indexing, and teams can lock it down with Entra ID, private endpoints, and their own encryption keys. Calling models from SQL through AI Functions and AI Pipelines is still in preview. The same holds for Fabric HorizonDB, a serverless variant inside Fabric that provisions in seconds and pauses when nobody uses it, and for a DMS path that moves existing Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers onto HorizonDB.

On Azure Managed Redis, the Redis 8 preview folds JSON, search, time-series, and vector search into a single version. Anyone who wants to develop against Azure SQL Database on a laptop can pull a preview container that needs no Azure subscription.

According to recent reports, the Microsoft Copilot SDK 2.0 is generally available, built on a native Rust runtime, supported in six languages, and using the same agent harness Microsoft and GitHub run internally. The GitHub Copilot app now takes Azure DevOps repositories from clone to merge and runs tests in a real, signed-in browser. Copilot code review adds local reviews in the CLI and app, secret detection, adaptive review effort, and cross-repository context. Copilot Code, a natural-language app builder with cloud and local sandboxes, is in the Frontier program, with general availability planned for December and a macOS local sandbox still to come.

According to recent reports, the Copilot app now brings Chat, Cowork, Code, and Autopilot into one experience, and Office in Copilot puts Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside it as a generally available feature. Autopilot, a long-running personal agent with its own identity, memory, and tool access, is rolling out to Frontier customers. Salesforce in Copilot entered preview with more than 38 prebuilt sales skills, and zero-copy data federation between Salesforce Data 360 and Fabric OneLake is generally available. For spend control, Agent 365 FinOps previews cost visibility, policies, alerts, and Fabric-based chargeback.

Cost tracking also featured in practitioner reactions. In his newsletter, Microsoft principal AI apps architect Anurag Karuparti wrote that tokenomics is among the top challenges his customers raise, and he proposed a different unit for agent ROI:.

It has been revealed that the metric that matters isn't just tokens consumed. It's cost per successful business outcome. That's how I think enterprises should start measuring agent ROI.

Writing for business leaders, Aaron Reich, CTO of the Accenture and Microsoft joint venture Avanade, built his Ignite analysis around trust rather than speed:.

According to recent reports, speed isn't the bottleneck anymore, trust is. As AI drives the cost of knowledge toward zero with apps being easier to build, agents doing more work, and abundant intelligence, the scarce things are hard and need more attention: institutional knowledge, judgment, accountability and trust.

At the Microsoft Hub, where he spent the week answering customer questions, Microsoft MVP Muhammad Atif noticed a change in what customers wanted to know:.

How do we actually put this into production? How do we scale AI and agents across the organisation? How do we govern and secure them? How do we control the cost as adoption grows?

Industry observers note that entra now assigns Agent IDs automatically to discovered local agents, starting with GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, and previews an MCP Firewall that controls access to MCP servers, tools, prompts, and transports. Agent 365 now has a generally available tools registry that lists the plugins, skills, MCP servers, and connectors agents use; MCP governance is in preview through Azure AI Gateway and LiteLLM; and Dynamic Agent Risk combines runtime, posture, and blast-radius signals into risk levels for each agent. Microsoft Perception, formerly Project Perception, is now generally available, with its Triage Agent covering about 80% of alerts in a typical Defender queue.

(Source: Microsoft Tech Community, Agent 365 blog).

Treat agents like apps and you'll spend 2027 cleaning up after them.

GeoIntelX confirmed on November 26, 2026, a collaboration with the Instituto Geológico de Angola and Ivanhoe Mines’ exploration team to apply artificial intelligence to more than a century of Angola’s historical geological records.

It has been revealed that ivanhoe Mines is funding the platform’s implementation in Angola, including digitization of historical geological maps, reports and other physical records held in the country’s geological archives. IGEO is the government institution responsible for managing those national archives, so the work combines a firm-funded exploration tool with digitization of a public collection.

Ivanhoe is conducting its Angolan work through Cuando-Recursos, its wholly owned subsidiary. The copper exploration program covers more than 22,000 square kilometres in the Moxico and Cuando provinces. GeoIntelX describes the package as one of the region’s largest greenfield programs targeting sediment-hosted copper deposits.

Industry observers note that tim Williams, Ivanhoe Mines’ vice president of geosciences, said the collaboration should accelerate evaluation of prospective targets, letting his team concentrate on the most promising areas and surfacing geological insights that could otherwise take years to uncover. The expected results are more efficient exploration and a better chance of discoveries, alongside local geological and technical skills development.

GeoIntelX claims its GIX platform digitizes and structures historical reports, georeferences geological maps and integrates the information through geospatial search. For maps and reports created separately, that location-based structure allows them to be searched as one body of evidence. The process is intended to turn physical material into accessible data for identifying and evaluating prospective mineral targets.

The platform also provides chat-based access to AI agents trained for geological work, which GeoIntelX states lets geoscientists, executives and operations leads assess geological potential, economic constraints and infrastructure needs from available information. Exploration teams internationally already use the technology.

Co-founder and CEO Gilad Hoshen said making historical data accessible again could help exploration teams “avoid unnecessary data re-acquisition, assess opportunities faster and make better-informed decisions.”.

IGEO’s mandate includes promoting and coordinating geological research and mapping, studying Angola’s mineral resources and rocks, and managing information produced by geological and mining studies authorized in the country. The archive work therefore affects more than Ivanhoe’s workflow: it concerns how Angola preserves and accesses geological knowledge gathered by companies and institutions.

Recent findings suggest that josé Manuel, IGEO’s chairman and CEO, mentioned the initiative could improve access to information, support the identification of prospective areas and contribute to better-informed decisions. Its institutional objectives include stronger national expertise in geosciences and digital technologies and expanded cooperation between Angolan institutions and sector partners. Manuel stressed technical rigor, coordination with national institutions, and preservation and responsible use of Angola’s geological information.

Sources indicate that the collaboration ties an active copper exploration program to the creation of a structured national archive. Its lasting significance will depend on whether the same records improve target evaluation and expand Angola’s own capacity to manage and apply its geological information.

#207009. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2197 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • According to recent reports, the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

According to recent reports, the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Recent findings suggest that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

According to recent reports, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

Sources indicate that the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

In a recent development, to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

Recent findings suggest that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Recent findings suggest that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

It has been revealed that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping manufacturer: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

Recent findings suggest that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Sources indicate that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

Recent findings suggest that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

Sources indicate that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Recent findings suggest that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cournot Protocol said in a November 26, 2026 announcement that it had raised $5 million in strategic funding co-led by Paper Ventures and Beam Foundation. The capital will fund a verifiable intelligence layer for onchain applications and AI agents.

Cournot’s stated mission is to expand what oracles can do beyond structured data, using AI to interpret real-world events while preserving a record that allows the resulting judgment to be checked. The funding consequently centers on verification infrastructure for automated decisions, where the path to an answer matters alongside the answer itself.

Sources indicate that in a May 14, 2026 product description, Cournot said its system aggregates multiple sources in real time and applies multi-agent reasoning to reach a judgment. Under that design, the sources, intermediate reasoning and final conclusion can each be proven cryptographically onchain, allowing the resulting judgment to be checked.

It has been revealed that the multi-agent component coordinates the analytical work, while the cryptographic record supplies an audit trail for the inputs and steps behind a conclusion. Cournot is addressing whether an answer can be inspected and substantiated, a separate concern from generating a fluent or plausible response. The approach also makes the reasoning process part of the oracle’s output, giving verification a defined role within the system.

Cournot is building for BNB Chain, where it wants markets, autonomous agents and other onchain applications to use these judgments when settling against real-world outcomes. A settlement can depend on the judgment such a system produces. Building verification into that process gives the application a way to examine the evidence and reasoning attached to an outcome when deciding how to settle.

In its May 14, 2026 cohort announcement, YZi Labs listed Cournot among the EASY Residency Season 3 graduates and described the problem it was targeting: probabilistic AI answers that lack checkable reasoning, addressed by organizing intelligence into structured claims that can be audited.

YZi Labs runs EASY Residency as its main global incubator, bringing together founders working across Web3, AI and biotechnology. The cohort presentation identified markets, governance and science as high-stakes domains for Cournot’s work, where verifiable reasoning was presented as a prerequisite for placing capital and trust on AI-generated conclusions.

The fresh round follows earlier backing from YZi Labs through that residency. Both the incubation thesis and the product design focus on converting probabilistic model outputs into structured claims whose evidence and reasoning can be audited. The new capital supports the development of that mechanism as infrastructure for other applications and agents.

In a recent development, cournot’s approach changes what its oracle is expected to deliver: a judgment accompanied by an examinable basis for relying on it. For settlement and other high-stakes uses, that verifiable basis connects probabilistic AI output to the automated action Cournot intends to support.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-upcoming web administration UI funded by NLnet.
  • The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present newly introduced features and give some information on what's coming next.
  • This is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-upcoming web administration UI funded by NLnet. We also discuss many other small news: Helm chart repository release, Garage v1.x EoL, Garage v3.0.0 beta 1 and an outlook on upcoming work on S3 versioning.

The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present newly introduced features and give some information on what's coming next.

This is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander. We started this collaboration in 2024 when it was clear that a user interface was one of the most sorely lacking feature of Garage. We are very grateful that NLnet has again engaged with us and provided funding to make this a reality.

Here's a minimal example to test 2.6.0 right away:.

Running 2.6.0 or above, you can access the web interface on the garage admin API port, by default port 3903, so http://localhost:3903/ if you are running garage on your machine with the example above.

Logging in requires a garage admin token. The example above prints it on the command line. If you have set the admin_token configuration variable in your configuration file, you may use that token. Otherwise, you'll need to create a separate token from the command line with garage admin-token create.

It has been revealed that one world of caution: administering a remote cluster over plain HTTP is NOT safe, as your admin token is transmitted in plain text with each request. You'll need to setup an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of your Garage node to encrypt the connection, or/and access your node through a VPN such as Wireguard to make sure no one can eavesdrop the credentials.

Once logged in the cluster, you will be greeted by a cluster overview screen that looks like the following (this is a live example from our Deuxfleurs cluster):.

The web interface follows a similar pattern to the CLI: cluster monitoring, layout configuration, bucket and access credential management are all available as you expect. Here are example videos (now included in the Quick Start guide as well) showing the setting up of a new cluster from scratch:.

Industry observers note that from a development standpoint, the web UI currently lives in a separate Git repository so please report any challenges there and not in Garage's main issue tracker. Tixie will continue being the maintainer of the UI moving forward.

In a recent development, this has also been one of the longstanding requests from our Kubernetes people, and it's now done! Starting today you can deploy Garage on Kubernetes easily thanks to our self-hosted Helm repository. Both "regular" (tgz+index.yml) helm chart repository as well as OCI artefacts are available. Instructions in the documentation have been updated accordingly. Happy Helming!

Sources indicate that thanks to Boris M. and Maximilien for contributing this improvement to Garage, along the many contributors that participated in finding the right way to make this work.

The Garage helm chart follows its own version scheme, with the current version being 0.10.7.

The last release of the 1.x branch was v1.3.1 in January 2026, almost a year ago. Many significant bug fixes, including security fixes, are currently only present on the v2.x branch. At this point, it would be too much work to backport them to 1.x and it didn't seem there was any ask to do so from the community either. So we are officially deprecating Garage v1.x and urging all people still on this branch to patch to v2.x as soon as possible. The release note has been updated accordingly.

In a recent development, we have published a first beta release of Garage v3.0.0. This release does not yet include S3 versioning (sorry!). This unfortunately needed to be a major release because of a few breaking changes we wanted to release without waiting for s3 versioning to come though:.

We are looking for testers for this beta so please give it a try and report any findings on our issue tracker!

This beta release also marks the first step toward having a reliable Fjall metadata engine so please report to us not only problems, but also cases of successfully running a Garage cluster on Fjall with significant activity, so that we can gain confidence that it works well and potentially mark it stable soon. This also means we'll take bug report for Fjall concerns, something that we explicitly disregarded so far for the 2.x experimental implementation.

As per the release notes, the most key breaking changes for users to be aware of are:.

To finally align with industry standard, most Prometheus metrics have been slighly renamed, we provide an updated Grafana dashboard.

It has been revealed that the Fjall major version update breaks compatibility with the Garage 2.x Fjall as data files from older versions are not supported. If you were using Fjall on v2.x, you will need to migrate manually: convert your metadata to another format (LMDB or SQlite) with garage node convert-db before upgrading. You can convert back to Fjall once you successfully upgraded to v3.

It has been revealed that the complete list of breaking changes can be found in the changelog linked above. Happy testing!

Finally we want to close this post with an enhancement on S3 versionning.

In 2027 we will start a latest collaboration with Armaël to implement what is certainly the most requested feature in Garage: S3 object versioning.

We understand that there has been growing impatience for this feature to be implemented in Garage, and rightfully so as it would enable upcoming use-cases such as for long-term archiving where compliance is important, or as a backup target that cannot be tampered with.

Recent findings suggest that we thank the community for their patience, and kindly ask them to understand why this hasn't been done before: while there have been several attempts by community members, this is a deep problem that requires intricate understanding of how Garage stores metadata, and implementing it without taking this into account leads to code that, while it might appear to work on the surface, is in fact incorrect. A correct implementation requires a significant rewrite of core parts of Garage, which we believe can presently be accomplished only by experienced maintainers. We will also take this rewrite as an opportunity to fix some performance problems, such as those arising with extremely big objects.

I would like to make an notable note on object locking and WORM: we will provide an implementation of locking primitives/WORM per the S3 API specification, however note that due to Garage's lack of a consensus algorithm, this implementation will not be fully correct. This means that Garage will implement best-effort detection of access requests that would violate locks, but will not be able to guarantee that it upholds locks in all cases. More precisely: using conditional writes (If-Match, If-None-Match) as a substitute for a distributed mutex or to discriminate between concurrent write requests will obviously not work, but ensuring that a successfully uploaded object cannot be overwritten after the fact should work in most cases. We will take care of properly documenting what works and what doesn't, but in practice, this means that locking and WORM will be gated behind a feature flag (a configuration parameter) that requires cluster administrators to acknowledge that they might be running unsafe workloads if they don't understand exactly what the feature does.

Thanks for reading, and for your continued support in our journey to a robust and resilient distributed storage system.

Alex, Maximilien and Tixie, The Garage (and Garage UI!) Maintainers.

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done.
  • It has been revealed that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • Recent findings suggest that figure 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

It has been revealed that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

It has been revealed that then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

According to recent reports, so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Industry observers note that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Industry observers note that table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

It has been revealed that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Sources indicate that figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Sources indicate that in a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

In a recent development, thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly newly introduced solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

It has been revealed that in our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

It has been revealed that and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

It has been revealed that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 indicates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Sources indicate that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Recent findings suggest that table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

Recent findings suggest that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Industry observers note that pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

In a recent development, table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

Recent findings suggest that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

According to recent reports, figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

According to recent reports, selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

According to recent reports, every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each patch generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

Sources indicate that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

It has been revealed that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

According to recent reports, why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

Recent findings suggest that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

It has been revealed that the question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

It has been revealed that we used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

Recent findings suggest that we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO enhancement.

It has been revealed that figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

It has been revealed that when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

In a recent development, nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:.

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

Industry observers note that the public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Keep the three repositories side by side:.

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:.

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Industry observers note that start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:.

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Industry observers note that follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BharatGen introduced Patram 1.5 on November 25, 2026, a 7.8-billion-parameter open-weight vision-language model for document intelligence.
  • According to recent reports, A text-first extraction pipeline can flatten information that gives a document meaning.
  • OCR 3.0 turns the prompt into the extraction specification.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BharatGen introduced Patram 1.5 on November 25, 2026, a 7.8-billion-parameter open-weight vision-language model for document intelligence. Its two central additions are prompt-controlled OCR and abstention, the ability to hold back an answer when evidence is missing or conflicting, the input is unreadable, or the question is ambiguous.

According to recent reports, A text-first extraction pipeline can flatten information that gives a document meaning. Patram instead processes page images directly, preserving visual cues such as table rows and columns, blank form fields, tick boxes, signatures, stamps and the relationships inside diagrams. Its six task areas cover document and element parsing, question answering, key-value extraction, OCR 3.0 and abstention, with inputs including handwriting, complex tables, charts and formulas.

OCR 3.0 turns the prompt into the extraction specification. A user can select a whole page, a region or a semantic element; exclude unwanted material; retain text, structure, styling, layout or readability information; and request text, Markdown, HTML, JSON, LaTeX or Mermaid output. Field names can come from the user, structures can be flat or nested, and personal details can be masked during extraction.

One BharatGen example asks for only the electricity-bill months above 2,000 units and returns four JSON records containing month, units and amount, rather than the entire bill. That illustrates how extraction can move filtering and formatting into the model request, reducing the separate parsing work around it.

Abstention addresses a different failure: a confident value that the page cannot support. BharatGen’s triggers include an absent answer, source material that cannot be read as requested, an ambiguous question, a false premise and conflicting evidence. The model can answer the readable portion, explain what is missing, assign confidence to individual values, request a clearer copy or identify a best guess for review.

Recent findings suggest that that behavior connects to BharatGen’s workflow design, in which the model reads and extracts, code checks the details, and people handle decisions that need review. For regulated or sensitive paperwork, the practical value is a documented reason for routing doubtful values to a person while allowing clearer answers to proceed.

BharatGen evaluated Patram 1.5 on 15 PatramBench tasks and 34 public benchmarks against 27 other systems: 20 vision-language models and seven OCR or parsing systems. Every reported score came from BharatGen’s own runs under the same settings. The overall score equally weights the PatramBench and public results.

On that combined measure, BharatGen reports 83; its component scores are 85 on PatramBench and 81 on the public benchmarks. Patram is level with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, listed at 403 billion and 763 billion parameters respectively. Those larger models each scored 82 on the public component, compared with Patram’s 81, so the overall parity does not mean it led every part of the evaluation.

Industry observers note that bharatGen’s token comparison uses the same 10 question-answering tests. It reports that Patram produced 21 answers in the number of tokens Qwen3.5-9B used for one thinking-mode answer, while both scored 85. The measurement covers tokens written, not inference speed, so the result concerns output efficiency and leaves comparative response speed unresolved.

In a recent development, the published evaluation has explicit language limits. Its 15 PatramBench tasks contain 11,828 items drawn from 8,773 English document pages, while the public benchmarks use English test items only. The stated language scope is English and code-mixed pages. The full PatramBench account of its pages and 86 tasks is still forthcoming, while the AIKosh listing says a technical report detailing limitations and failure modes will follow.

BharatGen notes the model can run on a single GPU. Together with the downloadable weights, that gives organizations the option of processing sensitive documents on their own servers or cloud, keeping pages inside their own systems.

In a recent development, the vision-model page describes a limited Playground preview with 1,000 free credits per user. It includes Chat, Parse, Extract, Classify, Split and Section tools, plus ready-made workflows for identity verification, loan underwriting, health claims and contract work. API access remains on a waitlist.

For researchers and document-heavy organizations, the release offers a compact model they can examine and run locally, with promptable extraction shaping the data and abstention marking the values that still need human review. That combination addresses two practical barriers to document automation: keeping sensitive pages under the user’s control and concentrating review on uncertain values instead of every field.
