💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • According to recent reports, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

According to recent reports, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

Recent findings suggest that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We blueprint to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script rolls out its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

Sources indicate that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

  • Industry observers note that mock Service Worker, the API mocking library maintained by Artem Zakharchenko, has released version 3.0, nearly three years after the Fetch-based v2.0 rewrite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Mock Service Worker Releases v3.0 with ESM-Only Build, Socket-Based Interception and GraphQL Subs.

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read.

Industry observers note that mock Service Worker, the API mocking library maintained by Artem Zakharchenko, has released version 3.0, nearly three years after the Fetch-based v2.0 rewrite. The release ships as ESM-only, completes the library's GraphQL story with subscription support, and introduces a socket-based interception algorithm in Node.js that Zakharchenko describes as going as deep into the runtime as JavaScript will allow without recompiling Node.

The headline breaking change is that MSW is now distributed natively as ECMAScript Modules only, with support for Node.js v18 and v20 dropped in favour of v22, v24, and v26. TypeScript 5.9 is now the minimum supported version. Several transitive dependencies have been removed, including graphql (now a proper optional peer), path-to-regexp, picocolors, and statuses. The result is a library tarball that drops from 416KB to 234KB, with type definitions shrinking by half, from 190KB to 90KB.

Alongside ESM, v3.0 introduces granular entrypoints that replace the single msw import with designated paths for each protocol:.

GraphQL subscription support, a long-standing community request on the project's tracker, lands in this release. Building on the WebSocket interception shipped previously, subscription handlers can now be defined against a graphql.link() and publish events on demand, closing the gap between MSW's HTTP, WebSocket, and GraphQL coverage.

An experimental defineNetwork API is introduced as the eventual replacement for setupServer and setupWorker. The new primitive splits interception into sources (where traffic comes from) and handlers (how it is answered), allowing teams to replay HAR files, combine custom interceptors, or hand control of request timing to a test runner. The first ecosystem package to expose it directly is @msw/cloudflare, which wraps the API for Workers environments.

The most technically significant change sits in the underlying Interceptors library. Zakharchenko writes that after seven attempts at the problem, the team has moved network interception in Node.js down to the TCP and TLS wraps, the JavaScript bindings for Node's C-level network code. Moving any lower, he notes, would require recompiling Node.js itself. The fresh architecture supports arbitrary socket-based protocols, with SMTP cited as an early example. Nock already relies on the Interceptors library for its Node.js support.

A GitHub discussion reports failing tests after upgrading, traced to MSW now intercepting the browser-issued OPTIONS preflight requests that previous versions quietly ignored. Separately, a developer in discussion #2771 challenged the earlier decision to deprioritise Jest and JSDOM, arguing that a runner with 46 million weekly downloads warrants a formal breaking-change note rather than a quiet docs change.

In the Node-only space, MSW continues to compete with Nock, fetch-mock, and undici's built-in MockAgent, though as a recent comparison notes, none of those cover both browser and server with a single handler definition.

Industry observers note that teams on v2 should consult the official 2.x to 3.x migration guide before upgrading. Full release notes are available on GitHub.

According to recent reports, mock Service Worker is an open-source, MIT-licensed JavaScript library for mocking network traffic using Service Workers in the browser and runtime-level interception in Node.js. It is used widely for frontend and full-stack testing, and now covers HTTP, WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and GraphQL including subscriptions.

It has been revealed that the presented system combines equipment and software from several companies into one clinical workflow. Hon Hai characterized the unveiling as progress from technology development toward validation in an actual medical setting, with the project intended to reduce staff exposure to high-risk drugs and the burden of repetitive work.

Industry observers note that the work follows an October 23, 2025 strategic smart-healthcare agreement between the two organizations. Alongside that agreement, Hon Hai noted it would donate NT$300 million over three years for related projects. The original research agenda covered smart-hospital automation, multimodal medical AI models and home healthcare.

Chemotherapy compounding and distribution carry strict safety requirements and traditionally involve substantial manual work and coordination across hospital departments. The compounding stage combines Yuyama Manufacturing’s ChemoRo the Spike equipment with Kawasaki Heavy Industries’ dual robotic-arm technology to perform automated preparation steps. Hon Hai stated this stage is designed to reduce staff’s direct contact with high-risk medicines.

After compounding, FARobot’s SMR30-MedDrawer autonomous mobile robot handles medication delivery along routes integrated with hospital elevators. Hon Hai’s Nurabot then connects to the hospital information system, using biometric authentication to link patient identity, medical orders and nurse confirmation while supporting delivery management and nursing-station work. Hon Hai remarked the connected process is intended to support safe, accurate medication handoffs and reduce the time clinical staff spend transporting items.

Nurabot uses NVIDIA’s Jetson AGX Orin system module for edge AI computing. Hon Hai also used NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to create a digital twin, a virtual representation of the medical site, for equipment simulation, workflow validation and system optimization. Later work will explore agentic AI, intelligent scheduling and deeper integration with hospital information systems, extending automation toward coordination across systems and departments.

The Beihai AI Center’s stated role is to combine the hospital’s clinical experience and medical data with Hon Hai’s AI computing, robotics, hardware-software integration and edge-cloud capabilities. The partners intend to use those resources for technology validation and to translate research results into medical applications.

Taipei Veterans General Hospital superintendent Chen Wei-ming stated pharmacists and nurses remain central to care as robots assume dangerous and repetitive tasks, returning time to medical staff. His vision for the center includes medical personnel serving as technology validators and innovators, rather than only users.

Health and Welfare Minister Shih Chung-liang inspected the compounding robot and said the ministry would continue developing a trustworthy, verifiable environment for medical AI. He identified the Healthy Taiwan Deep Cultivation Program as a mechanism for helping hospitals adopt smart technology and spreading successful results beyond a single hospital.

Industry observers note that hon Hai chairman Young Liu noted the project applies the organization’s experience in smart manufacturing, automation and systems integration to reducing repetitive and high-risk healthcare work. Its broader healthcare agenda also includes multimodal medical AI, medical automation and smart care.

The Taipei site’s importance now rests on clinical validation: showing that the multi-vendor workflow can operate safely and efficiently as a whole is the foundation for Hon Hai’s stated goal of developing replicable, scalable smart-healthcare systems.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM3 is our fresh generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • According to recent reports, LFM2 highlighted that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our fresh generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

According to recent reports, LFM2 highlighted that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

Sources indicate that the payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

It has been revealed that every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:.

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

According to recent reports, reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a latest in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

According to recent reports, reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

If you use this work, please cite the release blog:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reuters reported on November 26, 2026 that Dragos chief research officer HD Moore had identified MiniMax as the previously unnamed Chinese AI developer in a wider investigation of nearly two million seeded AI prompts. Researchers found private web links being opened later, including when people requested no storage or retention.

Reuters mentioned the public attribution and the Moscow-region findings were being reported for the first time. The evidence concerns particular URL fetches and later attempts to retrieve code; it does not establish that every prompt or model response sent to MiniMax was disclosed.

The November 19, 2026 research post described the method: prompts carried unique URLs and canary credentials, test secrets with no legitimate use, so later connections to controlled systems would reveal that someone had seen the original request. The testing ran from July through November 2026. For the then-unnamed lab, systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of prompts sent to its models between July and October 2026. The same happened to roughly two-thirds of requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention (ZDR), a setting intended to prevent storage of prompts and responses; fetches typically arrived two or three days later.

Moore told Reuters that links sent through different providers were repeatedly opened from a Singapore internet connection. The pattern appeared when requests were forwarded to MiniMax’s cloud, not when other companies independently ran its models. For customers, that makes the hosting and forwarding path as consequential as the model they selected.

Sources indicate that one incident involving a link sent to MiniMax extended beyond automated fetching. The link appeared in a channel on Feishu, ByteDance’s workplace messaging platform, 24 days after the original prompt and was opened within two minutes on three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. Because Dragos had disclosed only the link’s first eight characters to the provider, the researchers inferred that whoever shared it had access to a stored copy of the full prompt.

Researchers later observed attempts to clone private software repositories referenced in MiniMax requests. Reuters reported that the activity appeared after URL scraping seemed to stop on October 22, 2026; who initiated it and whether any code was obtained remain unclear. Researchers also detected unusual internet activity from the Moscow region involving links submitted to MiniMax, but the evidence did not establish that those links were opened from Russia.

MiniMax said in a November 24, 2026 statement that its internal security system extracted URLs and IP addresses from forwarded web traffic into security logs for checks against threat intelligence. Automated security programs and agents subsequently probed some logged URLs. The monitoring was enabled by default on endpoints receiving forwarded requests and included traffic marked ZDR or no data collection.

MiniMax mentioned the process recorded extracted addresses rather than full request or response content and did not retain full conversations. Its examination found no evidence that prompts or model responses were disclosed to third parties beyond the URL activity. The company deleted the affected URLs, disabled the mechanism and verified that links were no longer opened on the identified path for current business-to-business traffic. The statement did not address the repository-download attempts or the Feishu incident.

Atlas Cloud said in an updated security notice that MiniMax’s explanation matched its finding that links were opened after prompts reached MiniMax, not on Atlas Cloud infrastructure. The company stopped forwarding requests to MiniMax’s official API and warned customers who used MiniMax M3, M2.7 or M3.1 Flash to treat submitted secrets as exposed and revoke affected credentials, tokens or links. Atlas had selected MiniMax’s Singapore data centers to avoid processing customer data in China, a choice that still left information potentially exposed after it reached MiniMax.

Sources indicate that novita stated in a privacy notice that a routing-configuration issue sent some MiniMax requests to the official API instead of Novita-hosted infrastructure between May 28, 2026 and November 11, 2026. The affected paths included direct Novita traffic and requests routed through OpenRouter. The investigation found accesses to embedded URLs and hostnames, with no observed use of test markers for Amazon Web Services credentials. Novita advised customers whose requests contained live credentials or other secrets to revoke or rotate them.

It has been revealed that openRouter stated in a broader November 22, 2026 response that it had off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility and notified potentially affected customers. The platform found no breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself; continuing work included adapting the researchers’ testing and verifying network paths.

According to recent reports, miniMax’s explanation accounts for the automated probes of logged links, while the Feishu sharing and repository-download attempts remain unattributed. The episode makes the full routing path central to AI privacy: no-retention settings did not stop systems along that path from extracting and later using embedded URLs.

#206994. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that language models can do a lot.
  • It has been revealed that say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

It has been revealed that say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Industry observers note that computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's latest speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

In a recent development, the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

According to recent reports, qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

Industry observers note that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

According to recent reports, downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Recent findings suggest that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

Sources indicate that the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

In a recent development, these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

Recent findings suggest that what's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

It has been revealed that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

It has been revealed that if you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

It has been revealed that emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

Sources indicate that the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

According to recent reports, reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

In a recent development, raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Industry observers note that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

Sources indicate that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

According to recent reports, like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

In a recent development, both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Industry observers note that each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Complications and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

The strategy connects consumer access, brand fulfillment and merchant decision-making. It also places customer-facing agents within a broader product framework covering advertising, commerce and data, tying service interactions to subsequent business activity.

The planned Consumer Agent would handle everyday needs and connect people to services directly inside chats. Brand Agent, delivered through official accounts, would integrate brand service workflows and complete customer tasks. LINE Biz AI is the Business Agent, intended to combine data insights with operational recommendations and execution support for merchants.

For brands, the upcoming AI agent platform will sit inside OA Plus, the administrative backend for official accounts. Businesses will be able to choose appointment, sales or customer-service agent roles and describe their requirements in natural language, with AI guiding the setup. They will also be able to combine basic and advanced functions according to their operating needs.

Industry observers note that LINE Biz AI is designed to use the customer context created by those interactions. Within OA Plus, it would combine appointment records, product or service preferences, official-account interactions and membership information, automatically tag customer profiles and identify audiences. For a nail salon, that could mean recognizing a customer who has not booked recently, recommending a return-visit offer and sending messages when the merchant directs it to do so.

LINE first detailed the official-account platform in an October 13, 2026 announcement, which said brands could connect their own point-of-sale, customer relationship management, membership, reservation and scheduling systems alongside standard templates. LINE planned to begin brand cooperation and validation at the end of 2026 and targeted a formal launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that LINE Biz AI has a separate, staged rollout. It became available on the LINE Biz-Solutions website in November 2026 to provide AI Q&A about products and services. LINE looks to bring it into OA Plus in the first half of 2027 for operational decision and action support, then gradually integrate AI capabilities across products in the second half of 2027 so it can assist across services.

In a recent development, the surrounding products are intended to connect agent interactions to transactions. The Chat Ad format in LINE’s LAP advertising system lets a consumer enter a brand conversation after clicking an ad and ask about a product or service before deciding whether to add the official account as a friend. A separate Cross Buy and LINE Gift test uses previous purchasing and gifting behavior to anticipate future gifting demand, generate ads from LINE Gift product assets and direct consumers back to LINE Gift to complete a purchase.

Physical stores provide another entry point. With LINE Touch, a shopper can tap a phone to open a brand’s LINE MINI App, collect coupons and redeem them in-store without downloading a separate app. LINE reports that a FamilyMart trial combining the two products reached a maximum coupon redemption rate of 91%.

In a recent development, for campaign planning, LINE Data Hub is designed to show audience profiles before ads run and use campaign results afterward to inform subsequent plans. AI Persona uses semantic analysis across LINE cross-service behavior labels, official-account friend data and user research, allowing brands to explore audience characteristics in natural language and receive suggestions for messaging and ad creative. LINE also plans partnerships under its DMP Alliance data program with Invoice Monster operator Chun Shu Technology, ECPay DATA and uTagGo to add spending, payment, ecommerce and mobility data sources.

Recent findings suggest that together, those products describe an operating loop in which an ad starts a conversation, an agent completes a service task and the resulting customer information informs the next action. With the main brand and merchant capabilities scheduled in stages through 2027, the practical test is whether those releases form a shared operating loop across OA Plus and LINE’s commerce and data tools, rather than a set of isolated chat features.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WaterSense announced on November 26, 2026 that it had raised a combined €5.75 million in pre-seed investment and grants to expand AI-supported water-quality monitoring across Europe, including a plan to monitor the Oder River continuously from its sources to its mouth.

The pre-seed round was co-led by b2venture and Movens Capital, with participation from vastpoint. The announcement separately identifies €3.5 million from Poland’s National Centre for Research and Development for further sensor development and satellite-data integration. That work is intended to add measurements for ammonium ions, nitrates, orthophosphates, fluorides, lead and E. coli, extending analysis from individual stations to entire water bodies and watercourses.

WaterSense is addressing a monitoring gap created by manual sampling: field teams collect water at individual sites and send it to laboratories, producing accurate results that can arrive days later and describe only past conditions. Its model replaces those isolated readings with continuously operating autonomous stations connected to a cloud analytics platform, giving utilities, industrial operators and public authorities a current view of rivers, lakes and industrial water systems.

In a recent development, the hardware uses hundreds of inexpensive miniature printed sensors, automatically replaced inside the station instead of relying on one expensive sensor that must remain stable through long exposure. WaterSense says this limits the impact of biofouling, the buildup of aquatic organisms on equipment, and reduces servicing needs. The sensor design originated in founder Filip Budny’s doctoral research at Warsaw University of Technology.

In a recent development, waterSense’s product description lists more than 25 water-quality parameters measured every ten minutes. The stations use hybrid solar and optional hydro power, supporting continuous operation without cables or external power infrastructure.

In a recent development, field readings create a growing reference database connected to satellite observations and deep-learning models. WaterSense states the models can forecast water-quality changes up to 72 hours ahead and that AI agents turn the combined data into alerts, operational conclusions and decision support. The operational goal is earlier warning for intake protection and better-informed treatment decisions.

The ASIR research project, which is developing an autonomous Internet of Things system for water-quality monitoring and threat identification, runs from September 1, 2024 through August 30, 2027. Alongside the station, it includes cloud-based anomaly detection and an interactive national river-pollution risk map for planning measurements and station placement. Warsaw University of Technology leads a consortium whose other members are the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management, MAGLY and NEBUCODE.

According to recent reports, waterSense reports monitoring more than 80 points for over 30 customers in four European countries. Its customers include industrial operators, large water utilities, cities and regional authorities. They receive continuous measurements, alerts, analysis and decision-support tools through a Data-as-a-Service subscription, under which WaterSense supplies the monitoring infrastructure and customers avoid building their own field teams and measurement systems.

According to recent reports, deployments include alpine lakes in Austria and urban water systems in large European cities. In Kitzbühel, Austria, the monitored parameters include water temperature, conductivity, pH, dissolved oxygen and phycocyanin, a pigment that serves as a blue-green algae indicator. The continuous view is intended to help local teams track changes between field visits and proposal environmental stewardship and tourism activities.

In a recent development, the upcoming capital is intended to move WaterSense beyond individual installations toward a denser monitoring network across European rivers, lakes and water systems. WaterSense indicates each deployment adds to a geographically varied reference dataset and strengthens its predictive analytics. The Oder project would extend continuous observation and decision support from selected locations to the full length of the river.

The announcement cites the 2022 ecological crisis along hundreds of kilometres of the Oder, which affected water utilities and river-dependent businesses, as an example of decisions being made with information that arrives too late. The planned river-wide deployment gives the manufacturer’s network model a concrete test: consistent field measurements and useful forecasts would need to support decisions across connected stretches of water, where pollution can affect owners far beyond an individual monitoring point.

Breaking: Typed indexes in Zig

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lvignoli

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.
  • The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me.
  • In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.

The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call @backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me.

In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type.

In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming.

Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes:.

We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes.

Its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example.

Sources indicate that our spreadsheet has now several fields: a title, and row and column properties. When iterating over them, we have two kinds of indexes: row indexes and column indexes. Adding typed indexes is attractive to prevent callers from mixing them up.

According to recent reports, this enum gives us a way of referencing all the struct fields for which we will construct a typed indexed. If all fields were to be indexed, we would have used std.meta.FieldEnum(Sheet), but our spreadsheet has a title.

This checks at compile time that each Field enum variant name is indeed a field inside Sheet. As we’ll see later, we will have to access Sheet’s fields by name, so it’s good to check the names of Field variants match the names of Sheet fields.

This defines the kind of type indexes we’ll construct: one for row data slices and one for columns data slices. Each indexed field of Sheet has one correct typed index kind. We match them with an exhaustive switch over Field.

We now have all we need to construct the two typed indexes of kinds .row and .col. A generic function returning a type at comptime is how to do it.

Industry observers note that the typed index type for row is Sheet.Index(.row), and for colum it is Sheet.Index(.col). Note the title case of the Index function, matching Zig’s convention for types.

Remains to give a way of making use of these types.

Recent findings suggest that this part may look complex if you are not familiar with comptime-enabled generics in Zig, so let’s be precise. This defines a method on Sheet that requires f to be a Field instance known at compile time. This allow to infer at compile time both the type of i and the return type.

Index(kindOf(f)) is just a chain of function calls on a known value. So it is comptime known. And most importantly, the type of i is bound to the one of f at compile time. Given the body of Sheet.kindOf, it’s easy to see that s.at(.row_width, i) will compile only if i has type Index(.row)!

The return type of Zig function must be comptime known, and it is the case here by using some reflection. @FieldType(Sheet, name) returns the type of the field of Sheet named name (given as a []const u8). @tagName(f) gives just that for the input enum variant. std.meta.Elem returns the element type for a collection type (here a slice). Finally, we return a pointer to allow the caller to mutate, but a value would work just fine for a read-only case.

This gives us a clear usage at call site.

The Sheet.Index(.row) syntax is particularly lovely: a method call feeling like a qualified concrete type.

In a recent development, still, as I hinted earlier, this design it not completely hermetic to bugs. Nothing prevents you from forging a Sheet.Index(.row) from any integer with @fromBackingInt. And opaque types are really just for interaction with C.

Also, any caller can access Sheet fields directly (Zig has no notion of private fields.).

As for all Zig code, one must follow documented usage (“Direct access is discouraged. Use Sheet.at.”) and make good use of the public methods by proactively inspecting types.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

Recent findings suggest that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super notable for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That mentioned, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

It has been revealed that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

Industry observers note that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

Sources indicate that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing revealed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

According to recent reports, the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Industry News: .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload.
  • Nov 26, 2026 3 min read.
  • Microsoft released .NET 11 on 10 November, and .NET MAUI in .NET 11 changes the default runtime from Mono to CoreCLR on all supported platforms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload.

Nov 26, 2026 3 min read.

Microsoft released .NET 11 on 10 November, and .NET MAUI in .NET 11 changes the default runtime from Mono to CoreCLR on all supported platforms. It also adds incremental XAML hot reload, implicit XAML namespaces and new test project templates. The work spanned seven previews and a release candidate, and the documentation describes product quality as the release's focus. Overall, this release consolidates more than it expands.

It has been revealed that .NET MAUI (Multi-platform App UI) is Microsoft's cross-platform UI framework for Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst and Windows apps built from one C# and XAML codebase. .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support. Microsoft notes that MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the runtime's STS and LTS lifecycle.

The runtime switch is the most significant change. According to Microsoft, CoreCLR puts mobile and desktop apps on the same runtime as the other .NET workloads. Release builds use composite partial ReadyToRun by default. On Apple platforms, which disallow JIT compilation, code that isn't precompiled runs in the CoreCLR interpreter. Native AOT is an opt-in publishing option, and its Android support is still experimental. Microsoft recommends developers to test app libraries before choosing their deployment model.

It has been revealed that XAML gets four main improvements. First, incremental hot reload, still in preview, patches live instances of pages and controls without recreating them. It is on by default in Debug builds, works with dotnet watch, and can be disabled with EnableMauiIncrementalHotReload. Second, implicit namespace declarations are now on by default, so the root xmlns and xmlns:x are optional. Third, lazy ResourceDictionary loading makes large dictionaries initialise up to roughly eight times faster when XAML source generation is used. Finally, RelativeSource bindings with a resolvable AncestorType now compile to trim-safe code.

Handlers keep replacing the legacy renderers with newer implementations. Windows uses the fresh CollectionView2 handler by default, Android Shell is now handler-based, and iOS and Mac Catalyst now use handlers for NavigationPage, TabbedPage and FlyoutPage. The old renderers remain available as a manual fallback. On iOS, Appearing now fires before a page is pushed rather than after it becomes visible, and secondary toolbar items move into an overflow menu. Developers who depend on the old timing should switch to NavigatedTo.

Industry observers note that controls get smaller additions. Maps gain clustering and custom pin icons, plus an Azure Maps-backed implementation on Windows. TabbedPage gains badges, BoxView a Fill brush, and LongPressGestureRecognizer becomes configurable. Shell also supports route templates such as trip/{tripId}.

Animation methods now accept a CancellationToken, and their non-Async variants are obsolete. On the platform side, a fresh Passkeys class in Microsoft.Maui.Authentication wraps WebAuthn creation and assertion, while the server still has to validate challenges and attestation. Permissions.PostNotifications now works on iOS, and splash screens can have dark-mode variants.

For Android, the minimum API level rises from 21 to 24, and x86 architecture is no longer supported. The release notes report shorter builds: an incremental build after a managed source change dropped from 68.3 to 52.3 seconds. They also report startup gains of 2.4 to 4.5 per cent from partial ReadyToRun, at the cost of a slightly larger package. Apple targets now require iOS, tvOS and Mac Catalyst 18.2 and macOS 15.2, with Xcode 26.4.

Several changes break existing code. The Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships, the Color record is now sealed, Java.Lang.Object.JavaFinalize() is obsolete, and non-font SwipeItem icons are no longer tinted automatically. When upgrading, Microsoft advises to focus on throughly testing navigation, custom handlers and trimmed publishing.

It has been revealed that the full list of changes, including per-preview release notes, is in the .NET MAUI documentation. .NET MAUI ships as a workload with NuGet packages, so a project can pin specific versions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ROBOTERA disclosed in a November 26, 2026 announcement that 45 of its humanoid robots are being tested for parcel induction at China Post’s Hangzhou Postal District Center.

Industry observers note that china Post’s Hangzhou center officially launched the testing program in April 2026. ROBOTERA describes it as the largest deployment of robots for testing in comparable postal operations nationwide.

Industry observers note that parcel induction here covers the handling work that moves packages onto induction platforms within a sorting operation. The robots can independently pick parcels, reorient them, identify and reject irregularly shaped parcels, place parcels onto those platforms, and handle operational exceptions.

According to recent reports, that is a broader assignment than a single pick-and-place motion. It combines object recognition, physical manipulation and accept-or-reject decisions with responses to exceptions, giving the fleet several functions within one induction workflow. The testing therefore examines whether humanoids can handle varied parcels and disruptions at a postal facility, rather than only repeat a fixed movement.

ROBOTERA reports that multiple rounds of iterative optimization raised induction efficiency from 500–600 parcels per hour during initial testing to approximately 1,200 parcels per hour during specific testing periods, with operational accuracy above 90% and improvements in motion smoothness, recognition accuracy and handling precision.

Recent findings suggest that those figures describe different aspects of the work: throughput measures speed, while accuracy and handling precision bear on whether parcels are processed correctly. The higher rate applies to particular testing periods, so it represents performance reached during those tests rather than a sustained fleet-wide production average.

The Hangzhou disclosure follows a separate Guangdong rollout revealed on November 17, 2026, which covered 11 postal hubs in eight cities. That project began with a pilot at the Guangzhou Postal District Center in March 2026. ROBOTERA reported an average induction rate above 1,500 parcels per hour there, comparable to the performance of experienced human workers. The rates have different measurement bases: Guangdong’s was an average, while Hangzhou’s higher result came during specific testing periods. The earlier project also spanned a provincial network, whereas Hangzhou concentrates the disclosed fleet at one facility.

Recent findings suggest that china Post’s Hangzhou branch said it plans to accelerate adoption of automated equipment, including intelligent sorting and security-inspection systems, across more operational scenarios to improve postal-delivery quality and efficiency. That blueprint would extend automation beyond the induction work covered by the current robot tests.

In a recent development, hangzhou now provides a concentrated counterpart to the distributed Guangdong project: a single facility where fleet size, multi-step handling and test performance can be assessed together. The branch’s planned expansion into sorting and security inspection broadens the stakes, leaving the operational question of whether the induction results can be maintained as automation covers more of the facility’s workflow.

#206981. Tech Report: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1305 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Sources indicate that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Sources indicate that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to blueprint for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

In a recent development, but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

It has been revealed that project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

Sources indicate that the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

It has been revealed that figure 1. Fresh public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

According to recent reports, when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an notable part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

In a recent development, publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

Industry observers note that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Sources indicate that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

According to recent reports, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

It has been revealed that teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

  • Industry observers note that the flagship 708B-A41B uses approximately 41B active parameters per token, compared with roughly 3.8B for the compact 37B-A4B.
