📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the GigaChat Team announced GigaChat 4 on November 26, 2026, releasing 708B- and 37B-parameter mixture-of-experts models with native one-million-token context windows. Both activate only a subset of their parameters per token, support tool calling and multi-step agent tasks, and allow Instant or Reasoning responses to be selected per request within one checkpoint.

Industry observers note that the flagship 708B-A41B uses approximately 41B active parameters per token, compared with roughly 3.8B for the compact 37B-A4B. Both were trained on sequences extending to the full context length for work with long documents, collections of sources and large codebases. This arrangement replaces GigaChat 3.5’s separate instant and reasoning checkpoints.

It has been revealed that both models use a 3:1 mix of Gated DeltaNet layers and multi-head latent attention layers enhanced with DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). Gated DeltaNet maintains a fixed-size recurrent state, while DSA selects up to 2,048 earlier positions for each query rather than computing attention over the entire sequence. The companion technical report says indexer and selection overhead can outweigh the attention savings at short contexts or small decode batches.

It has been revealed that the flagship has 64 decoder layers and 256 routed experts, selecting eight per token together with one shared expert. The compact model has 32 layers and 192 routed experts, using the same combination of eight routed experts and one shared expert.

According to recent reports, for the 708B model, context extension progressed from 32K to 128K tokens before indexer training and joint optimization at the native length. After supervised fine-tuning, specialist models underwent reinforcement learning in mathematics, coding, tool use and multi-turn agent workflows. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation then consolidated their capabilities into one model offering both response modes.

According to recent reports, under the team’s evaluation protocol, the 708B model scored 71.26% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 in Reasoning mode and 60.47% in Instant mode, versus 30.30% and 12.94% respectively for GigaChat 3.5. Its reported Reasoning results also include 80.89% on SWE-bench Verified and 79.55% on BFCL v4, although GLM-5.3 is listed higher at 86.67% on SWE-bench Verified.

It has been revealed that the compact model’s reported Reasoning results include 85.00% on LiveCodeBench v6, 70.80% on SWE-bench Verified and 72.00% on BFCL. For the flagship, evaluation combined public runners and scoring code with the team’s own implementations, including seven-hour timeouts for specified agentic benchmarks.

The team’s demonstrations emphasize tasks that chain artifacts and tools: the flagship modified a Mario cartridge’s palette in its binary file and ran the game on a Mac M4, produced an STL vase for 3D printing, and used MCP access to the Cadenza music workstation to compose a track before building an accompanying visualization site.

According to recent reports, the flagship model card lists FP8, BF16 and GGUF instruction-tuned variants, along with base and intermediate checkpoints, and releases its instruction-tuned checkpoint under the MIT License. The compact model card lists the same variant categories but uses the Noncommercial License for Individuals 1.0. The detailed technical report right now covers the 708B model; a dedicated report for the 37B model is planned for later.

According to recent reports, both cards document SGLang and vLLM serving, per-request mode selection and OpenAI-compatible tool calling. They recommend Pi for agentic tasks, with Codex CLI and DeepSeek Harness as alternatives for interactive terminal work.

The flagship’s documented FP8 configuration uses two nodes with eight H100 80 GB GPUs each. The compact model’s example uses one H100 80 GB GPU, with approximately 40 GB required for its weights before attention caches, recurrent states and activations.

In a recent development, gigaChat 4 makes deployment terms part of the model choice alongside benchmark scores: the flagship combines MIT licensing with a two-node example, while the compact model offers a single-GPU path under noncommercial terms. For prospective people, the compact checkpoint’s usage restrictions are therefore as consequential as its lower hardware requirement.

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The package adds public-private cyber responders, an AI-focused team run by the economic ministry, and more leeway to use the government's newly introduced active cyber-defense powers.

To read this story in Japanese, please click here (translation by our internal AI tool).

With Japan facing a surge in cyberattacks and breaches, the Japanese government has passed a ¥10 billion ($63 million) emergency cybersecurity package aimed at establishing teams of industry and government experts to quickly respond to attacks and better secure its infrastructure.

The four pillars of the strategy include thoroughly implementing basic cybersecurity measures country-wide, including adopting AI for cyber-defense, strengthening the nation's cyber-investigations capabilities, better supporting the victims of cyberattacks, and partnering with private industry to jointly respond to cyberattacks.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for the cybersecurity measures to be implemented "promptly and effectively" to enhance the nation's cyber resilience.

Industry observers note that "Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities," Takaichi said in a published statement announcing the emergency package on November 6. "Let us mobilize the full resources of the Government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks.".

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進.

A surge in cyberattacks has caused significant damage to Japanese companies and government agencies. In the first nine months of 2026, more than 600 cybersecurity incidents were publicly reported, surpassing the 594 incidents in all of 2025, according to data from TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm (formerly TrendMicro). The public reports are a conservative estimate: Japan's privacy regulator logged 2,094 breach incidents (original in Japanese) from April through mid-October, also above the total for all of fiscal 2025.

While AI has aided attackers elsewhere, TrendAI has not established a firm link between the increases and the use of AI by attackers, Ryan Flores, co-lead for threat research at TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm, said in a statement on the threats.

In a recent development, "Cyberattacks are increasing globally, and so are the breaches and data leaks as a result," he noted. "While AI might not be directly involved, its ability to help the attackers find targets and automate their operations makes cyberattacks scalable. Organizations need to shrink their cyber exposure and close the vulnerabilities in order to lower the odds of being victimized.".

Recent compromises include ransomware attacks on business, such as frozen food giant Nichirei and brewery and food giant Asahi, and data breaches targeting GMO Internet Group. While many of the attacks are criminal in nature, the worry is that the stolen information could be used by other criminal groups and nation-state actors against the Japanese public, states Mihoko Matsubara, chief cybersecurity strategist for Japanese telecom giant NTT.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes.

"If attackers can collect and aggregate enough personal information, they can build detailed profiles of Japanese citizens, from personal preferences to economic activities," she states. "That data could potentially be used for influence operations against Japan, such as targeted disinformation campaigns to manipulate public opinion or undermine trust in Japanese institutions.".

The Japanese government intends to use the emergency funding to pursue four broad initiatives to improve its overall cybersecurity posture. Pointing out that many recent breaches could have been prevented by good hygiene, the government's first initiative is to ensure organizations are implementing basic cybersecurity measures, according to the published Japanese notes of the ministerial meeting.

According to recent reports, the second major initiative is to improve investigation and information collection capabilities, allowing better analysis that can then be delivered to the public to better prepare them for attacks. Third, the government will strengthen its response to cyberattacks, establishing international partnerships and implementing active cyber-defense measures. Finally, the government plans to create the capability and infrastructure to support victims so that citizens can recover damages and businesses can remain operational.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk.

Sources indicate that "Accessible consultation points and direct expert support will be expanded so that affected organizations and individuals can connect to support without confusion, and communication to prevent secondary harm will be strengthened," the Japanese notes stated. "Work will also begin on building a nationwide mechanism for flexibly dispatching public- and private-sector specialists.".

On October 1, Japan's Active Cyber Defense legislation came into effect, authorizing the police and the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to take strong measures against any cyberattacks that pose a risk to Japan’s national security.

"Many countries would be keen to learn how quickly Japan could respond to which kind of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity," notes NTT's Matsubara, adding: "This emergency package is ... necessary to translate the law’s framework into practical capabilities across the broader economy, preparing organizations of all sizes to prevent, detect and respond to attacks as they become increasingly likely.".

However, the funds are only enough to get started, and more will be necessary to continue Japan's investment in cybersecurity, she claims.

Recent findings suggest that "The key aspect about this package is that it recognizes that cybersecurity cannot be left entirely to individual organizations," Matsubara claims. "Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SIMMTECH’s board approved two KRW 150 billion private perpetual bond complications on November 26, 2026 to expand production of AI-oriented SOCAMM module substrates and high-layer MSAP substrates, according to convertible-bond and bond-with-warrants decisions filed through South Korea’s DART corporate-disclosure system.

Recent findings suggest that the Series 11 securities are unsecured private perpetual convertible bonds; Series 12 comprises unsecured, non-detachable private perpetual bonds with warrants. Each filing designates the full amount as facility funds for the two substrate categories from December 2026 through December 2027, with no allocation to working capital or debt repayment. Subscriptions occurred on the approval date, while cash payment is scheduled for December 4, 2026, so the disclosures cover an approved financing before the proceeds are received.

SIMMTECH approved KRW 274.2 billion in an August 25, 2026 capacity-investment decision for a dedicated AI-oriented SOCAMM module-substrate factory and additional high-layer MSAP substrate capacity through December 31, 2027. That decision cited increasing demand for both product categories and identified internal resources or external financing, excluding a rights offering, as the funding sources. The November approvals supply a defined external financing structure for the same two substrate categories, rather than marking a change in product direction.

Industry observers note that both series carry an initial 3% coupon and maturity yield and mature on December 4, 2056. Full conversion or warrant exercise for either series would produce 1,409,906 common shares at KRW 106,390 per share, equivalent to 3.54% of SIMMTECH’s existing shares for that series. Conversion and exercise rights open on December 4, 2027 and run through November 4, 2056.

The Series 11 capital-securities terms and corresponding Series 12 terms allow SIMMTECH to defer interest at its discretion, with unpaid amounts accumulating additional interest. The company can also extend maturity on the same issuance conditions, while holders have no right to demand early redemption.

From December 4, 2029, the coupon and maturity yield increase by four percentage points, followed by annual one-percentage-point increases capped at 19%. SIMMTECH may redeem either series quarterly beginning on that date, giving it a scheduled route to retire the securities as their cost rises.

In a recent development, SIMMTECH reported preliminary third-quarter 2026 results showing consolidated revenue of KRW 535.9 billion, up 43.7% from a year earlier, and operating profit of KRW 101.8 billion, up 721.6%. The figures are unaudited and subject to change during accounting review. The resulting operating margin is roughly 19%, calculated from the reported revenue and operating profit.

The disclosures frame the expansion’s financing trade-off: SIMMTECH has arranged long-dated capital for AI-substrate capacity, investors hold routes into common shares, and the company faces escalating coupons on securities left outstanding. The balance among conversion, warrant exercise and redemption after the step-ups begin will shape whether the larger effect comes through dilution or interest expense.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding newly introduced expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these newly introduced features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this revision. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the latest multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

According to recent reports, that is what makes AI regulation an operating challenge in 2027. Businesses will need a usable account of where the product may go, what it may do there and which obligations travel with the use case.

According to recent reports, the timetable itself requires care. The European Commission says the AI Omnibus entered into force in July 2026. The promise of one global product will increasingly require a more detailed release package. In 2027, suppliers will publish market-specific configurations or documents that distinguish the customer's role and intended use. The underlying model can remain shared. In a recent development, one underlying model can support many products, and one product can create different obligations depending on its purpose, owners and deployment location. Map market access requirements onto the release process before promising worldwide availability. Buyers should ask whether the supplier's documentation covers their actual use case. A generic claim that a model is compliant can obscure obligations that arise only when the buyer deploys it.

In 2027, buyers of EU high-risk applications will ask earlier for operational evidence. Compliance cannot remain a one-time launch assessment when both the legal framework and the product are changing. A latest downstream use, a revised model or a changed implementation date can invalidate assumptions used in an earlier sales process.

In a recent development, the difference between the 2026 Omnibus change and earlier implementation summaries illustrates the operational problem. Now, I went to the database and I retrieved other chunks that are going to be the negative answers. In this process, I've created to myself three samples. Each sample contains one question, one answer, and one document that is positive documents, and then seven negative documents.

Industry observers note that I wanted to take a look at the data to see and check two things. On the top, I wanted to check the number of tokens for each part. I wanted to see what is the distribution of tokens for the questions, and you see it's roughly between zero to 50. This is a sample. Then I wanted to see what is the token distribution for the positive answers, which are roughly up to 1,500. Then I wanted to see what is the distribution of the negative answer, which are the same, up to 1,000, but we add a little bit more. This is vital because the model is limited by context, so you want to make sure that you don't have very large context. Second thing is the cosine similarity distribution. As you see below, I wanted to compare the distribution of the question and the positives, and the question of the negatives.

According to recent reports, what would you expect it to be? In a perfect world, I would expect that the distribution of question and the positive document would be very high, and take it to the right, the green one should be on the right. The distribution of similarities between negatives and the question would be to the left, very low similarities. As you can see here, it's a start where they are pretty similar. My goal, or what I will check after I'm going to train, is if I manage to create that separation, meaning the similarities of positives are going to be on the right side, and similarities of negatives are going to be on the left side. One more thing about fine-tuning with Auto Research. Some of you have trained models in the past. You know that, at least in the past, it was babysitting the models. You have a lot of parameters to play with in the model, learning rate, batch size, whatever it is.

In a recent development, every time, you do a round, you wait a few hours, and then you start with different parameters. I think a month ago, Andrej Karpathy released what they called Auto Research, and he remarked, I just created an md file. I told the model, it's an LLM training an LLM. That's what it is. I gave my Claude Code, I think it was Opus 4.6. I told it, here is a training loop, here is the configuration file. You are only allowed to play with the training code and the parameters and the configuration, nothing else. Don't stop until the human stops you. Just make experiments. Each experiment should last 10 minutes, and then check the loss. If the loss goes down, keep those parameters. Loss goes up, remove those parameters, and move on. I just let it run overnight, and it really did save me a lot of time, because I came up, I looked at the experiment he made. I must say that there were some stupid stuff he did, but I chose one of the experiments that I liked, and I set up the learning rate, and the batch size, and everything, to what just the model told me. It was a nice experiment, and I think it is saving time.

In a recent development, I wanted to tell you a little bit about the setup for training. First of all is, I ran on four H100 GPUs. After all, I work at Dell, they have a lot of infrastructure. The number of negatives is 7. I used batch size of 128, and remember, the training data was Confluence spaces of almost all Dell. I counted the tokens, it was around 9 billion tokens in total. Then I wanted just for us to talk, or have a pick on distributed training. Let's take a look at the first part. If I have four GPUs, and I say I have 128 batch size, what does it mean in terms of documents? It means that I have 128 queries, or questions, and then I have, for each one of them, one positive answer, seven negative answers. I ended up with 1,024 additional documents on each GPU. Each GPU is getting one model, and 1,024 documents plus 128 queries.

It has been revealed that we go to stage two. We start with the forward path. We put in the text, and we get vectors. What is interesting with this forward path is that, first, it is done in batches. It is done in batches of 32 in order to minimize memory consumption, but also, it is done in a way, we don't save any gradients, or the computational graph, let's call it. If you use PyTorch, so when saving a computational graph, it means you save the whole million parameters model activations, and it takes a lot of memory. When you don't save it, reduces the memory. What do you end up with after you do the forward path? You end up with vector. You started with text, now you have vector. Each vector is a dimension of 768. If we have 128 questions, so only for those, you end up with a matrix of 128 over the dimension of the vector, 768.

This is only for the queries. What else do we have? We have all the documents. We have 1,024 documents that are converted now to vectors in the size dimension of 768. What happened next? You have the all-gather. Each GPU now is collecting all the information from other GPUs. Now each GPU holds 4,096 vectors in a dimension of 768. Now we want to compute the loss. Remember the loss that we presented in the past where we want to compute similarities between the questions and positive answers and negative answers. This is where it is done. What is interesting here is that each GPU is seeing one question, one positive answer, and all the rest are going to be the negatives. You are getting now 4,095 negatives to compare against one positive. Why is it good? Because this is a harder task when the model is training. If you manage to train the model well, this is going to be a high-quality model because the task was differentiating between one question and 4,095 negative answers. Eventually when we do loss backward, there is the GradCache and surrogate trick to reduce memory when you calculate gradients. After we calculate the gradients on each GPU, you average them and then you update the model weights and start all over again.

It has been revealed that this was a little bit about the distributed training at a high level. Now I want to go back to my EDA before on similarities. Remember that we noted that we have similarities, the green one is the similarities between positives and questions, red is negative and questions. I wanted to say that I want to separate between them. You see the distribution before training and after training. As you can see, after training, you can see better separation, which means that it gives me a good signal or it gives me a signal, ok, the training did something well. Because now I see a separation, I see that the similarities of the questions and positive answers are a little bit more to the right. The question and the negative answer are a little bit more to the left. Yes, it's not perfect, there is still an overlap, but it's better than what it was.

Recent findings suggest that said, ok, good signal, let's continue. What do we need to check now? Let's talk about the evaluation setup. We have gathered what we call a golden dataset of 300 SME-verified questions, answers, and sources. Sources are like, if I ask you, how do I get Windsurf access? Then you will get an answer, but you will also get the links for Confluence that provide this answer. What I wanted to check is the recall @k, meaning, basically the question is, when I retrieve now, do I have the right sources? Did I retrieve the right URLs or not? When I say recall @1 is when I retrieve from the vector database, then it's top 1. Recall @10, it's top 10, organized by similarity. What we discovered is that, yes, we managed to fetch more correct sources when using the fresh models. I checked, let's say, top one or top five, but in reality, when you do a search system, you don't take top three or top five.

You take like more top 20. This is just for comparison to understand, ok, did I manage to get more or did I not? It seems like I did manage, at least in 12%, to get more resources right. Then, what is more interesting is eventually we are talking about a system that will provide eventually an answer to the user. What I care about is, did we provide the right answer? We did it, again, on the benchmarks that we built, using LLM-as-a-judge. LLM-as-a-judge has different aspects. One of them is question to answer. I want to know, does the text directly address the question? A2A is answer to answer, meaning does the answer match the ground truth? Because I have the ground truth. Here we saw an increase of a little bit more than 4%. It seems like, I would call it a good improvement, yes? Not a great success, but a very good improvement.

We noted, ok, let's deploy it. What do you do in order to monitor? You would fine-tune your model. You have now a newly introduced model, and you want to say, do I need to retrain? What do I do? The first thing we do is we check the rate of data change. If we are talking about Confluence, we can check within a month, how much did it change? Do we have 1 million new pages? This is already a reason to start retraining. Check for data drift. You can check the distribution of the training data and compare it to your production data. The last thing is we actually have signs from our systems. If people are using our web application, they have the ability to put thumbs up and thumbs down. Also, we check if they click on the actual sources we provide on the website. If they stop clicking, it gives us a bad sign.

Sources indicate that I hope that you will take away the importance of embedding. I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked. People are talking about embedding, but they don't understand how beautiful it is. Also wanted to talk a little bit about when fine-tuning is needed, a peek into the data preparation we did there and how we train, and why is it key to monitor and evaluate.

Sources indicate that participant 1: Before and after fine-tuning, did you compare with providing the documents in the context? Without fine-tuning, did you use RAG approach by sending the related document to the model and getting the answers and comparing that with the fine-tuned embeddings?

Rachel Shalom: Yes. We have RAG. We are using RAG, but not only. Like, when the user is asking questions and we let the router decide, do we need RAG or do we need an API call itself? We did test only the RAG, and it's not exactly testing. We saw at the beginning that this RAG is failing. It's failing normally in specific areas when we have documents that are very specific to Dell, like product relationships and acronyms that are at Dell, this is where there were failures that we tested at the beginning. Again, when you have failures at RAG, and there are many, you ask yourself, ok, so it could be a problem of indexing, it could be a problem of the wrong chunking, there could be many things. This was one of the hypotheses, that it might be that the model doesn't understand the context, and we need to retrain.

Participant 2: You mentioned images as one of the data sources. I was wondering, how does the embedding for images happen at Dell? Are the images embedded as raw content, or do you have some kind of an OCR that describes the images as text, and then the embedding happens?

It has been revealed that rachel Shalom: You are asking about like images, or attachments, or whatever. For different components, we did different things. For images, we took a multi-modal model that described the image and converted it into text, and this is how we chunked and then embed. Same thing for tables, I think. We understand the table structure, and the table start and end. Think about, you have now a table with 200 lines, and very complex. Since we know the dimensions of the table, so when you chunk it, then we always put the name of the columns for each chunk, and we always have in the metadata that this is part of the same table. This is for tables. What else? Attachments. Attachments are PDFs, and PPTs, and all others are parsed and chunked as part of the chunking and embedding. After chunks, we embed it.

#206966. Tech Report: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1283 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • It has been revealed that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

It has been revealed that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

According to recent reports, our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

In a recent development, A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

Sources indicate that for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

Industry observers note that one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

Recent findings suggest that we then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

Industry observers note that the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

In a recent development, we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

According to recent reports, the Llama 4 Scout shrink report highlights what this looks like on a major model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Recent findings suggest that our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a upcoming model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a upcoming model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

Industry observers note that so we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

Latest Update: Improving Human Impersonation, as the Web Closes Up Against AI

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.

Industry observers note that of course, domains subject to this treatment often considered RPA to be more akin to ‘data exfiltration’ and/or ‘hacking’ than any definition of ‘browsing’. Prior to the current era of AI, web scraping emerged from obscurity quite rarely, as a marginal form of pest; until LinkedIn introduced an ultimately-doomed lawsuit against HiQ Labs, an ‘intelligent automation’ provider, and one of many corporate concerns that challenged LinkedIn’s right to harvest publicly, profit privately.

Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the fresh gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.

In practical terms, defending against any kind of web scraper is about pattern-matching, and looking for evidence of algorithmic access, such as screenshotting non-selectable text, or polling the CSS stylesheets, or the other underlying structures of a page.

These actions in themselves, no matter who or what executes them, are often considered evidence of automated processes rather than human interaction; personally – and especially at Yandex – I often have to complete CAPTCHAs because I make ‘uncommon’ or technical queries; and the more protective and protected domains are generally intolerant of anything but ‘mom ‘n pop’ baseline browsing behavior.

It has been revealed that however, that’s still a relatively rare and heavy-handed experience. For the most part, anti-scraper logic and algorithms are looking not so much at the actions as for the way they are enacted – and especially for repetitive usage patterns for keyboard and mouse interaction. This could mean that a played-back RPA human interaction that works at first will shortly become blacklisted, because its lack of variation reveals it over time as a routine, and not a person.

Because of the growth of AI scraping, the tools of the RPA industry have suddenly become of great interest both to AI and intelligence companies that consider publicly available data ‘fair game’ in spite of any interstitial defenses (a stance theoretically supported by LinkedIn’s defeat in the aforementioned lawsuit – at least in the US); and the defending domains that in most (but not all) cases don’t have quite enough market capture to retain their profitable user base behind a login-wall, and would prefer to keep access open.

In the latter case, the companies have hardened themselves against the customary dedicated ‘headless’ browsers common in RPA, and against dedicated RPA frameworks such as Microsoft’s Playwright, and its derivatives and forks.

The security sector has taken an interest lately in whether AI-powered web agents can actually still be recognized by sites that are on the defensive against such activities. After all, these incursions may not be running on a CRON job, but neither are they ‘human’.

In this regard, a newly introduced paper† from Canada proposes an AI-powered web agent designed to test the effectiveness of current anti-bot defenses. By combining a modified version of Chromium with AI models trained to reproduce human mouse and keyboard activity, the new system achieved access (non-rejection of browsing) in 89% of tests on a benchmark of protected websites – 12 percentage points above the best previously-published result:.

In a recent development, comparative test results for bypassing eleven categories of web bot protection. Figures indicate successful page access as percentages, with test counts in parentheses. The fresh paper’s system, DarkAgent, achieved the highest overall score across 80 tests, compared with previously published results for nine other browser configurations. Source.

The system, dubbed DarkAgent, consists of Browsium, a customized Chromium browser engineered to conceal evidence of automated control; and Behavium, a framework incorporating two machine learning models: MouseGen, and KeyboardGen, which, together, simulate human interaction with the browser:.

The DarkAgent workflow. Browsing decisions are translated into simulated human interactions, executed through Browsium’s native input mechanisms. The resulting page changes are fed back to the planning agent to determine its next action.

The architecture, shown above, addresses four categories of evidence available to bot detection systems, namely interaction patterns; browser and device characteristics; evidence of automated browser control; and network protocol characteristics.

Recent findings suggest that the aforementioned KeyboardGen was trained on the Aalto keyboard dataset, derived from a study of 136 million keystrokes, to reproduce typing rhythms, errors and corrections. MouseGen was trained on the Boğaziçi Mouse Dynamics dataset, with additional scrolling data sourced from the Attentive Cursor dataset:.

Examples of mouse movements, in coordinate and interpreted form, from the Attentive Cursor Dataset. Source.

It has been revealed that both generators use Transformer architectures, while the browser modifications were implemented through conventional programming. OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 was used to decide which actions to perform during the benchmark tests.

Sources indicate that the browser’s reported identity and the simulated user behavior are coordinated throughout each session, so that the various signals presented to a website remain consistent with one another. To support this, a separate JavaScript-based environment within Chromium allows the agent to inspect web pages without exposing its presence to the website’s own scripts:.

Comparison of conventional browser automation (top), using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to inspect and control web pages, and the new paper’s approach (bottom), where a private communication channel reduces the evidence of automated activity visible to websites.

It has been revealed that the simulated mouse movements and keystrokes are then processed by the browser as genuine user input, with the same trusted status granted to physical mouse and keyboard activity. Variations in mouse trajectories and typing patterns, learned from recorded human activity, facilitate different sequences of movements and actin timings, reflecting the natural inconsistencies of human interaction.

DarkAgent was evaluated using Stealth Bench V1, a benchmark developed by Browser Use, comprising 80 short mouse and keyboard tasks on live websites, requiring no login and covering eleven categories of protection: Cloudflare; PerimeterX; DataDome; Akamai; reCAPTCHA; Kasada; Shape; GeeTest; hCaptcha; Temu; and (unspecified) site-specific anti-bot systems.

Industry observers note that the tests were conducted in August 2026*, using geographically-matched residential proxies, with success measured solely by whether page access was obtained, and discounting task completion. Comparative results were drawn from earlier baseline tests conducted by the benchmark’s authors.

To establish the individual contributions of DarkAgent’s components, 30 browsing sessions were scheduled for each of 18 configurations on a website hosted by the researchers, with identical prompts, tasks, planning models, and limits on the number of actions.

For this, standard Chromium and Browsium were tested with and without Behavium, and with MouseGen and KeyboardGen enabled independently.

Additional comparisons were made with Firefox; Camoufox; the Playwright derivative Patchright; CloakBrowser; and publicly-available human behavior simulators Ghost Cursor; HumanTyping; and CloakBrowser’s Humanize.

The browsing sessions were evaluated using FP-Agent (an existing bot-detection system); additionally, JA4DB (a database of network connection fingerprints) was used to check whether the browser’s reported identity was consistent with its network activity.

Beyond the initial Stealth Bench V1 results presented earlier, all browsing sessions conducted without behavioral simulation were identified as automated by FP-Agent, while every session conducted with Behavium enabled in either Chromium or Browsium was classified as human:.

Recent findings suggest that bot detection results across 18 browser configurations, based on 30 sessions per configuration. P(Human) indicates the average probability of human activity assigned by FP-Agent, Verdict indicates the most frequent classification, and the final column identifies the browser engine inferred from the network connection.

Similar results were obtained with Ghost Cursor and CloakBrowser’s Humanize, indicative of a weakness in FP-Agent (which doesn’t examine how fast the mouse moves, or how its speed changes).

Recent findings suggest that in AgentShield tests, all 139 form-filling sessions from the benchmark’s existing automated agents were flagged as bot activity, as were all ten sessions conducted with Browsium using standard automated input. With DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize, all ten trials per configuration were completed successfully without detection:.

Results of the AgentShield form-completion tests, showing successful submissions, bot detection rates, detection scores, mouse movements and keypress durations. DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize escaped detection, though DarkAgent’s keypress durations were considerably closer to those of human owners.

In a recent development, when new fields appeared in the form, they were attended to by DarkAgent within an average of 3.74 seconds, compared to 4.72 seconds for human customers. The greater variation in human response times suggests, the authors contend, that bots could still be identified by the length and consistency of the pauses between actions.

Although this almost-impenetrable paper is not likely to gather many adherents to the cause, web scraping is one of the most interesting challenges for the dataset-builder and proponent of agentic AI.

However, it’s fast-becoming a Quixotic pursuit; even sites that may be indifferent to data acquisition routines are now likely to become defended against RPA and agentic AI in the very near future, simply because it is becoming a default position.

While data of the kind dealt with in this research can be extracted from human engagement farms in Asia, such data will inevitably form recognizable patterns in the aggregate, so that the routines that are part of them can be specifically blocked – a familiar pattern in a new cold war that’s starting to heat up.

Projecting the scenario to an extreme, truly effective RPA countermeasures could signal the wholesale revival of the crowdsourced worker – lately an eclipsed figure.

† Titled ‘Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion’.

* Relevant only because GPT4.1 was available then.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

It has been revealed that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

It has been revealed that every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

It has been revealed that of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Recent findings suggest that every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

Sources indicate that -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#206958. How WinHelp files work

How WinHelp files work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Quin

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them.
  • Sources indicate that microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco.
  • A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.

Sources indicate that microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco. Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.

A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: |SYSTEM holds the title and settings, |TOPIC holds the text, |FONT holds the fonts, |CONTEXT holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like |bm0.

The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.

In a recent development, all the text lives in |TOPIC, which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.

Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a latest topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.

It has been revealed that winHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, says whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:.

The length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, x followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes xxxxxx.

One fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.

On top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.

Sources indicate that winHelp 3.1 keeps the table in |Phrases. In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:.

The lowest bit of the code states whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.

The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across |PhrIndex and |PhrImage. Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in 01 starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, 011 starts a run of literal bytes, 0111 means a run of spaces, and 1111 means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte.

|PhrIndex doesn't store where each phrase starts. It stores how long each one is, packed into as few bits as it can get away with. Each length is a unary count in steps of some power of two, followed by the remaining low bits to add on top. The step size is set once for the whole file.

Sources indicate that my first version always read at least one remainder bit. That works until a file uses a step of one, where there's no remainder to store. Then every length reads one bit too many, and everything after the first phrase is garbage. The fix was a single bits > 0 check.

It has been revealed that when a help author wrote a topic, they gave it a context string, a name like SaveFile. You'd expect a link to store the position of the topic it points to, but it actually stores a hash of the target's name. To follow a link, you hash its target name the way WinHelp does and look the result up in |CONTEXT, which maps hashes to positions.

Each byte goes through a lookup table that gives uppercase and lowercase letters the same values, so links are case insensitive. The table's entries are signed, so anything at or above 0x80 subtracts instead of adding. Get that wrong and almost every hash still comes out right, so it's really easy to miss. Oh, and an empty name hashes to 1, not 0, because that's what WinHelp does.

Recent findings suggest that text doesn't store its own formatting. A paragraph says "switch to font 4", and |FONT says font 4 is the bold one. Links are drawn the same way. WinHelp underlines a link by switching to an underlined font, so libhlp has to tell that underline apart from underlining the author actually asked for.

WinHelp is older than Unicode, so text is stored in whatever Windows code page the author used, which might be a double-byte one for East Asian languages. Sometimes the file's language ID says which one. When it doesn't and the text is mostly non-ASCII, libhlp guesses the code page from the text itself.

Industry observers note that then there's WinHelp 3.0, the version from Windows 3.0, which is different enough to almost be its own format. Its topic blocks are 2 KB and never compressed, its records give the distance to the next record instead of its position, its topic headers are 12 bytes instead of 28, and its links point at topic numbers instead of hashes. libhlp reads it, but it took its own commit.

It has been revealed that and then there are the files that only share the extension. Borland's help compiler and MS-DOS QuickHelp both made .hlp files that have nothing else in common with WinHelp, so libhlp just turns those away.

Industry observers note that it reads the text, titles, tables, emphasis, links and pictures of every WinHelp version I know of, from 3.0 to the Windows 95 compiler, and it bounds checks everything. Paperback uses it to open .hlp files, so if you've got an old one sitting around, now you can read it.

Entering the Geminispace

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jmmv

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread.
  • According to recent reports, however, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/.
  • Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread. I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that.

According to recent reports, however, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/. The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post.

Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.

A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC.

In a recent development, A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network.

Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page:.

… and break down the introductory and only paragraph:.

Gemini is a upcoming internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents.

It has been revealed that you can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead.

That’s not a latest idea, but it’s not old fashioned either.

Recent findings suggest that exactly. Gemini is like the WWW, or “the web” in more colloquial/modern parlance. In fact, Gemini is a parallel community to the web. Obviously, that’s not a upcoming idea because the web dates back to 1989, and we are now 37 years after that.

The idea is not unique either because Gopher, a much lesser-known option, exists as well. Surprisingly to me, I realized that Gopher came after the web in 1991 while researching this article. I had always assumed Gopher was first and that the web came to replace it because of Gopher’s rigidness. But that’s not quite what happened.

It’s timeless, and deserves tools which treat it as a first class concept, not a vestigial corner case.

In a recent development, humans have shared written documents since around 3400–3100 BCE (roughly 5,100–5,400 years ago) in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and that’s probably (hopefully?) not going away. It’s true, though, that at this point, text sharing is not the primary thing that the web does, as you well know. We have morphed the web from a document distribution tool into an app platform, for better or worse.

A little confession: I worked at Google for 12 years, starting right at the time they published Google Wave (2009), which to me marked the start of truly interactive web apps—more so than Gmail (2004) did. In the back of my mind, I knew I was helping turn the web into how we run apps, destroying the traditional desktop paradigm—a feeling I never liked. And… it happened. Obviously, it’d have happened without me, a little pawn in the game, but it bothered me regardless.

Gemini isn’t about innovation or disruption, it’s about providing some respite for those who feel the internet has been disrupted enough already.

It has been revealed that (That comma splice hurts.) As we have established earlier, Gemini’s ideas are not newly introduced, so it’s indeed not innovative. And seeing how little people read these days, or even how unable to pay attention to long-form text they are, it’s not going to disrupt anything either. But respite is key: having a separate place where you know you’ll only find some sort of counter-culture sounds entertaining.

According to recent reports, fun fact: I wasn’t quite sure what respite meant and originally took it to be similar to spite. That meaning would have worked equally well here, if not better?

It has been revealed that we’re not out to change the world or destroy other technologies. We are out to build a lightweight online space where documents are just documents, in the interests of every reader’s privacy, attention and bandwidth.

According to recent reports, here is the interesting thing. Gemini claims that it has been designed to minimize the chances of becoming bloated, and I’m not exactly sure how you can prevent that. For example: articles can provide links to images, but images are not auto-loaded. OK, says who? The auto-loading part is something the client browser controls, and it’d be trivial to create a Gemini browser, or modify an existing one, to auto-load and render images. That’d go against the spirit of Gemini, but if enough people wanted it, it’d happen. Same story as the browser wars.

And that’s the key: “enough people”. As long as Gemini stays under the radar and only like-minded people gravitate towards it, these properties will be maintained. But if for any reason it becomes more mainstream… unwanted changes will happen.

Gemtext is the native format of documents stored in the Gemini network, with a MIME type of text/gemini and a .gmi extension. Gemtext documents are typically grouped in capsules—which is just another name for “website”.

The format itself is like a super-diluted version of Markdown, supporting just these features:.

Workable for sure, but weak. In my opinion, Gemini missed the boat of creating a truly semantical web, but for that you need additional primitives to represent more concepts. In any case, you can read through the long FAQ to know that this was discussed and eventually ruled against, so know that a lot of thought was put into its design.

Yet another fun fact: just two days ago, I stumbled upon “Good morning and welcome to my idea of a upcoming web”: the proposal of a “browser” that just renders Markdown documents. This feels quite similar to the idea behind Gemini, but using a better (not a great) format with more markup abilities. And I say fun fact because, as I was learning about Gemini, I was imagining developing this exact alternate idea.

One curious bit is that Gemtext is also the format for subscription feeds. Sure, you can offer an RSS feed for your capsule, but RSS is a monster spec that feels out of place in a minimalistic network like Gemini’s. So you can abuse Gemtext to create a feed by creating a page that’s primarily links with a de-facto YYYY-MM-DD Title format. Again, it’s simple, and it works.

The significant benefit of Gemtext’s simplicity is that clients can also be super-simple. You can rest assured that all clients will be able to display the same content, consistently. So far I’ve tried Elpher within Emacs, Lagrange on the desktop, and Buran on my Android phone. All are simple. All display text in the same way.

Recent findings suggest that I definitely do not recommend using the Gemtext format to persist your original content, but that doesn’t mean you have to write in Gemtext. Which brings us to Markdown again.

It was at that point that I committed to converting my golden copies to Markdown even though authoring in Markdown was more inconvenient. And believe me: it is inconvenient, especially when having to insert images. But now I own my content in a format that’ll survive for years to come.

It has been revealed that which brings us back to Gemtext. The thought that crossed my mind when I stumbled upon Project Gemini again three weeks ago and that triggered this whole thing was: can I write a script to convert my Markdown docs into a capsule? And with “I” I really mean AI, because this is the kind of experiment I was not going to code myself.

And of course I could. After just one simple prompt, I had a converted site that I could browse. Granted: the conversion Python script was literally awful, and the converted format was not great either, but having something I could play with inspired me to try harder.

So I threw everything away and started over, again with AI, to write a conversion tool for my blog (codenamed gengems for now) that takes the existing Hugo layout and spits out a capsule end-to-end in just 300 milliseconds while processing 1000 documents. The tool is obviously written in Rust, and by now supports enough configurable features that I’m increasingly tempted to throw Hugo away for the web version and create my own static site generator too. Because, you know, while Hugo works, it isn’t the greatest in usability and its recurrent incompatible changes are annoying. I’ll resist the urge to do that for now… I think.

Let’s dive a tiny bit into gengems. First of all, this second iteration is still entirely vibecoded. Oops, first sin. I have not looked at the code because it’s working for what I need it to do, it’s fast, and it’s not going to be used by anyone else… unless you want it, but then I’d probably rewrite it once more now that I know what the final feature set looks like.

Industry observers note that now, for this second iteration, I was so close to running out of my $20 weekly OpenAI quota that I pivoted from my favorite GPT 6.1 Sol model to GPT 6 Luna to see how far I could go. Luna is so cheap that you can do a ton with it, and I actually got gengems to work well enough within just a few iterations.

But oh dear. Luna is cheap, but it’s also kind of crap for coding. It stops half-way. It doesn’t think through enough corner cases. It doesn’t produce enough tests. The plans it produces are very vague. You have to be extremely prescriptive when asking it to do things and even that leads to mixed results. Out of curiosity, when my weekly cap was reset, I asked Sol to review what Luna did, and oh boy did it have things to say. From design problems to key missing tests, passing through outright bugs. I let it fix those complications, and I continued building with Sol.

In a recent development, right now, I’m actually pretty happy with the results of gengems. I can configure the mapping of pages to templates in a much more explicit way than in Hugo. I can use MiniJinja for templating. I can specify cross-site links. I can handle inline links, figures, and even tables. I can generate archives/feeds for the site, for each year, for each month. I can process blog posts, and also standalone pages. All in all, the results are very satisfactory given the close-to-zero effort I put into it.

In a recent development, with the site exported to Gemtext, I needed a server. There are a lot of options out there, but the one that piqued my interest was Agate: a minimalistic Gemini server written, of course, in Rust. You run the binary pointing it at the directory containing the generated site and, voila, it works. Agate even takes care of auto-generating SSL certificates because all Gemini traffic is TLS-protected, and the fact that it’s automated is a relief because dealing with certificates is a pain.

Industry observers note that but running Agate once, interactively, and making it serve in the background are different stories. I am running FreeBSD on my server and I could have used the prebuilt agate package, but then I encountered a crashing bug and wanted to add a feature, so I had to pivot to building from source. And, as you can imagine, Cargo leaves a lot to be desired if you want to install the resulting product to a running system.

Now, of course you can copy the built binary to, say, /usr/local/bin/agate, but there is typically much more than a binary in a distribution: think about documents, examples and, for a server program in particular, startup scripts. Mind you, Agate’s source tree does include a FreeBSD rc.d script, but it was buggy, insufficient, and it also required manual copying. So I created a PR to revamp the installation system based on earlier experience with setting up similar infrastructure in other Rust services I run.

I mentioned briefly above that I wanted to add a feature to Agate and that it was the reason I had to build from source. And that feature is… analytics, which are the second sin right there.

“Oh no, ah-nah-ly-tics! Privacy enemy number one! How dare you add analytics to something in the Gemini network!?!”.

But wait a second. What are analytics? You do realize that Agate prints and saves a log of incoming connections (with IPs redacted by default), right? That’s par for the course for any Internet server out there, because in order to serve requests… well, the server actually needs to know what those requests are and where to send the responses to. So you can always analyze the log to gain some insights on traffic.

In a recent development, and that’s pretty much what I did. I just wired this exact same information to my own analytics service for visualization. The only thing I see are the pages that are being downloaded, when they are downloaded, and the originating country (computed from the requester’s IP after truncating the last octet to mask it). Essentially… good old page counters from the 1990s.

Industry observers note that the way I implemented this is generic though: I extended Agate to add optional support for an SSI-style URL inclusion primitive and then added such a call to the capsule-wide footer template given to my Gemtext generator. As a high-level primitive, it can serve other purposes, like sourcing comments for each page by making the footer download a pre-rendered .gmi chunk. I haven’t implemented that yet in my comments service, but it should be pretty easy.

Sounds interesting? I might try to contribute this SSI feature upstream to Agate, but I predict that this collides with the goal of a lightweight server and that it’ll be rejected. But I’ll try anyway. I want to get the FreeBSD-related bug fixes and related improvements merged first, because those are helpful to everyone, I hope.

That’s about it! If you are in the U.S. you are about to have 4 days off, so spend that time falling into the Gemini rathole. And if you are elsewhere, do the same! It’s entertaining.

From now on, remember that you can also read this blog via gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ if you want a super-fast, distraction-free experience. To get started, visit the Gemini software page for a long list of clients to choose from and install.
