#206949. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1730 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • It has been revealed that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

It has been revealed that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer looks the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide claims and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one notes, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

Sources indicate that each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

Recent findings suggest that we trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

Industry observers note that there's no public corpus of intends, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

Industry observers note that "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

According to recent reports, the teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

According to recent reports, what fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Recent findings suggest that consumers often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the blueprint and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Industry observers note that figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Industry observers note that even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

Sources indicate that first, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

In a recent development, the key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

Sources indicate that to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

In a recent development, presentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

It has been revealed that we also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

Slack vs. ClickUp: Which Is Better for Teamwork and Project Delivery?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review.
  • In a recent development, A busy channel is good at surfacing a request and much less reliable as a delivery proposal.
  • Choose Slack when your biggest need is communication across departments and the tools you already use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

In a recent development, A busy channel is good at surfacing a request and much less reliable as a delivery proposal. Slack and ClickUp overlap more than a simple chat-versus-tasks comparison suggests: Slack has Lists and workflows, while ClickUp includes Chat and collaborative Docs. The decision is which environment should organize the team’s daily work.

Choose Slack when your biggest need is communication across departments and the tools you already use. Choose ClickUp when tasks, dependencies, time, and reporting need one accountable home. We prefer ClickUp as the delivery system for a project-heavy team, with Slack retained when its wider communication network already has value.

Both products appear in our best AI collaboration tools guide. This comparison evaluates where each belongs in a real team workflow, including where using them together is more useful than replacing one with the other.

It has been revealed that consider a product team preparing a website launch. Design must finish before development, copy needs approval, and analytics must be ready before release. A marketing lead needs a quick answer about launch risk, while individual contributors need to know what to do next.

Slack is a natural place to create the launch channel, bring design and engineering into the same thread, and capture the decision behind a change. A Slack list can assign small follow-ups with dates and status. A canvas can keep the brief and key links visible, reducing the time new participants spend asking for context.

Industry observers note that clickUp gives the launch a more explicit delivery structure. Tasks can carry an assignee, due date, status, and custom fields; subtasks separate work that belongs under a larger deliverable. Dependencies make the relationship between design, development, and approval more visible. A manager can move between a task list and a schedule view without reconstructing the proposal from messages.

Sources indicate that for a small, straightforward launch, Slack Lists may be enough. Our recommendation moves toward ClickUp when there are repeated handoffs, several debuts, or a need to track effort and report progress consistently. ClickUp’s flexibility brings setup work of its own: too many statuses and custom fields make a simple project harder to use.

In Slack, a useful AI request starts with work the team has already discussed: summarize the open questions, explain a decision, or prepare a brief for someone joining the project. Slackbot’s value comes from the relevant context it can access, not from replacing an accountable owner. The official example below shows research being organized into a canvas; it is a vendor product example, not a result from our own test.

It has been revealed that clickUp Brain can work with project context, and the action-item menu shown below illustrates the connection between writing and follow-up work. The useful result is a proposed set of actions that a team can assign and refine. For the launch example, we would keep those actions in the project so that a summary and the delivery record do not drift apart.

Recent findings suggest that slack is the stronger choice when the question is who remarked what, why a decision changed, or which colleague needs to join the discussion. ClickUp is the stronger starting point when the output needs to become managed project work. Neither AI output settles a dependency or commits a deadline on its own; a project owner still needs to approve the change.

According to recent reports, proposal choice matters for this workflow. Slack Free and Pro provide a limited Slackbot preview; Business+ includes 15 messages per member each week, with additional usage available through the applicable credit arrangement. Permission and connected-app scope determine what the assistant can use. A paid communication plan and unrestricted AI usage are different purchases.

Sources indicate that slack’s official overview below shows how AI fits into the communication workspace. Use it to understand the product’s approach alongside the concrete work examples above.

It has been revealed that slack AI | AI that works where you do. Video: Slack.

The ClickUp overview provides a second view of the decision: how AI can support project follow-through rather than just summarize discussion.

How to Streamline Project Management With ClickUp Brain. Video: ClickUp.

ClickUp’s Slack integration can create tasks from messages, show rich previews, and post activity updates to chosen channels. That supports a practical handoff: a customer issue arrives in Slack, someone turns it into a ClickUp task, and the channel receives meaningful progress changes rather than a second manually maintained task list.

Use one authoritative task record. If the same deliverable lives independently in a Slack list and a ClickUp task, somebody will eventually update only one. ClickUp documents the integration as available across prepares, but particular automation and connected-search capabilities have their own blueprint requirements. An integration is also not permission for every user to see every private task.

The examples below use standard USD annual-billing rates, expressed as a monthly equivalent. They exclude tax, temporary promotions, and additional AI usage. Annual billing means paying the annual commitment, rather than buying a month at the displayed equivalent.

For ten people, Slack Pro plus ClickUp Core comes to a $162.50 monthly equivalent, or $1,950 billed annually, before tax and optional usage. Slack Pro plus ClickUp Business is $242.50 per month equivalent, or $2,910 per year. The combined stack is easier to justify when Slack already connects departments or external collaborators beyond the project team.

ClickUp’s current Core pricing includes a Brain trial, while Business includes Brain with a pooled credit allowance. Do not treat a trial label as a permanent unlimited AI entitlement. Slack Pro is also different from Business+ for ongoing Slackbot use. For an AI-centered comparison, the higher tiers and actual credit consumption matter more than the cheapest paid seat.

Sources indicate that choose Slack if colleagues need a better way to coordinate, ask questions, and act on information from several business tools. Its strongest case is a team whose work already spans departments and needs a shared communication layer.

According to recent reports, choose ClickUp if work has dependencies, time tracking, repeated assignments, or reporting needs that outgrow a lightweight list. Its integrated Chat may also reduce the need for a separate messenger within a self-contained project team.

We recommend Slack for teams whose coordination spans many departments and business tools, and ClickUp for teams whose main problem is executing projects reliably. For an established Slack organization, connecting ClickUp is often a better move than migrating every conversation just to improve task management.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reuters reported on November 26, 2026 that Z.ai had fallen behind schedule on GLM-5.5, its next flagship designed with roughly 3 trillion parameters, a measure of model size, while Moonshot AI had begun distilling from Google and Meta models as training data from OpenAI and Anthropic models became harder to obtain.
  • According to recent reports, distillation uses answers generated by a more capable model to train another system.
  • It has been revealed that two people familiar with the matter mentioned Z.ai had planned to release GLM-5.5 in November 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reuters reported on November 26, 2026 that Z.ai had fallen behind schedule on GLM-5.5, its next flagship designed with roughly 3 trillion parameters, a measure of model size, while Moonshot AI had begun distilling from Google and Meta models as training data from OpenAI and Anthropic models became harder to obtain.

According to recent reports, distillation uses answers generated by a more capable model to train another system. A person familiar with Moonshot’s operations remarked anti-distillation safeguards had also slowed its development, and that Google’s and Meta’s latest releases had made their models attractive alternative data sources. Moonshot is also seeking substitute computing: a separate source said it had intensified efforts to rent capacity in Europe, corroborating earlier CNBC reporting, and planned to approach Chinese chipmakers about training on their processors.

It has been revealed that two people familiar with the matter mentioned Z.ai had planned to release GLM-5.5 in November 2026. One of them said increasingly effective anti-distillation safeguards were partly responsible for the hold-up and that newly introduced US computing restrictions could push the launch into the first quarter of 2027 or later, despite the earlier goal of finishing training and releasing it by the end of 2026. Z.ai, Moonshot, Google and Meta did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Recent findings suggest that the disclosures put simultaneous pressure on the resources behind Chinese developers’ low-cost challenge to US rivals: outputs from more capable models and overseas access to advanced chips. Anti-distillation measures constrain unauthorized extraction of model outputs, while the fresh licensing rule targets overseas arrangements that let developers use Nvidia processors without importing them.

Moonshot is particularly exposed to the fresh US Commerce Department rule because it rents computing power to train its models and prioritizes overseas providers, a person with knowledge of its operations stated. The rule took effect on November 19, 2026 and imposes licensing requirements for covered computing arrangements at data centers outside the US above a threshold roughly equivalent to 750 Nvidia H100 chips. Operators already providing covered services before the rule took effect have 90 days to obtain licenses.

It has been revealed that A person with knowledge of Moonshot’s operations said domestic computing capacity could not fully replace its overseas supply if access were cut off entirely, a scenario that could stretch its usual six-month interval between major releases to 12 months or longer and push Kimi K4 to around mid-2027. Moonshot released Kimi K2 in July 2025, K2.5 in January 2026, and K3 in July 2026.

According to recent reports, Z.ai announced GLM-5.4 on November 23, 2026, describing it in the model’s technical release as its first flagship built on a Loop Transformer. The architecture reruns a shared block of layers to refine internal states without adding parameters. The 750-billion-parameter model loops 28 layers from the GLM-5 base for two iterations; Z.ai adapted an already pretrained base through continued training rather than starting from scratch.

Z.ai says the design reaches intelligence comparable to models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters. To control deployment costs, the second pass reuses the first pass’s attention indices and combines shared and sliding-window key-value caches, which store prior context, rather than creating another full-context cache.

The company also acknowledged that GLM-5.4 can enter excessively long reasoning loops, although it mentioned the resulting reflection and self-correction improve accuracy beyond the model’s parameter count. The model is available through Z.ai’s chat and coding products; API access is listed as coming soon, and open weights are planned after safety hardening.

In Anthropic’s September 2026 threat-intelligence report, the company defines illicit distillation as industrial-scale, covert extraction without authorization and attributes more than 23 million exchanges to Moonshot between May and July 2026 and more than 3.4 million to Zhipu, branded outside China as Z.ai, over 17 days in June and July 2026.

Sources indicate that anthropic said Moonshot silently relayed customer requests to Claude and used fraudulent proxy accounts and cross-session replay techniques to extract reasoning transcripts for training, while Zhipu used Claude to clean and normalize harvested transcripts, judge model outputs, filter training data, and support other post-training work. Anthropic’s layered defenses combine proxy-network attribution, extraction classifiers, account bans, identity checks, and summarized or encrypted reasoning intended to make stolen transcripts less useful.

Moonshot previously told China’s National Business Daily in July 2026 that Kimi K3’s gains came from original architectural changes, rejecting suggestions that they resulted from distillation.

GLM-5.4 demonstrates how architectural efficiency can extend an existing model, but it does not resolve the constraints around the next generation. The reported GLM-5.5 and Kimi K4 schedules are exposed to tightening access to large-scale computing and training data drawn from rival models, pressures that reusing a pretrained base cannot fully address.

Latest Update: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
  • Recent findings suggest that in April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms.
  • According to recent reports, OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

Recent findings suggest that in April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

According to recent reports, OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

Sources indicate that however, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

In a recent development, run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

It has been revealed that say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

It has been revealed that the choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

It has been revealed that the base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:.

It has been revealed that all three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Industry observers note that cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

It has been revealed that SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

Industry observers note that on a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

According to recent reports, parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

InfoQ Homepage News Building a Production-Ready Culture and Skills Through SRE-based Training.

Nov 26, 2026 4 min read.

Recent findings suggest that training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. In her talk, Engineer Confidence with Reliable Training Programs at GOTO Copenhagen, Jennifer Petoff showed how we can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself.

It has been revealed that software ownership is a human challenge as much as it is a technical one. Most formal education programs are geared towards the first 10% of the software development life cycle, the build phase, Petoff said. Engineers and operators are tasked with maintaining, debugging, securing, and evolving systems they may not even have written:.

There’s this implicit assumption that coding proficiency translates seamlessly to operational confidence, but it doesn’t. Without systematic training, this may create imposter syndrome, stress, and maybe even attrition in your organization.

AI has magnified the relative cost and complexity of post-build operations. Petoff suggested thinking about how to equip developers and operators with skills to run their services scalably in production.

It has been revealed that culture is not some grand mindset you need to shift. It’s much more tactical. You can change your culture by changing what people do every day, Petoff said. Training people acts as a confidence engine, giving engineers the self-efficacy to adopt new operational behaviors. When behaviors are repeated over time and across teams, they become habits, and those habits comprise your organizational culture. Petoff suggests avoiding a sink-or-swim mentality (letting people fend for themselves rather than training them), as it can breed stress or frustration.

Recent findings suggest that training needs depend on the maturity of your organization in adopting key principles and practices, the familiarity of engineers with the organization and infrastructure, and the experience of individuals. For organizations starting their DevOps or SRE journey, she suggested addressing skill gaps and tailoring the message to who is on your team. Organizations that already have well-developed production best practices should aim at reinforcing their culture and building upon their practices to foster confidence.

Your training program should take into account the size of your organization and how fast it’s growing to get the most from your investment. If your organization is small and growing slowly, focus on one-on-one knowledge transfer through mentoring and shadowing, Petoff suggested. For a large and slowly growing organization, invest in ongoing education. When it’s small but growing rapidly, invest in onboarding. If you’re both large and growing rapidly, invest in a full life cycle training program, onboarding, all the way through ongoing education and beyond, she mentioned.

The foundational principles of SRE and elements of the service reliability hierarchy can be applied to the training program itself, Petoff explained:.

Recent findings suggest that monitor through attendance tracking and survey feedback. Address complications that surface via the monitoring. Write postmortems when something goes wrong to learn from that failure. Observe concrete job-related behaviors to more effectively tie the training to business impact.

Recent findings suggest that to scale production safety training to tens of thousands of developers, they created a self-paced training and piloted it with a 1% cohort, making changes based on audience feedback before scaling it up. Petoff mentioned they automated the distribution, enrollment, and escalation notifications up the management chain.

A production-ready workforce and organizational culture is non-negotiable in the generative AI era, Petoff stated. Learning drives confidence, confidence drives behavior, and behavior repeated over time drives culture. You need to look at the training costs and benefits to make the right level of investment based on the specific organizational situation. Applying SRE principles to the training program itself led to a more consistent, reliable, and scalable experience, she concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Jennifer Petoff after her talk.

InfoQ: How can we tailor the training message to individual team members?

Jennifer Petoff: In the Generative AI era, we are all moving faster than ever, and it’s easy for training to get sacrificed as something vital, but not urgent. Developers and operators may also look upon training with skepticism: Is this training tied to some fleeting corporate hype that will quickly be forgotten?

According to recent reports, you need to convince them "what’s in it for me?" (WIIFM). The answer ties directly to what motivates people and varies among team members.

These "WIIFM" elements can be conveyed in written communications, through talking points to managers, or peer-to-peer discussions incorporated into the program.

InfoQ: How did you observe job-related behaviors?

Petoff: We built a hands-on training environment using real production infrastructure, but without real-world consumers and associated stakes. We could "break" our training infrastructure on demand, and students would work in groups of three to troubleshoot realistic production challenges.

In a recent development, by structuring the training in this way, instructors could directly observe how participants used system diagrams, diagnosed production complications, and mitigated an outage. We looked at how people engaged with production during the exercises instead of quizzing them or asking for a simple nod of understanding.

InfoQ: What have you learned from applying SRE principles to training programs?

Petoff: Reliability is about mastering the operational "how" of any complex initiative. Training programs are just the tip of the iceberg. I believe that you can "SRE" anything in work, life, and for your well-being. Building is time-bound, but operations are forever. Planning a project beyond launch to include mechanisms to streamline operations and drive continuous improvement will pay you back tenfold and free up time to work on more impactful initiatives without getting buried under a mountain of toil.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • We've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Industry observers note that getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

Sources indicate that we declared Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Sources indicate that phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Sources indicate that phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the crucial things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Recent findings suggest that the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

It has been revealed that developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that the Open TTS Leaderboard is a very upcoming project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a upcoming inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It has been revealed that it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

In a recent development, A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Industry observers note that phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a fresh one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

Sources indicate that we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Sources indicate that phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

In a recent development, congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

Sources indicate that one line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly demonstrates where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

We’re excited to announce a fresh collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗.

It has been revealed that with these fresh accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:.

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
  • Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least vital experts (in each layer independently).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency complications which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least vital experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

Industry observers note that in this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly notable, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

It has been revealed that unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

Sources indicate that because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣.

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}.

Industry observers note that this F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It demonstrates the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

Industry observers note that in terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

It has been revealed that notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

It has been revealed that HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

Industry observers note that as expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more crucial. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

According to recent reports, notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

It has been revealed that HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

Recent findings suggest that the calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

In a recent development, to complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:.

It has been revealed that HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916.

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

Decision Models in Hugging Face

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
  • Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.
  • In a recent development, "I was charged twice for my subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.

In a recent development, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.".

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

In a recent development, typeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

In a recent development, the community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models).

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:.

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:.

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

In a recent development, if we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

In a recent development, zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

Industry observers note that one common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

Consider these three approaches:.

According to recent reports, the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:.

According to recent reports, the state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

In a recent development, questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:.

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:.

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

Here, KKK is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:.

In a recent development, ∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:.

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​.

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

How urgent is this customer request?

The model again produces a probability distribution:.

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:.

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​.

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7.

The reported score is therefore 1.7.

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Is the customer requesting a refund?

It has been revealed that rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let YYY represent a binary outcome:.

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p).

It has been revealed that P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:.

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​.

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:.

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997.

It has been revealed that notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:.

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

It has been revealed that transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:.

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:.

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:.

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:.

The default server runs on port 9931.

Sources indicate that we can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

It has been revealed that hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it indicates the parts that matter:.

In a recent development, first-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is upcoming, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Sources indicate that great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that notes whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

In a recent development, I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator.

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Industry observers note that nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

In a recent development, the state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

Release notes: https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1-1?utm_source=huggingface&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=hf_decision_blog.
